title: Splat2Act: From Captured Scenes to Personalized VLA Manipulation
authors: Xiaomeng Ye,Krishna Jaganathan,Gyubeum Lim,Gunjan Chhablani,Muhammad Zubair Irshad,Zsolt Kira
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Yet even a strong generalist like π0.5\pi_{0.5} achieves 0% pickup success in our captured deployment scenes without adaptation, and collecting real demonstrations in every user’s environment is prohibitively expensive. We present Splat2Act, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that personalizes a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a specific scene and object set using only a handheld phone scan and images of the user’s objects. Unlike prior real-to-sim work that reconstructs individual tabletops, Splat2Act operates on building-scale indoor environments: it builds a photorealistic digital twin with 3D Gaussian Splatting and collision geometry, automatically discovers tabletop and non-tabletop receptacles, constructs feasible pickup tasks, and generates successful demonstrations with a privileged simulation oracle, with only scene and object capture required from a human. Applied to 101 scanned campus environments with a median navigable area of 104.87 m2 and 7 receptacles, the pipeline yields 852 receptacles and over 68,000 pickup demonstrations. We fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5} in two stages: Stage 1 adapts to over hundreds of public object assets, drawn either from the deployment scene alone or from all 101 scenes; Stage 2 personalizes to the user’s own objects on the deployment scene’s receptacles. Our strongest personalized policy reaches 62.5% aggregate pickup success in the target scene. Deployed on a real Stretch 3, the same policy achieves 63.9% success on a 12-task subset, closely tracking its 66.7% simulated success on those tasks. We find that Splat2Act is able to adapt to the target scene and objects from only simulation oracle data, suggesting an alternative way for personalizing VLA manipulation training using an automated real-to-sim-to-real approach.
introduction:
Consider a mobile manipulator deployed in a user’s home. The user wants it to fetch a pill bottle from the shelf and a can of soup from the side table. Generalist VLAs promise this kind of open-world capability [1, 2], but deployment exposes a gap: in our experiments, pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} achieves 0.0% pickup success rate (SR) in two target scenes (Sec. V-C). Closing this gap through fine-tuning is standard practice, but the required data has traditionally come from teleoperation, policy rollouts, or human intervention in the target environment [3, 4], a cost that recurs for every new user, receptacle, object, or configuration.

Simulation demonstrations and evaluation metrics help further improve generalist models, but they often rely on mesh-based rendering of generic scenes with simplified lighting conditions, matching deployment configurations marginally [5, 6]. Current real-to-sim-to-real systems use scene reconstructions through 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to improve visual fidelity and close the sim-to-real gap through demonstration generation and evaluation with privileged information [7, 8, 9, 10]. However, these either still require human demonstration or annotation, or are often reconstructed at the level of individual tabletops, making it still laborious for deployment in a user’s full environment.

To address these challenges, we present Splat2Act, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline for VLA manipulation training and evaluation within a large building-scale scene and custom objects. The pipeline combines 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) appearances with collision geometry from scenes scanned with a hand-held device. Target and distractor objects can be either chosen from publicly available 3D assets or generated using single images of real objects. The pipeline detects valid receptacles and uses a privileged-state geometric oracle to generate successful pickup demonstrations in simulation. The resulting environments also provide task resets and success predicates for policy evaluation. The only human input to Splat2Act is a 20-30 minute handheld scan of the scene plus one image and the dimensions of each target object; no robot, operator expertise, or per-task repetition is needed. The same half hour of teleoperation would yield demonstrations for only one receptacle and one object set, before accounting for robot setup and operator training.

Our pipeline scales to 101 scanned indoor environments with a median of 104.87 m2 navigable area, from which we generate 68,021 successful pickup demonstrations across 852 automatically discovered receptacles. We will make this dataset publicly available upon acceptance. Using a selected subset of this data, we study different approaches to personalization across broad adaptation sources and conduct sim-to-real experiments in target scenes and out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We find that same-scene broad adaptation followed by personalization yields the strongest policy, improving over direct personalization by 17.5 percentage points on aggregate and reaching 63.9% real-world SR where it scores 66.7% in simulation, and a personalized policy fine-tuned from diverse multi-scene adaptation retains robustness to unseen receptacles

Our contributions are:

An automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that converts scene captures and real objects into feasible manipulation tasks and demonstrations with no human effort beyond scene and object scans.

A large-scale simulation dataset generated from our pipeline, constructed from 101 building-scale indoor scenes with 852 diverse receptacles, with corresponding task metadata and demonstrations.

An empirical study on how broad simulation adaptation and personalization affect pickup performance on a user’s scene and objects, with controlled simulation and real-world evaluation.

1. An automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that converts scene captures and real objects into feasible manipulation tasks and demonstrations with no human effort beyond scene and object scans.

2. A large-scale simulation dataset generated from our pipeline, constructed from 101 building-scale indoor scenes with 852 diverse receptacles, with corresponding task metadata and demonstrations.

3. An empirical study on how broad simulation adaptation and personalization affect pickup performance on a user’s scene and objects, with controlled simulation and real-world evaluation.

title: Noise Space Learning for VLA Adaptation
authors: Junjie Lu,Chuheng Zhang,Yucen Wang,Yuhua Jiang,Xinyao Qin,Min Xu,Li Zhao
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly combine pretrained visual-language representations with continuous action generation. Early VLAs such as RT-2 [3] predict discretized actions as tokens. Octo [20] subsequently combines a generalist robot transformer with a diffusion action head to model continuous, multimodal behavior. More recent VLAs, including π0\pi_{0} [2] and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [23], use flow matching to transform standard Gaussian noise into action chunks, with the flow generator conditioned on visual observations and language. This progression has made flow matching an increasingly prominent approach to continuous action generation. The broad manipulation priors of flow-matching-based VLAs provide a starting point for deployment, but precise alignment, contact handling, and dynamic manipulation still require adaptation to the target task.

The central challenge in VLA adaptation is to acquire task-specific behavior efficiently while preserving useful pretrained priors. Full-parameter updates to a large VLA are costly and can disturb these priors when training is limited to narrow task experience. For example, low-data supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can leave a policy fixated on training objects or spatial targets, even when a new instruction specifies a different target [12]. A parameter-efficient alternative is low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which keeps the VLA backbone fixed and trains low-rank adapters. This approach can better preserve VLM-derived visual-semantic recognition than full-parameter fine-tuning [35], and retain earlier skills with substantially less forgetting in continual VLA adaptation [11]. These observations motivate efficient adaptation that freezes the VLA backbone and learns a small task-specific module.

Keeping the VLA backbone fixed can help preserve pretrained priors and improve adaptation efficiency, but does not by itself ensure effectiveness. Different ways of adapting a fixed backbone face different limitations. Adapting only the action head can underfit task execution despite better preservation of visual-semantic knowledge [35]. Inference-time candidate selection can improve task success, but seeking better actions through a broader search requires generating and scoring more candidates, increasing inference cost [34]. Residual adaptation learns action corrections, but keeping these corrections close to the base policy for stable learning can limit the behavioral changes it can achieve [1]. These trade-offs motivate a central question:

How can we adapt a VLA effectively and efficiently while preserving its priors?

To address this question, we study noise space learning (NSL) for flow-matching-based VLAs. NSL trains a lightweight noise actor to produce a context-conditioned distribution over the noise that initializes action generation while keeping the VLA backbone fixed. This formulation builds on learning a conditional noise actor in DSRL [33] and noise supervision obtained by inverting corrective actions in UniSteer [18] and FlowDAgger [19]. NSL targets effective adaptation by favoring useful behaviors already represented by the generator, supports efficient learning through lightweight actor updates, and preserves the pretrained noise-to-action mapping. The practical challenge is how to optimize the noise actor to realize these benefits. We develop NSL variants based on three reinforcement learning paradigms: on-policy policy optimization with PPO [27], off-policy actor–critic learning with SAC [9], and advantage-weighted regression (AWR) [22] that uses supervised learning as subroutines.
We study how these variants are impacted by different implementation techniques such as noise limit, task balancing, and success/failure balancing.
Based on these results, we conclude which algorithms are effective and which implementation choices yield strong performance, aiming to establish best practices for NSL under different resource and deployment constraints.

We evaluate NSL on two simulation benchmarks, LIBERO [17] and RoboTwin [5], and four real-robot manipulation tasks, cup stacking, toy fishing, sequential insertion, and bead placement, under the following constraints:
The interaction constraint refers to the sample budget for adaptation, which differs between simulation and real-robot experiments and influences algorithm choice.
The computation constraint refers to the computational effort allowed in adaptation and may limit the performance.
The execution constraint concerns the safety of learned behavior on physical robots. We observe that noise distributions far from standard Gaussian can be tolerated in simulation but are associated with unsafe motions and safety interventions, such as emergency stops, on real robots.

Our contributions are threefold.
First, we formulate NSL as a VLA adaptation interface that maximizes success rate through a context-conditioned noise actor that steers action generation while keeping the VLA backbone fixed.
Second, we analyze NSL’s adaptation efficiency through an information-theoretic comparison with generator adaptation and residual adaptation.
Third, we develop NSL variants based on PPO, SAC, and AWR through implementation refinements, and evaluate them on simulation and real robots.
Our experiments show that NSL-SAC performs well in simulation with ample interaction budgets and requires more computation. However, its noise distribution can deviate from standard Gaussian, with associated unsafe motions and emergency-stop interventions on real robots.
In contrast, NSL-AWR is better suited to interaction-limited real-robot adaptation, combining lower computational cost with safer execution.
NSL-PPO also achieves competitive performance in simulation, benefiting from more rollouts while showing limited average gains from additional updates.

title: Chronos Policy: Learning Robot Policies on Physical Time
authors: Changhao Wang,Jaden Clark,Shuran Song
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed-rate observation--action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. This assumption breaks when observation rates or delays vary, or when inference latency changes. We introduce Chronos Policy11
1
          
          
          
        “Chronos” is the Greek word for time, reflecting that the policy reasons directly over physical time., which makes physical time explicit by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE). We find that time-aware RoPE is more robust, allowing attention to depend directly on physical time while keeping token content unchanged. During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi-rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real-world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi-static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing. Project website: https://changhaowang.github.io/chronospolicy/.
introduction:
Real robot systems rarely run on a fixed clock. Consider a robot grasping a moving object from a conveyor belt: the same displacement between two images can correspond to very different object velocities depending on whether the images were captured 20 ms or 200 ms apart. Likewise, the appropriate grasp depends on when the predicted action will actually be executed. Successful control therefore depends not only on what the robot observes, but also on when observations are captured and when actions execute.

More generally, robot learning systems are exposed to timing variation at every stage of sensing and control. Sensors operate at different rates and latencies, inference takes time, controllers may execute at different frequencies. Yet many imitation learning methods convert demonstrations into fixed-rate observation–action sequences, using sequence position as a proxy for physical time. This assumes a consistent relationship between sequence position and elapsed time; when that relationship changes, the policy cannot tell how much time has passed between observations or how far in the future an action will execute. Prior work has addressed specific deployment-time effects, such as latency matching (Chi et al., 2024) and asynchronous action-chunk execution (Black et al., 2026). We take a different approach: instead of treating timing variation as an external mismatch to correct, we represent it explicitly as part of the policy input.

Concretely, we formulate the policy as:

A key design choice is how this timing information should enter the policy. One option is to encode timestamps and add them directly to the token embeddings, mixing what a token represents with when it occurs. We instead find it more effective to keep the token content unchanged and use physical time only as positional encoding in attention. Chronos Policy therefore replaces index-based positional encoding with time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE): observation tokens use their capture times tot_{o}, while noisy action tokens use their queried execution times tat_{a} as rotary coordinates. Attention then depends on elapsed time ti−tjt_{i}-t_{j}, directly representing observation-to-observation, observation-to-action, and action-to-action timing while remaining invariant to the choice of clock origin.

Timestamps also allow us to vary the timing of training examples. We randomly change which observations are selected and when the action chunk starts. Because the policy sees these timestamps, it can correctly interpret each sampled sequence even when its timing differs from the nominal training setup. This exposes the policy to timing variations that may occur at deployment and lets it use measurements that fixed-rate downsampling would otherwise discard.

We evaluate Chronos Policy across three types of tasks: dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing affects the correct control; multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters; and standard quasi-static tasks, where precise timing is less critical. Across simulation and real-robot experiments, Chronos Policy improves robustness to sensing and inference variation while preserving performance on quasi-static tasks where timing matters less.

Our contributions are threefold:

We formulate robot policy learning in physical time by conditioning on observation capture times and queried action execution times.

We introduce Chronos Policy, a diffusion transformer with time-aware RoPE that learns directly from asynchronous, multi-rate observations, without aligning them to a fixed temporal grid.

We develop benchmarks that implement realistic timing variation and show that Chronos Policy improves dynamic manipulation through better observation–action timing and multisensory manipulation through better observation–observation timing, while preserving nominal performance on standard tasks and improving robustness to deployment-time mismatch.

1. We formulate robot policy learning in physical time by conditioning on observation capture times and queried action execution times.

2. We introduce Chronos Policy, a diffusion transformer with time-aware RoPE that learns directly from asynchronous, multi-rate observations, without aligning them to a fixed temporal grid.

3. We develop benchmarks that implement realistic timing variation and show that Chronos Policy improves dynamic manipulation through better observation–action timing and multisensory manipulation through better observation–observation timing, while preserving nominal performance on standard tasks and improving robustness to deployment-time mismatch.

title: BT-Agent: Deploying Onboard Robot Agents with Behavior Trees and Multi-Fidelity Evaluation
authors: Fabio Hübel,Adam Lilja,Yue Yin,Siming He,Claire Tomlin,Shankar Sastry,Jonas Frey,Marco Pavone
abstract: Deploying language-model agents onboard mobile robots requires task reasoning and responsive execution within limited compute and memory. We propose BT-Agent, an onboard architecture combining LLM-driven task decisions with predefined behavior-tree (BT) skills. These skills enforce execution conditions and return structured failure feedback. We demonstrate fully onboard operation with a 9B model on a quadruped across five task categories. Intervention tests show that local checks stop ongoing navigation without waiting for another model decision, while the agent remains active to retry or report constraints. To compare agent designs efficiently, we introduce a 161-task multi-fidelity benchmark, evaluated in text on all tasks and in Habitat on 39. Text supports 10.9× higher evaluation throughput, while simulation reveals how perception and motion failures change task outcomes. BT-Agent’s largest success gains over the strongest Act/ReAct baseline occur at 4B and 9B: approximately 10 and 5 percentage points. Ablations identify structured tool calls and informative failure feedback as the most useful components.
introduction:
Mobile robots increasingly receive high-level goals that require sequences of physical actions.
During search, inspection, and manipulation, they need to track partial
information and adapt when an action fails [1]. For
operation independent of remote compute, this reasoning must run onboard,
sharing finite memory and compute with perception and control. Deploying an
agent on an embedded platform therefore involves both task-level decision
making and responsive physical execution.

Language-model robot agents interleave task-level reasoning with action through
skill selection, execution feedback, and programs over robot APIs
[2, 3, 4, 5]. These
methods primarily address what the agent should do next. There is, however, no
shared interface across these approaches for how selected robot skills expose
execution state, enforce conditions, and support interruption. Behavior trees
(BTs) provide a modular, robotics-native basis for such an
interface [6].

To this end, we propose BT-Agent, a deployment-oriented architecture that
separates task-level model reasoning from reactive robot execution through
predefined BT skills (Fig. ). An onboard Actor selects
skills and arguments using the task, state, and previous observations. A
supervisor BT starts each skill and returns structured feedback, forming a
reasoning-and-acting (ReAct) loop [7]. Within each skill, guards
recheck conditions on every tick and can interrupt a running action without
another model decision. The Actor cannot modify skill implementations or
guards, so their logic can be reviewed and tested independently of the
task-level policy. This combines established BT execution mechanisms with
flexible, feedback-driven task reasoning: the model adapts its decisions,
while the BT enforces the conditions under which each skill can run.

Evaluating this architecture means checking both the agent’s decisions and
how its skills perform. We need controlled comparisons across models and
harnesses, alongside trials where perception and motion can fail. We therefore
construct a multi-fidelity benchmark with 161 text tasks derived from Habitat
and Isaac scenes, sharing task goals and skill interfaces with simulator
execution. Text trials support inexpensive
comparisons of task performance, inference cost, and responses to injected
faults such as navigation timeouts and observation failures. Paired trials on
39 primary Habitat tasks examine where perception and motion change the outcome. Robosuite
experiments [8] additionally examine task-level orchestration
in manipulation. Finally, real-robot trials demonstrate fully onboard task
completion with a 9B model, while intervention tests validate the architecture’s
reactive skill execution.

In summary, our contributions are:

An agentic robot architecture, BT-Agent, for onboard deployment, combining
model-driven task decisions with predefined BT skills, reactive execution
checks, and structured feedback.

A multi-fidelity evaluation methodology connecting a 161-task
text benchmark, simulation-informed fault injection, and physical execution
through shared task goals and skill contracts.

An empirical evaluation across model sizes and execution
backends, characterizing task success and inference cost, demonstrating
fully onboard deployment with a 9B model, and achieving
10.9×\times higher evaluation throughput in text than in Habitat at eight
concurrent workers.

We will release the BT-Agent implementation and benchmark code under the
Apache-2.0 license.

title: HorizonNav: Geometry-Guided Video Diffusion for Anticipatory 3D Robot Navigation
authors: Hajira Amjad,Valerii Serpiva,Viacheslav Liubimov,Didar Seyidov,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract:
We present HorizonNav, a video diffusion-based framework for anticipatory robot navigation that transforms a single RGB image and a text prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding 3D space. Given the initial observation and a textual description of the reconstruction objective, a vision-language model, guided by designed instructions, interprets the scene and constructs structured prompts for a video diffusion model. The resulting video sequence provides plausible future observations of the environment, which are subsequently processed using monocular ORB-SLAM3 for camera pose estimation and Video Depth Anything for dense depth prediction. Our central contribution is a geometry-guided depth alignment stage that combines the estimated camera poses with triangulated visual landmarks to constrain dense depth predictions across multiple views. This alignment improves the geometric consistency of the reconstructed 3D environment, addressing inconsistencies that temporal coherence of the generated video alone cannot resolve. The experimental evaluation of navigation in imagined 3D environment shows that across a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes increase from 13/19 at P20 to 15/19 at P81, while successful RRT trials increase from 62/90 to 75/90. In a separate corridor study, 6 of 25 evaluable generated-camera trajectories violate the reconstructed collision constraints; RRT planner recovers feasible alternatives in 5 of those 6 cases. A larger archive contains 58 usable reconstructions from 67 attempted cases, of which 36 support a downstream plan and 22 do not, exposing reconstruction and free-space failure modes rather than hiding them without lidar
Across 15 corridor reconstructions, the mean reconstruction error is approximately 0.30 m at matched structural landmarks.
introduction:
Autonomous navigation in unfamiliar environments requires robots to act before their surroundings are fully explored. Visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) reconstructs observed scene structure, while regions outside the current field of view remain unknown. A robot that can form plausible spatial hypotheses before motion may be able to evaluate candidate routes earlier, but such hypotheses are useful only if their geometry is treated cautiously rather than as ground truth.

Recent generative world models use predicted observations for navigation and action reasoning. Navigation World Models [1] predict action-conditioned observations, while ImagiNav [2] combines language-guided video generation with trajectory extraction. WonderWorld [3], WorldExplorer [4], and GEN3C [5] further demonstrate that generative models can expose spatial structure beyond a single image. However, a generated trajectory need not be safe to execute, and generated views may contain deformations or inconsistent occlusions that alter free-space connectivity.

Dense depth estimation provides per-pixel depth information for generated observations, but it does not by itself enforce a geometrically aligned 3D reconstruction across views. Video Depth Anything [6] produces temporally coherent depth maps and explicitly achieves this without introducing geometric priors or video generation priors. However, temporal consistency alone does not necessarily guarantee accurate multi-view geometry. In contrast, methods such as VGGT [7] and Depth Anything 3 [8] explicitly target multi-view geometric estimation, while World Reconstruction From Inconsistent Views [9] addresses contradictions between generated observations through non-rigid alignment. These developments motivate combining exploratory video generation with explicit geometric constraints to transform temporally consistent depth predictions into spatial representations that are more geometrically coherent and useful for robot planning.

We present HorizonNav a framework that transforms a single RGB image and a language prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding space. Starting from one RGB observation and a language task, a vision-language model produces structured exploration instructions and Wan 2.2 generates complementary virtual camera motion. ORB-SLAM3 [6] estimates the corresponding virtual camera poses and sparse 3D landmarks, whereas Video Depth Anything predicts dense relative depth maps for the generated frames. We align the dense depth estimates with the sparse geometric structure recovered by ORB-SLAM3, jointly resolving scale and geometric consistency across views. A measured scene reference resolves monocular scale, after which RRT [7] searches the resulting obstacle representation independently of the generated camera motion. HorizonNav combines exploration-oriented VLM prompting, sparse-landmark-guided depth alignment, and multivideo map fusion to connect generative visual exploration with explicit spatial reasoning for navigation.

This design deliberately separates three questions that are often conflated: whether generated frames contain enough repeatable visual structure for multi-view reconstruction, whether the resulting spatial hypothesis preserves free-space connectivity well enough for planning, and whether a map-feasible plan transfers to the physical robot.

title: Mapless, Stabilizing, and Anti-Stuck Flipper Control for Articulated Tracked Robots
authors: Valentýn Číhala,Pavel Sarga,Martin Pecka,Tomáš Svoboda,Karel Zimmermann
abstract:
Nearly every autonomous or semi-autonomous flipper controller assumes access
to an elevation map of the terrain under and in front of the robot. The terrain beneath the chassis is occluded in the sensors, so the map is remembered through odometry integration, whose drift corrupts it. We present
Stabilizing Anti-Stuck (SAS),
a mapless controller that combines a stabilization term for body roll
and pitch with an anti-stuck term that frees the robot when it gets stuck. As input, SAS uses the IMU, the flipper joint angles, and a motion cue that only
tells whether the robot is moving. The cue is computed over a short window and never
accumulated, so SAS does not inherit the odometry-integration drift that corrupts the
map. We deploy SAS on a tracked robot with four flippers and evaluate it against manual
teleoperation and prior flipper controllers in a large comparison, both in
simulation and on a real obstacle. In simulation and on the real robot, SAS achieves traversal quality comparable to state-of-the-art
map-based controllers. On a log hidden in tall grass, invisible to the LiDAR, the best map-based controller gets stuck
while SAS traverses the hidden obstacle without a problem.
introduction:
Tracked and wheeled robots cannot ascend an obstacle taller than their leading wheel.
Articulated tracked robots address higher obstacles with flippers,
independently actuated sub-tracks that reshape the robot’s morphology on the fly: they
can be used to reach beyond the leading wheel to ascend what tracked and wheeled robots cannot, and to
free the robot when it gets stuck [1, 2, 3].

Prior flipper controllers assume an elevation map.
Across the literature, semi-autonomous and autonomous flipper controllers share a
precondition: they consume an elevation map of the terrain under and in front of the
robot as their dominant
input [2, 4, 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8].
Fully manual teleoperation needs no map because the operator sees the terrain from a
third-person view but must drive all four flippers by hand.

On a real robot, the map is a dead-reckoning artifact.
Where the estimate of that terrain drifts due to body occlusion, the commanded flipper
angles are computed for incorrect terrain. Onboard sensors
observe what is ahead, but the body occludes their view of the terrain beneath it.
Dedicated underbody sensors could measure it, but they are rarely fitted and have very
low resolution. That terrain can therefore mainly be remembered: observed earlier, accumulated into an elevation
map, and carried beneath the robot as it advances by
integrating wheel or LiDAR odometry [9]. Every stage of this
pipeline is a dead-reckoning process: point-cloud deskewing warps each scan by the estimated
sensor trajectory, and elevation mapping registers successive scans through the
estimated motion [10]. On the loose, deformable,
step-like terrain where flippers are needed, odometry is least reliable: tracks slip, and
the chassis pitches and drops abruptly, saturating the IMU; therefore, inertial integration cannot
recover the estimate either [11]. Reflected, invalid LiDAR returns add obstacles that do
not exist, such as the spike behind the robot in Fig. 1.

The hardest case is a hidden obstacle.
When a rigid obstacle is hidden (Fig. 3), optical sensors, such as LiDAR or cameras, return the
compliant canopy above it, while the load-bearing obstacle beneath remains invisible until the
chassis stalls on it. Neither a dedicated underbody sensor, which is blinded by the same vegetation, nor foliage-penetrating radar, which is bulky and low-resolution, resolves this in practice.

Our contribution: control of the flippers without a map and without an accumulated
pose.
We present Stabilizing Anti-Stuck (SAS), a reactive controller that requires no
elevation map. It has two terms: a
stabilization term that stabilizes the robot body regardless of the terrain, whether
climbing or descending an obstacle, and an anti-stuck term that frees the robot when it
gets stuck by driving the flippers down. To tell a stuck robot from a moving one, the
anti-stuck term needs a motion cue: a thresholded answer to whether the robot is
moving, which requires neither an accurate nor a metric estimate of the motion. Because the
cue is computed over a short window and is never accumulated, SAS never inherits the drift that corrupts the map.

Contributions:

We propose SAS, a mapless flipper controller that needs only a
thresholded motion cue, combining continuous roll and pitch stabilization with a reactive
anti-stuck term under a safe directional-priority blend.

We measure the degradation of the elevation map caused by body occlusion and
odometry drift by evaluating map-based baselines under both a ground-truth map and
the onboard map, in a large comparison in simulation of SAS against twelve
map-based baselines and two manual baselines on a twelve-obstacle course; every controller
drives the full course ten times, with the perception stack reset at each obstacle.

We perform the large comparison in a real obstacle arena with AprilTag ground
truth: on a four-track robot, each controller drives ten times over a pallet obstacle.

title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
authors: Jingwei Song,Zhisheng Chen,Bingfan Zeng,Jing Tang,Yubo Hou,Jinhao Jing,Zhengwei Xie,Linfeng Zhang
abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source–target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source.
introduction:
One of the central ambitions of autonomous intelligence is recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Chen et al., 2026): an agent should use experience from its own actions to become more capable over time. The goal is larger than learning one policy or storing one successful trajectory. An RSI system should turn experience into a capability, retain it, and apply it when the task, world, or required action changes. This loop is central to long-horizon autonomy: as tasks become harder, the agent must build on what it has already learned.

This view differs from evaluation settings in which training is separated from testing and improvement is summarized by a single score (Ren et al., 2026). For RSI, the important question is whether a gain remains useful after the original interaction has ended. A capability should survive a change in local conditions, help with a related goal, and combine with actions that were not part of the source task. RSI is therefore a systems problem: learning, memory, planning, and physical interaction must work together, while the resulting gain remains visible and attributable.

Embodied agents make this problem concrete and difficult. Their behavior depends on both internal state and physical state. A later success may reflect a tool left in the inventory, a changed world, a favorable location, or more source interaction rather than a reusable capability. A useful benchmark must therefore show that improvement survives a reset and appears in observable behavior.

We study this question through later behavior. A memory, skill file, or model update shows that an agent changed internally. It does not show that the agent gained a useful capability (Li et al., 2025b; Park et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). The evidence must link internal change to later action. It must also distinguish capability from favorable execution. To test that claim, we compare target behavior after a world reset and check both task outcomes and stage-level records.

Existing benchmarks address parts of this problem. MCU (Zheng et al., 2023) evaluates diverse and combined Minecraft tasks with automatic verification. LifelongAgentBench (Zheng et al., 2025), EvoAgentBench (Gao et al., 2026), and PAST-Bench (Xue et al., 2026) study learning across tasks, transfer, and persistent state in other settings. Embodied evaluation also needs to separate world resources from agent state, match source budgets, and record where a task chain fails (Ni et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025). Otherwise, a score difference may reflect an easier world, more source interaction, or an early failure that hides later behavior.

Minecraft makes these controls practical. Collecting resources, crafting tools, and using them create visible task dependencies. A task-state graph represents these relations, and environment evidence verifies each stage. Resetting the world and inventory removes physical carryover, while stage records show progress before a chain stops (Guo et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025).

We introduce MC-EvoBench to evaluate embodied RSI in Minecraft. Figure 1 shows its mechanism: measure progress, transfer only a declared agent artifact, and use matched controls to assess experience gains. Table 1 compares this design with representative Minecraft benchmarks (Guss et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2022; Hill et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025). MC-EvoBench provides a task catalog, verifiers, and three short probe families for wood-species crafting, wooden-tool transfer, and stone-tool transfer. The framework can study capability formation, transfer, retention, and composition. This paper focuses on forward transfer between graph-related tasks.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Embodied RSI as attributable capability change. We formalize an agent as a policy, a persistent state, and an update rule, and separate this persistent state from the world state. A gain counts as experience-driven only when it appears after the target world is reset, only a declared artifact crosses the source–target boundary, and matched unrelated and shuffled sources rule out alternative explanations.

Embodied RSI as attributable capability change. We formalize an agent as a policy, a persistent state, and an update rule, and separate this persistent state from the world state. A gain counts as experience-driven only when it appears after the target world is reset, only a declared artifact crosses the source–target boundary, and matched unrelated and shuffled sources rule out alternative explanations.

MC-EvoBench, an executable audit of experience-driven improvement. It instantiates this definition in Minecraft with a task-state graph of 80 tasks, 111 states, and 369 typed edges organized into 19 chains; stage-level verifiers with three complementary metrics, Task Success Rate (TSR), Weighted Graph Progress (WGP), and Verified Milestone Progress (VMP); and a four-condition paired protocol with matched environment-step budgets and provenance records.

Controlled evidence on embodied transfer. Controller-based agents clearly outperform planner-backed variants in direct capability. Under matched controls, the reference method shows no stable transfer gain, even though its related sources earn more verified progress and, on the longer probes, more computation, and early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks leave later capabilities unobserved. Future RSI methods must therefore first clear these execution bottlenecks, and their gains should be claimed only after a controlled audit.

Section 2 reviews related benchmarks and agents. Section 3 defines the framework and benchmark. Section 4 reports the reference results. Appendices A–G give the task, environment, protocol, and reproduction details.

title: When LiDAR Fades, Radar Takes Over: LiDAR Reliability-Aware Adaptive Localization Under Airborne Obscurants
authors: Moumita Mukherjee,Avijit Banerjee,Anton Koval,George Nikolakopoulo
abstract: LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is widely used for real-time localization and mapping, but its reliability can degrade substantially in subterranean environments affected by smoke, dust, and other airborne obscurants, whereas radar remains comparatively robust. This article presents a one-class temporal learning framework for LiDAR degradation detection and reliability-aware localization under such conditions. A broad set of degradation-sensitive cues, including spatial, cross-modal, geometric/motion, intensity, and measurement-recency features, is evaluated to characterize changes in LiDAR sensing quality. Their temporal evolution is modelled over sliding windows using an LSTM autoencoder trained exclusively on nominal operation, enabling deviations from healthy sensor behaviour to be detected without requiring labelled degradation data. The resulting LiDAR reliability estimate governs adaptive selection between LIO and radar inertial odometry (RIO), retaining LIO during reliable sensing and transferring localization authority to RIO when degradation is detected. The framework is evaluated using real-world ground robot data collected in GNSS-denied subterranean tunnels under nominal and dense-smoke conditions. Experimental results demonstrate degradation detection, adaptive modality switching, and continued localization output under severe LiDAR degradation. A feature family ablation study further shows that a reduced feature representation can improve degradation-aware localization performance in the evaluated dense-smoke scenarios, highlighting the importance of feature parsimony in one-class sensor degradation detection. The code will be released as open source to support reproducibility and further research.
introduction:
The rapid advancement of LiDAR technology has significantly improved localization, mapping, and three-dimensional perception in challenging environments. However, in GNSS-denied subterranean environments such as tunnels and underground facilities, dense smoke, rain, and other airborne particulates can substantially degrade LiDAR measurements [1, 2].

Such degradation may reduce the number of valid returns, alter their spatial distribution, and change pointcloud density, thereby reducing the reliability of LiDAR-based perception in real-world deployments
 [3, 4]. Although radar is comparatively robust under degraded visibility, LiDAR remains valuable for its high-resolution geometric information. Reliable localization therefore
requires both complementary sensing modalities and the ability to identify when LiDAR measurements become unreliable, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

This motivates degradation-sensitive LiDAR feature extraction that captures changes in spatial occupancy, density, temporal consistency, and related sensing characteristics. LiDAR
degradation may be observed as abrupt changes, missing observations, or persistent deviations from nominal behaviour. Existing anomaly detection methods include distribution, clustering, distance, and density based approaches [5, 6, 7].
However, these methods typically operate on individual observations and do not explicitly model the temporal evolution of sensor degradation. This limitation motivates the sequence based formulation adopted in this article.

LiDAR pointclouds are unordered and variable in size, making direct temporal modelling computationally demanding. Representations based on subsampling, projection, or learned point-wise features can reduce this complexity, but may suppress local variations in point concentration and spatial occupancy that are informative for sensor degradation [8, 9]. Voxel-based representations provide a structured alternative by preserving three-dimensional spatial organization while enabling compact characterization of return density and occupancy [10, 11]. These statistics provide interpretable reliability cues through changes in the number, concentration, and spatial distribution of valid LiDAR returns. Accordingly, the proposed framework combines voxel-based spatial statistics with complementary temporal, geometric, cross-modal, inertial, and intensity related features for sequence based degradation detection.

Conventional anomaly detection methods, including clustering, Isolation Forest, and support vector machines, can identify observations that deviate from nominal feature distributions [12]. However, such approaches typically assess individual feature vectors and do not explicitly model the temporal evolution of sensor degradation. This is important for LiDAR reliability monitoring, where degradation may develop progressively over consecutive observations rather than as an isolated outlier. Autoencoder based methods provide a suitable one-class [13] learning framework by modelling nominal sensor behaviour without requiring labelled failure data. Deviations from the learned nominal representation are reflected by increased reconstruction error. To capture temporal dependencies, the proposed approach employs an LSTM autoencoder [14] operating on sliding windows of multivariate degradation-sensitive features. By modelling the temporal evolution of nominal LiDAR measurements, the network identifies abnormal temporal patterns associated with emerging degradation.

Thus, the main contributions of this article are summarized as follows:

A compact and interpretable multi-cue LiDAR reliability representation is developed using voxel based spatial statistics, measurement recency, LIO-RIO pose consistency, point-cloud geometry, inertial motion, and LiDAR intensity features. A feature family ablation study quantifies the contribution of these cues under dense smoke conditions.

A compact and interpretable multi-cue LiDAR reliability representation is developed using voxel based spatial statistics, measurement recency, LIO-RIO pose consistency, point-cloud geometry, inertial motion, and LiDAR intensity features. A feature family ablation study quantifies the contribution of these cues under dense smoke conditions.

A one-class temporal LiDAR degradation detector based on an LSTM autoencoder is proposed to model nominal sensor behaviour over sliding windows and identify emerging degradation from reconstruction error deviations without requiring labelled failure data.

A reliability aware adaptive LIO-RIO localization framework is introduced, in which LiDAR health governs online estimator selection. LIO is retained during reliable sensing, while RIO is selected when LiDAR degrades or becomes unavailable. The framework is evaluated using real-world data from GNSS-denied tunnel experiments under nominal and dense smoke conditions.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Sections II and III present the problem formulation and the proposed LMRIO framework, respectively. Section IV presents the experimental evaluation, and Section V concludes the article.

title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
authors: Timi Owolabi,Hikmah Olawore,Frances Adelakun,Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Robot Learning with World Models Workshop. Code:this https URLProject:this https URL
abstract:
World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot’s actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices.
We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk’s attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step.
Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11×\times faster than its teacher with 18.5×\times fewer FLOPs and 3.2×\times less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
Code: github.com/iitimii/SmolWAM; project page: smolwam.vercel.app.
introduction:
World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot’s next actions together with the observations they should produce [15, 41, 23].
Cosmos Policy [15] builds one from the Cosmos-Predict2 video model [28] by treating actions, future observations, and values as latent frames of a single denoising sequence, and reaches 98.5% success on LIBERO [19].
Its inference stack, however, was built for video generation: a 4.8B-parameter T5-XXL text encoder [32], a VAE that encodes a 33-frame clip per query, and five denoising steps of a 2B-parameter transformer over 1,764 tokens, which cost 624 ms, 42.6 TFLOP, and 7.55 GiB per 16-action chunk on an A100 even with cached text features.

Efficient policies usually give up the world model or the video prior: compact vision-language-action (VLA) models such as SmolVLA [33] and TurboVLA [39] predict only actions, and Fast-WAM [42] skips future prediction at test time.
We ask whether a strong pretrained WAM can itself be made small while still predicting the future.

We present SmolWAM (Fig. 1).
Our premise is that much of the teacher’s cost comes from an interface designed for video generation, not from what control requires.
SmolWAM reuses the trunk’s weights, token positions, and rectified-flow readout; it encodes single frames through a small adapter, replaces T5-XXL with cached BERT features [8] padded to preserve the trunk’s attention sinks, keeps 12 of 28 blocks, and reads actions from 28 state-conditioned queries.
Most changes break the trunk zero-shot, so a distillation curriculum recovers from pruning before compaction.

We contribute (i) SmolWAM, which retains 97% of its teacher’s success at 11×\times lower latency; (ii) a method, with a diagnostic behind each step, for deriving compact WAMs from pretrained video WAMs (Sec. 3), including three pitfalls (attention-sink padding, jointly fatal blocks, and chunks that cannot be cut short); and (iii) findings that the compressed world head preserves motion forecasting, whereas latent-action cascades or visual-reward fine-tuning degrade control (Sec. 4).

title: Towards a Unified Taxonomy of Agricultural Harvesting Technologies: Linking Physical Interaction, Automation, and Selectivity
authors: Renato Cristiano Torres,Fabiano Mariath D Oliveira,Claudio Gottschalg Duque
abstract: Harvesting technologies have evolved from conventional mechanized systems based on bulk mechanical interaction toward increasingly automated and robotic systems capable of perception, decision-making, and localized actuation. However, this technological evolution has also created a classification problem. Harvesting systems are commonly described according to crop type, mechanical removal principle, sensing technology, robotic architecture, or degree of automation, making direct comparison between mechanized, automated, and robotic approaches difficult.
introduction:
The adoption of agricultural mechanization technologies must be understood within a broader historical, economic, and social context. In a comparative analysis of the history of agricultural mechanization, Binswanger [5] demonstrates that the introduction of machinery in agricultural systems does not occur in a linear manner, nor is it driven exclusively by technological availability. Factors such as relative labor costs, land tenure structure, capital availability, public policies, and agronomic characteristics of crops play a decisive role in the adoption or rejection of mechanized and automated technologies. These factors shape not only the feasibility of technological implementation but also its economic and operational sustainability across different production systems.

Mechanization is defined as the use of mechanical energy and machinery to replace or reduce human or animal labor [12], whereas automation refers to systems capable of monitoring, decision-making, and actuation through sensors, controllers, and actuators [14]. Although conceptually distinct, these two paradigms increasingly coexist in modern agricultural systems.

Harvesting is among the most labor-intensive and costly operations in agriculture, particularly in high-value horticultural and fruit production systems. Previous studies indicate that harvesting may account for approximately 30–50% of total production costs [3, 4]. Labor shortages and rising wages have intensified the adoption of agricultural automation technologies, a trend further reinforced by changes in consumer behavior, which increasingly demand consistent and high-quality products [17].

Unlike operations such as seeding and spraying, harvesting involves direct interaction with fragile biological materials, requiring simultaneous perception, decision-making, and precise mechanical manipulation [25]. The heterogeneity of harvested products in terms of size, shape, rigidity, and maturity stage significantly increases the complexity of harvesting operations. Despite advances in robotics, computer vision, and artificial intelligence, economic, operational, and crop-adaptation challenges continue to limit the widespread diffusion of automated harvesting technologies.

Modern agricultural machines increasingly incorporate GPS-based navigation, electronic controllers, onboard sensors, and yield monitoring systems. However, the incorporation of these technologies does not automatically change the physical principle used to harvest the crop. A machine may become more automated while still applying the same cutting, pulling, vibration, impact, or combined harvesting mechanism. In this sense, mechanization and automation are not mutually exclusive categories but different dimensions of a harvesting system.

This distinction creates a conceptual problem for comparison. Conventional harvesting machinery is usually described primarily by the physical mechanism used to detach, collect, or transport the product, whereas robotic harvesting systems are more frequently discussed in terms of perception, manipulation, motion planning, and autonomy. As a consequence, technologies belonging to different stages of harvesting automation are often described using classification criteria that are not directly comparable.

The problem becomes even more evident because increasing automation does not necessarily imply increasing selectivity. Automated navigation or automatic adjustment of process parameters may improve operational efficiency while preserving bulk harvesting. A qualitative transition occurs only when perception and decision-making begin to influence product-level actuation, allowing the system to discriminate between harvestable and non-harvestable targets.

Accordingly, this study argues that agricultural harvesting technologies require a unified classification framework capable of describing both their physical interaction mechanisms and their level of automation while explicitly evaluating selectivity. Two primary classification axes are adopted: (i) the physical principle governing plant–machine interaction during product removal and (ii) the degree of automation associated with perception, decision-making, and actuation. Selectivity is treated as an emergent functional attribute that expresses the biological and spatial scale at which the harvesting action is targeted.

The objective of this paper is therefore not only to review existing harvesting technologies, but to demonstrate the conceptual need for a unified taxonomy capable of positioning mechanized, automated, and robotic harvesting systems within a common analytical framework. The main contributions are:

to separate the physical mechanism of product removal from the automation level of the harvesting system;

to identify selectivity as a central linking attribute between physical interaction and automation;

to organize conventional mechanized, semi-automated, collaborative, and autonomous robotic harvesting within a common framework; and

to clarify the technological transition from distributed or bulk harvesting toward localized and selective product-level interaction.

title: Cooperative Aerial Transportation of a Payload with a Sliding Cable Attachment
authors: Sebastian Tilaguy Lezama,Diego S D'Antonio
abstract: This paper presents a dual-quadrotor hook-suspended transport system for cooperative aerial manipulation of a payload that is not rigidly attached to a fixed point along the cable. Two quadrotors are connected by a single inextensible cable that passes through a frictionless hook mounted on the payload, allowing the cable to slide between its two segments. This introduces a cable-distribution variable that couples the quadrotor motion, cable geometry, and payload dynamics. A feasible reference-generation framework is formulated using the desired payload pose, cable distribution, and system shape while satisfying the cable-length constraint and elliptical workspace. The quadrotors track the geometrically generated trajectories while maintaining positive cable tension and respecting actuator limits. The payload pose is estimated from the system geometry, and its measured position is used only to validate the desired trajectory. The approach is evaluated through experimental demonstrations.
introduction:
Cooperative aerial systems have expanded the capabilities of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) beyond surveillance and conventional logistics. Through distributed actuation and coordinated motion, multiple UAVs can perform tasks that exceed the physical limitations of a single platform, including heavy-payload transportation, infrastructure interaction, and emergency response
[1, 2, 3].
Aerial logistics has therefore received increasing attention for rapid operation in remote or hard-to-reach environments, motivating scalable and autonomous multi-robot transportation strategies
[4].

Cable-suspended transportation provides several advantages for aerial manipulation. By separating the payload from the aerial platform, the cable reduces the direct transmission of disturbances and allows the UAVs to maintain a safer distance from the transported object. It can also facilitate payload attachment and release while the aerial vehicles remain in flight
[5, 6].
Early studies primarily considered payloads suspended from a single UAV, which inherently limits the available lifting capacity and controllability of the payload. Cooperative multi-UAV systems address these limitations by distributing the payload weight among multiple aerial vehicles and coordinating the cable forces applied to the load
[7].

Several approaches have addressed cooperative cable-suspended transportation through differential flatness, coordinated rotorcraft motion, inertial sensing, autonomous hook-based grasping, and nonlinear model predictive control [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. These methods enable trajectory generation, cooperative transport, payload grasping, and constrained full-pose manipulation. However, they generally assume fixed cable attachment points and do not consider cable-length redistribution through a sliding payload-mounted hook.

Cable-suspended aerial lifting is commonly divided into setup, pull, and raise stages [13, 14]. While the pull and raise stages have received significant attention, setup often requires manual cable attachment, reducing autonomy and limiting operation in hazardous or inaccessible environments. A catenary robot, formed by two aerial vehicles connected by a flexible cable, can manipulate the cable to interact with objects [15]. However, engaging a payload-mounted hook allows the cable to slide, coupling UAV motion, cable geometry, payload dynamics, and cable-length distribution.
Motivated by this gap, this work introduces the Dual-Quadrotor Hook-Suspended Transport System (DQ-HSTS), shown in Fig. 1. Two quadrotors are connected by a single cable passing through a frictionless hook rigidly attached to the payload. Unlike conventional systems, the cable slides through the hook, redistributing its total length between the two cable segments.

This paper addresses quadrotor coordination for payload-pose and cable-distribution control without fixed cable attachments. The contributions are threefold:
i) the DQ-HSTS, in which a cable slides through a payload-mounted hook;
ii) trajectory generation parameterized by payload pose, cable distribution λ\lambda, and system shape γ\gamma; and
iii) coordinated trajectory tracking under tension, geometric, and actuator constraints, validated in experiments.

title: AutoBio+: Benchmarking Dexterous Manipulation with Dynamic Experimental Phenomena in Realistic Laboratories
authors: Xuanye Wu,Yue Shi,Yongcan Yang,Yiqun Wang,Zhaoqi Wan,Dayu Xia,Jiezhang Cao,Xiangfei Li,Yao Mu,Guangtao Zhai
abstract:
Automating biological laboratories requires robots to perform dexterous tool interactions
under realistic visual conditions while handling dynamic experimental phenomena,
presenting significant challenges for robotic manipulation. To enable systematic
evaluation under these conditions, we introduce AutoBio+, a simulation benchmark and
framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments.
AutoBio+ comprises 14 tasks across 4 robot embodiments, spanning functional tool use,
precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation.
We introduce controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor, and
bubbles, to capture the evolving visual conditions of laboratory procedures. To further
enhance environmental realism, we develop a hybrid rendering pipeline that integrates
interactive simulated foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed
from 6 real laboratory scenes. For efficient large-scale data generation and evaluation,
we further build a parallel simulation framework on top of mjlab, proposing Parallel
Finite-State Machine (PFSM) and integrating batched rendering with decoupled trajectory replay
for demonstration generation and model-independent closed-loop policy evaluation. Our
evaluation reveals substantial variation in policy performance across tasks, exposing
distinct strengths and weaknesses of current manipulation policies. Real-world experiments
further demonstrate a reduced sim-to-real gap, supporting the validity of AutoBio+ for
realistic manipulation evaluation. Supplementary materials are available at https://autobio-plus.github.io/AutoBioPlus.
introduction:
Automated laboratories, often referred to as AutoLabs, are transforming scientific experimentation by shifting routine
procedures from manual operation toward autonomous execution [9, 10]. Conventional laboratory automation,
however, typically relies on task-specific instruments and tightly coupled workflows. Although such
systems are efficient in structured settings, adapting them to new experimental protocols, tools,
or operating conditions often requires substantial hardware modification and system reintegration.
General-purpose robotic manipulators equipped with dexterous hands or grippers provide a more flexible alternative, allowing
laboratory procedures to be adapted through demonstrations and learned policies rather than
hardware-specific re-engineering. This flexibility is particularly important in biological
laboratories, where robots must perform fine-grained operations such as manipulating pipettes and
tweezers, inserting tubes, actuating instruments, and coordinating multiple objects over
long-horizon procedures.

Recent robot-learning methods, particularly vision-language-action (VLA) policies,
have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities in household
and industrial environments [11, 12, 13].
To evaluate these learned policies,
recent benchmarks have explored manipulation from several complementary perspectives.
General-purpose manipulation benchmarks such as RoboTwin 2.0 [14]
and LIBERO [15] provide diverse household and industrial tasks with
controlled object interactions. Scientific robotics
benchmarks [5, 8, 6] introduce
laboratory-specific objects and procedures, while dexterous manipulation benchmarks such as
DexJoCo [4], DexVerse [3], and
Bi-DexHands [2] focus on complex hand–object coordination.
Recently, Labimus [7] extends dexterous manipulation evaluation
to chemical laboratory scenarios. However, laboratory procedures often introduce temporally
varying visual conditions, such as flames, vapor, and bubbles, which are underrepresented in
existing manipulation benchmarks.

To address this gap, we introduce AutoBio+,
a simulation benchmark for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments.
AutoBio+ comprises 14 tasks across four robot embodiments, covering functional tool use,
precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation.
It incorporates controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor,
and bubbles, to capture visually evolving conditions during laboratory procedures.
To improve visual realism while preserving physical interaction, AutoBio+ proposes a hybrid
rendering strategy that combines interactive simulated foreground objects with
Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed from six real laboratory scenes.
Leveraging mjlab as the simulation foundation, we design a parallel simulation
framework centered around the Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM) policy,
together with batched rendering and decoupled trajectory replay,
enabling efficient demonstration generation and model-independent closed-loop evaluation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Multi-Embodiment Benchmark for Dexterous Laboratory Manipulation.
We introduce AutoBio+, comprising 14 laboratory manipulation tasks across four robot embodiments and covering functional tool use, precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation.

Dynamic Experimental Phenomena.
We incorporate controllable flames, vapor, and bubbles into laboratory procedures, introducing process-dependent visual changes for evaluating learned policies under
temporally varying and perceptually complex observations.

Photorealistic Hybrid Rendering.
We combine interactive MuJoCo-rendered foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds
reconstructed from real laboratories, improving visual realism while preserving physical
interaction and efficient batched rendering.

Parallel Data Generation and Evaluation.
Built on mjlab, AutoBio+ supports parallel demonstration collection with the proposed PFSM policy, rendering, and closed-loop policy evaluation, enabling efficient large-scale data
generation and benchmarking.

We introduce AutoBio+, comprising 14 laboratory manipulation tasks across four robot embodiments and covering functional tool use, precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation.

2. Dynamic Experimental Phenomena.
We incorporate controllable flames, vapor, and bubbles into laboratory procedures, introducing process-dependent visual changes for evaluating learned policies under
temporally varying and perceptually complex observations.

3. Photorealistic Hybrid Rendering.
We combine interactive MuJoCo-rendered foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds
reconstructed from real laboratories, improving visual realism while preserving physical
interaction and efficient batched rendering.

4. Parallel Data Generation and Evaluation.
Built on mjlab, AutoBio+ supports parallel demonstration collection with the proposed PFSM policy, rendering, and closed-loop policy evaluation, enabling efficient large-scale data
generation and benchmarking.

title: JitterVLA: A Replay Benchmark for Motion Quality in VLA-Driven Human-Robot Manipulation
authors: Faith Ogunwoye,Didar Seyidov,Konstantin Gubernatorov,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller’s effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy–discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0–14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.
introduction:
A person hands a manipulator an object, guides its target, or works beside it. The high-level policy produces a sensible action, but its targets arrive sparsely and at irregular times, so the low-level controller receives discontinuous goals. What the person experiences is not the predicted action but the motion the robot executes. VLA policies such as OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2025b) run at a few hertz, one to two orders of magnitude below the robot’s control loop (Jiang et al., 2026), and remote or shared inference adds network delay. Human-robot interaction (HRI) research links onset latency to teleoperation performance (Rakita et al., 2020; Khalil and Kwon, 2026) and robot motion to observers’ responses and perceived safety (Kulić and Croft, 2007; Rubagotti et al., 2022).

Timing is not only latency. A constant delay shifts every command, whereas timing jitter (variation in delay and arrival spacing, including bunching) changes which targets the controller sees and when. Remedies exist at several layers: action chunking and asynchronous execution (Zhao et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2025; Guo and Guo, 2026; Kim et al., 2025a), interpolation and jerk-limited trajectory generation such as Ruckig (Berscheid and Kröger, 2021), geometry-guided jerk reduction in VLA execution (Yun et al., 2026), and stiffness adaptation (Ferraguti et al., 2013). Each paper evaluates its remedy with its own inputs, delays, plant and metrics, so the remedies cannot be compared fairly. JitterVLA addresses that comparison problem. It evaluates the middle of the chain (command stream, timing, controller, executed motion) before candidate behaviours are shown to people. It does not replace human studies.

We ask four research questions (RQ1–RQ4). RQ1 (timing): how do timing irregularities change motion-quality proxies for identical command streams? RQ2 (control): how do stepped, interpolated, entropy-gated, constant-gain and jerk-limited strategies move the jerk–tracking trade-off? RQ3 (cross-source): do these relationships hold across synthetic, human and three VLA action representations, and on new episode draws? RQ4 (physical): are the contrasts observable on a real UR3 under a bounded protocol?

Contributions. (1) A paired replay benchmark and protocol that holds the command source and delay realization fixed while varying the controller. (2) An evaluation that progresses from controlled synthetic reaches to 20-person human motion, three VLA pipelines with a planned replication on 598 new episodes, and measured network traces (Table 1). (3) Findings: a consistent jerk–tracking trade-off for interpolation, representation-dependent uncertainty associations, and a failure of entropy gating on some inputs. (4) A bounded UR3 check, including a null result for the planned position-derived metric. Code, the transformed VLA streams, the human windows and the traces will be released.

Terms. Latency is delay; jitter is its variation. Command discontinuity is the spatial jump between successive targets or chunks. Jerk is the benchmark plant’s jerk proxy, or a sensor-derived estimate on the UR3. Tracking error is the root-mean-square error (RMSE) against the undelayed reference. Jerk, tracking error, log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) and spectral arc length (SPARC) (Balasubramanian et al., 2015) are motion-quality proxies; comfort, preference and safety were not measured.
