title: RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Xuhui Kang,Sung-Wook Lee,Yan Zhuang,Tianle Zhong,Yen-Ling Kuo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model’s generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts.
We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two-stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves pre-training demonstrations with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy’s representations of the target demonstrations with the pre-trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations.
Second, RARA fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine-tuning.
By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre-trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine-tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine-tuning by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines.

Project page: https://shua-kang.github.io/RARA_robot/
introduction:
Pre-training on large-scale robot demonstrations followed by fine-tuning on a small target dataset has become a standard practice in learning robot manipulation policies (O’Neill et al., 2024; Khazatsky et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025).
By leveraging supervision from large and diverse robot demonstration datasets, pre-training provides useful initial representations that help adaptation to a new task.
However, fine-tuning on limited target data can still overfit the policy to the narrow distribution seen during adaptation:
A policy may succeed on the target task under the in-distribution conditions, but fail when the camera viewpoint, background, or object properties change (Fei et al., 2026).
This vulnerability arises because standard fine-tuning on limited data can severely distort the representations learned during pre-training (Kumar et al., 2022; Kachaev et al., 2026; Yadav et al., 2026).
Therefore, robust policy fine-tuning, which requires learning a target task while maintaining generalization to out-of-distribution shifts, remains a critical challenge when adapting pre-trained robotic policies to new tasks.

Existing methods have explored several ways to preserve generalizable representations when adapting policies to new tasks.
One line of work constrains the adapted policy toward its pre-trained initialization, for example by regularizing fine-tuned weights toward the pre-trained weights (Huang et al., 2026), merging pre-trained and fine-tuned weights (Yadav et al., 2026), or aligning policy representations with those of a frozen pre-trained visual encoder (Kachaev et al., 2026).
Another line of work distills knowledge from multiple pre-trained models into a shared representation for downstream robot learning (Shang et al., 2024).
While these approaches preserve broad pre-trained knowledge, they do not provide a principled way to focus alignment to pre-training demonstrations that are most relevant to the target task.

We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), which uses task-relevant pre-training demonstrations as anchors for fine-tuning (Fig. 1).
RARA retrieves relevant demonstrations from the pre-training data by matching both task instructions and robot motions to the target demonstrations. For example, demonstrations of removing a pot lid may be retrieved for target tasks like opening a blender and remove a bottle cap.
The retrieved demonstrations support adaptation in two complementary ways.
Before fine-tuning, RARA aligns every target frame with the retrieved frames whose upcoming actions are most similar, so each frame is matched to the same stage of the motion in the retrieved demonstrations (e.g., a frame in which the gripper closes around the blender lid is matched to frames in which it closes around a pot lid).
The pre-trained policy has seen these stages under many visual conditions, so alignment lets the target frames reuse this robust representation instead of fitting the target demonstrations from scratch.
During fine-tuning, an anchor loss keeps the representations of the retrieved demonstrations close to their pre-trained values, so the small target dataset does not overwrite this robust structure.
Unlike a standard drift regularizer, the anchor acts only on the retrieved demonstrations. It therefore does not pull the target representation back, and it preserves only the pre-trained structure that is related to the target task.

We fine-tune a pre-trained Diffusion Policy on four RoboTwin tasks, and a DROID-pre-trained GR00T policy on five RoboCasa tasks and four real-robot tasks. We evaluate each policy in the conditions covered by its demonstrations (in-distribution, ID) and under new camera poses, backgrounds, distractors, objects or object positions (out-of-distribution, OOD). Across these 13 tasks, RARA improves the average success rates of fine-tuned policies by 9.59.5 % points in ID and 13.613.6 % points in OOD settings, consistently outperforming the baseline methods.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) we introduce RARA, a framework for robust policy fine-tuning that uses task-relevant pre-training experience to guide representation learning; (2) we evaluate RARA across different policies, simulated environments, and real-world manipulation tasks, measuring performance of target tasks and robustness to unseen conditions; and (3) we conduct extensive studies that separate initial alignment from representation constraints during fine-tuning, and examine how the choice of source data and network layer affects adaptation.

title: ATHLETE: Learning Reactive Humanoid Tennis via Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching
authors: Zhihao Tian,Zifan Wang,Enzheng Zhu,Xun Yang,Jialong Qin,Mengbo Wang,Junwei Liang
abstract: Humanoid tennis requires reactive whole-body coordination under rapidly changing ball dynamics, yet collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations that cover diverse approach states, contact locations, and timing conditions is costly. Inspired by how humans acquire new skills by combining reusable motor experience with task-specific demonstrations, we present ATHLETE, a framework for learning reactive humanoid tennis from generic locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos. ATHLETE combines LAFAN1 locomotion with video-derived striking motions and uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to construct diverse task-conditioned whole-body references. These references are transformed into a reactive policy through physics-based teacher–student learning with online DAgger distillation, followed by PPO fine-tuning for the tennis task. The resulting policy responds directly to robot and ball observations without requiring reference-motion inputs at deployment. On a real humanoid robot, ATHLETE achieves forehand and backhand hit rates of 90.00%90.00\% and 86.67%86.67\%, respectively, and enables multi-shot rallies with human players. These results demonstrate that ATHLETE can learn dynamic humanoid tennis skills from reusable locomotion data and video demonstrations. Result videos and code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ATHLETE2027/.
introduction:
Humanoid tennis requires rapid locomotion, precisely timed whole-body strikes, and continuous adaptation to incoming balls.
A central challenge is data coverage: a successful policy must handle diverse approach states, contact locations, and arrival times, while collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations for all such variations is costly.

Existing works such as LATENT [1] and AdaPT [2] demonstrate that human motion data can provide strong priors for humanoid tennis.
However, collecting or reconstructing task-specific tennis motions that sufficiently cover the combinations of locomotion, contact position, and timing remains difficult.
At the same time, public motion datasets such as LAFAN1 [3] and AMASS [4] already contain abundant reusable human locomotion, while ordinary tennis videos provide task-specific striking motions.
This raises a natural question: can dynamic humanoid tennis be learned by composing reusable locomotion experience with only sparse task-specific striking demonstrations?

We present ATHLETE to answer this question.
Our key idea is to treat locomotion and striking as complementary motion sources rather than requiring complete tennis demonstrations.
ATHLETE uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to compose generic locomotion with video-derived strikes under task, contact, and transition constraints, producing diverse whole-body approach-and-strike references.
These references are then converted through physics-based teacher–student learning into a reactive policy that no longer requires reference-motion input, online motion retrieval, or explicit motion planning at deployment.
The resulting controller directly responds to the robot state, ball observations, and task target.

Our contributions are threefold:

Task-conditioned motion composition from heterogeneous motion sources.
We introduce TGMM to combine abundant generic locomotion with sparse video-derived striking motions.
By explicitly enforcing approach, contact, and transition constraints, the method generates diverse whole-body tennis references without collecting dedicated tennis motion-capture demonstrations.

From composed references to reference-free reactive control.
We develop a deadline-adaptive teacher–student learning framework that transfers reference-motion and contact-timing supervision into a deployable reactive policy.
The final controller operates without reference motions, online motion matching, or an explicit motion planner.

Real-world humanoid tennis from low-cost motion sources.
We validate ATHLETE on a humanoid robot, achieving reactive forehand and backhand returns and multi-shot human–robot rallies, demonstrating that reusable locomotion data and sparse visual demonstrations are sufficient to support dynamic whole-body tennis skills (Fig. ).

title: Beyond Successful Robot Demonstrations: Learning from Human Interactions and Modeling Failure Dynamics
authors: Peiyan Tu,Cong Wang,Hanxin Zhu,Xin Jin,Zhibo Chen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Action-conditioned world models offer a promising foundation for generalist robotic intelligence by predicting the consequences of actions.
However, existing robotic datasets provide limited coverage of the diverse interaction dynamics required for generalizable world modeling. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer complementary interaction experience, yet the embodiment gap between human hands and robotic manipulators hinders effective cross-embodiment learning. Meanwhile, the predominance of successful demonstrations leaves failure dynamics substantially underrepresented, limiting the ability of world models to anticipate unsuccessful executions.
To address these limitations, we introduce HF-WM, an action-conditioned world model that combines Human interaction learning with Failure-aware post-training. To bridge the embodiment gap, we develop a dual-branch framework that couples video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction, using stabilized pointflow as a unified motion representation across human and robot interactions while suppressing egocentric camera motion. To improve failure modeling, we further perform Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training on perturbed actions derived from successful demonstrations, guided by action alignment and physical plausibility rewards, enabling the model to learn plausible failure dynamics without paired ground-truth videos.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation and exhibits strong utility for policy evaluation in downstream robotic tasks.
introduction:
With the rapid advancement of video generation models (Wan et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2026), world models have witnessed significant breakthroughs and are increasingly regarded as a promising pathway toward generalist robotics (Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). In particular, action-conditioned world models take robot action sequences as input and model the resulting state transitions to predict future states (Zhu et al., 2025). This predictive capability supports scalable data generation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning in generated environments (Sun et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Tseng et al., 2026), thereby closing the loop between imagination, evaluation, and policy improvement. This paradigm has emerged as a key foundation for learning and improving robot action planning systems.

Despite these advances, action-conditioned world models still struggle to accurately capture interaction dynamics and execution outcomes, largely due to the limited scale and coverage of high-quality embodied data (Mei et al., 2026).
To alleviate this limitation, recent studies have turned to large scale egocentric human object interaction datasets (Gao et al., 2026; Wu and Gao, 2026), leveraging human demonstrations to enhance model performance. 1) However, a substantial domain gap persists between human and robotic manipulation, and egocentric recordings are often affected by camera jitter and unstable viewpoints, which can obscure interaction-relevant regions and hinder the learning of physically meaningful representations. Consequently, effectively exploiting human egocentric data for embodied world model learning remains an open challenge (Mei et al., 2026).
2) In addition, existing embodied datasets are heavily biased toward successful demonstrations, with limited coverage of failure cases and off-target interactions (Yang et al., 2026a). Yet world models for embodied scenarios require not only modeling successful trajectories, but also capturing failure dynamics and counterfactual outcomes induced by erroneous or suboptimal actions (Ma et al., 2026). In the absence of failure demonstrations, how to effectively synthesize failure scenarios to improve physical reasoning remains an important open problem.

title: RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors
authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal,Abdelwahed Khamis,Mohammad Ali Armin,Lars Petersson
abstract:
Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions.
Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed.
We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor’s alarms enable useful interventions.
By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost.
We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches.
Recoverability depends on the state–intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at τ=0.5\tau=0.5, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions.
On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost.
Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0–3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early.
These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly capable of executing diverse robotic manipulation tasks from visual observations and language instructions [1, 2].
Despite this progress, long-horizon execution remains vulnerable to compounding errors, environmental perturbations, and out-of-distribution conditions.
Runtime monitors therefore aim to detect impending or ongoing failures from policy representations, observations, or predictive world models so that execution can be stopped, recovered, replanned, or escalated [3, 4, 5, 6].
These monitors are commonly selected using discrimination, calibration, or timing-aware detection metrics.

However, predicting failure and deciding whether to intervene are different problems.
A monitor may accurately distinguish failed from successful executions while still providing a poor intervention rule: an alarm may arrive after useful recovery has disappeared, or a false alarm may interrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed.
Conversely, an imperfect predictor may still be useful if it alarms while an effective and inexpensive intervention remains available.
Related agent studies similarly show that better failure prediction or calibration need not improve outcomes under intervention [7, 8].
In robotics, this distinction is particularly important because interventions alter physical state and may incur reset, delay, or damage costs.

Timing-aware evaluation addresses part of this problem, but elapsed time alone is insufficient. VLA-FAIL [4] incorporates detection time into monitor evaluation, PREFAIL [9] identifies an actionable intervention window for lift-and-place failures, and CheckVLA [5] defines an intervention-relative irreversibility time by testing whether a fixed set of repairs can still restore success.
CheckVLA establishes that actionability depends on available repairs, but leaves open how intervention value changes across the trajectory and whether acting remains preferable once false alarms and intervention costs are included [5].
The same robot-policy state can therefore have different value under continuation, recovery, or stop-and-reset.

We introduce RESCUE (Recoverability Evaluation of Stopping Criteria Under Execution), a counterfactual framework for evaluating existing runtime monitors as intervention rules.
As illustrated in Fig. RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? 
Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors, RESCUE restores simulator and policy states at action-chunk boundaries and evaluates alternative interventions, estimating action-conditioned task success under a declared intervention repertoire 𝒜\mathcal{A}, execution model ξ\xi, and remaining task budget BB.
Evaluating these outcomes across the trajectory yields a recoverability horizon: the latest checkpoint at which the declared repertoire satisfies a specified recovery criterion.
The horizon therefore depends explicitly on the available interventions, execution model, and task budget.

Recoverability establishes what can still succeed, but not whether intervention is worthwhile. Stopping a failed execution can save time, whereas an unnecessary stop incurs a reset and another attempt.
RESCUE therefore evaluates interventions in a common cost-to-completion space incorporating failure prevalence, alarm timing, false alarms, and intervention cost.
For stop-and-reset, this yields a closed-form break-even false-alarm rate computable from ordinary execution logs, allowing a monitor’s realised operating point to be compared directly with never intervening.

We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus [10, 11], comprising 1,562 trunk episodes and 128,340 counterfactual branches.
At τ=0.5\tau=0.5, only 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, while 34 of 66 clear under continuation or scripted recovery.
Under stop-and-reset, even an idealised detector that identifies every failure immediately can afford only a 2.78–3.32% false-alarm rate under the evaluated cost model.
A steps-since-progress monitor tuned to a nominal 5% operating point instead costs +0.0835+0.0835 reset-equivalents per completed task relative to never intervening.
Across matched evaluation sets, conventional detection and timing metrics admit the real monitors in 61 of 75 verdicts, whereas decision value admits none of 15 against never intervening.
These results show that failure-prediction quality alone does not establish intervention value.
Our contributions are:

title: Reflect-VLA: Internalizing Reflective Guidance via Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation for Autonomous Driving
authors: Yuechen Luo,He Chong,Fang Li,Shaoqing Xu,Hexin Zhang,Ruiqi Zhang,Ziying Song,Lei Yang,Zhi-Xin Yang,Fuxi Wen
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) substantially improves planning performance in autonomous-driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar trajectory rewards that measure overall quality but fail to identify specific planning errors or provide actionable correction signals. In long-tail scenarios, errors in scene understanding, behavior selection, and trajectory execution are compressed into a single score. We observe that Reflective Guidance turns trajectory evaluation into explicit diagnoses and corrective instructions, substantially improving planning accuracy. Yet such guidance requires an initial prediction and its evaluation results, making it unavailable for direct single-pass inference. We propose Reflect-VLA, which treats Reflective Guidance as training-time privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD). Unlike scalar-reward optimization, Dual-OPSD uses the driving score only to route student-generated trajectories. It distills dense token-level corrective distributions from the teacher for risky trajectories while applying self-imitation to preserve reliable ones. To provide reliable corrective distributions on student rollouts, the teacher is progressively constructed through Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. At inference time, Reflect-VLA generates trajectories in a single pass without explicit guidance or iterative refinement. Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive demonstrate competitive planning performance while reducing training time by over 90% compared with RL.
introduction:
Autonomous driving is shifting from conventional modular pipelines toward end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems (Jiang et al. 2025b). Unlike modular systems (Hu et al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2024) that coordinate perception, prediction, and planning through handcrafted interfaces, VLA models integrate visual observations, language instructions and action generation within a unified architecture. Recent driving VLA methods commonly adopt a multi-stage training paradigm (Li et al. 2025c; Zhou et al. 2025b; Luo et al. 2025a; Luo et al. 2026b; Lu et al. 2026). They first acquire domain knowledge from large-scale driving question-answering data, then learn trajectory generation through supervised fine-tuning, and finally improve the policy using reinforcement learning or planning-oriented objectives.

Despite progress, VLA models struggle to learn from planning failures, especially in complex and long-tail scenarios. A scalar planning score can identify a poor trajectory but cannot reveal whether the error arises from scene understanding, behavior selection, or trajectory execution, nor indicate how to correct it. Trajectory-level rewards collapse these heterogeneous failure modes into a single value, leaving the model without a direction for improvement. ELF-VLA (Luo et al. 2026a) alleviates this problem by introducing structured failure information, showing that detailed feedback can guide the correction of failed trajectories. However, how to convert feedback-assisted correction into an intrinsic single-pass planning capability remains underexplored.

We begin with a key observation: Reflective Guidance provides substantial planning gains. As illustrated in Fig. 1, a VLA model may produce an incorrect trajectory during direct inference, yet generate a markedly better trajectory when provided with evaluation-derived diagnoses and corrective suggestions (Yang et al. 2026; He et al. 2026; Chen et al. 2026b). Constructing the guidance requires both an initial trajectory and its evaluation results, whereas an autonomous driving system must produce an executable plan before acting. The central challenge is therefore not to perform iterative refinement at inference time, but to transfer the planning preferences induced by Reflective Guidance into the model’s direct trajectory-generation policy.

To this end, we propose Reflect-VLA, a training framework that treats Reflective Guidance as privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD). Starting from the same VLA checkpoint, the model supplied with Reflective Guidance acts as the frozen teacher, while the model receiving standard inputs acts as the student. The student first generates trajectories from the input available at deployment. A planning score then routes each trajectory to one of two learning paths. For risky or suboptimal trajectories, the teacher provides dense token-level distributions that encode corrective planning preferences. For reliable trajectories, a self-imitation objective preserves the student’s existing decisions. The scalar score is therefore used only for trajectory-quality-aware routing, while the teacher distribution supplies the fine-grained supervision required for correction.

Effective self-distillation requires a teacher that can refine trajectories drawn from the student’s rollout distribution. We construct this teacher using a progressive strategy comprising Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. The first two stages establish driving knowledge, direct trajectory generation, and guidance-assisted refinement. The final stage exposes the teacher to student-generated failures and retains verified refinements, reducing the distribution gap between offline refinement data and on-policy trajectories. After Dual-OPSD, Reflect-VLA performs single-pass trajectory generation without Reflective Guidance, an online planning evaluator, or an iterative correction procedure.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We construct Reflective Guidance that converts trajectory evaluation results into structured, trajectory-specific diagnoses and corrective suggestions, and use it as privileged information available only during training.

We propose Dual-OPSD, a trajectory-quality-aware self-distillation method that transfers corrective distributions for risky trajectories while preserving reliable planning.

We develop a progressive teacher-construction strategy that combines driving-knowledge pretraining, planning-and-refinement supervision, and self-refinement rejection sampling to support stable guidance internalization and efficient single-pass planning.

1. We construct Reflective Guidance that converts trajectory evaluation results into structured, trajectory-specific diagnoses and corrective suggestions, and use it as privileged information available only during training.

2. We propose Dual-OPSD, a trajectory-quality-aware self-distillation method that transfers corrective distributions for risky trajectories while preserving reliable planning.

3. We develop a progressive teacher-construction strategy that combines driving-knowledge pretraining, planning-and-refinement supervision, and self-refinement rejection sampling to support stable guidance internalization and efficient single-pass planning.

title: ManeuverFlow: Maneuver Hypothesis Generation with Future Evidence for Trajectory Evaluation and Refinement in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
authors: Yuhao Wei,Yong Chen,Chen Yang,Yingchen Wang,Delin Ouyang,Lingfeng Qi,Qi Lan,Zhanhua Zhang,Jie Li,Guofa Li
abstract:
End-to-end planning in complex scenes must model diverse driving intentions and select the most appropriate trajectory using scene context and future risks.
However, multi-query regression may collapse to one mode, while anchor-based and generative planners share a scaling bottleneck: small candidate sets limit maneuver coverage or discovery of high-quality trajectories, whereas large sets increase generation and scoring costs.
We propose ManeuverFlow to generate trajectories for distinct intentions in one step and evaluate and refine them using current and future evidence.
The model selects relevant maneuver modes, draws corresponding noise from the Gaussian mixture prior, and maps it to intention-specific trajectories through a maneuver-routed mixture-of-experts MeanFlow field.
Current features and future features predicted by the world model are aggregated along each candidate path into trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-factor prediction.
Using the same evidence, the refiner predicts local Frenet residuals for selected candidates; refined and retained candidates are then jointly re-scored for selection.
With a lightweight TransFuser-style ResNet-34 backbone, ManeuverFlow achieves 90.6 PDMS and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v1/v2 navtest, respectively.
On WorldEngine’s recent 3DGS closed-loop benchmark, it attains the highest listed PDMS∗ scores of 75.19 and 74.58 under logged and IDM-controlled traffic, respectively.

introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving maps sensor observations, ego states, and navigation cues directly to future ego motion, unifying perception and planning under a single objective (Chitta et al. 2023; Hu et al. 2022b; Hu et al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2023; Jia et al. 2023; Sun et al. 2025). Complex traffic scenes often admit multiple plausible driving hypotheses, so a single trajectory cannot capture the underlying decision space. Multimodal motion forecasting represents this ambiguity with fixed anchor vocabularies or mode-specific queries (Chai et al. 2020; Shi et al. 2022); recent planners further use learned queries, trajectory anchors, and diffusion- or flow-based generators to produce candidates, then select a final plan through candidate–scene interactions (Jiang et al. 2026; Li et al. 2024b; Liao et al. 2025; Xing et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2026). As shown in Fig. 1(a), learned queries without explicit mode-level structure may concentrate in similar regions of trajectory space, producing redundant candidates and risking mode collapse.

Standard diffusion and ODE-based flow sampling is iterative (Lipman et al. 2023; Liu, Gong, and Liu 2023), although recent driving planners reduce the process to two steps in DiffusionDrive (Liao et al. 2025) or one step in GoalFlow and MeanFuser (Xing et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2026). MeanFuser generates multiple proposals in one MeanFlow step, but its Adaptive Reconstruction Module (ARM) attends to and fuses them into a single output trajectory; the initial hypotheses thus do not remain explicit candidates for downstream evaluation, refinement, and selection (Wang et al. 2026). Fixed anchors encode predefined modes but may allocate part of the candidate budget to modes weakly relevant to the current scene. For a frozen generator, Fig. 2 retrospectively shows that larger pools expose stronger candidates. This motivates improving candidate quality under a compact proposal budget through scene-adaptive hypothesis generation and evidence-conditioned local trajectory refinement.

Candidate generation also requires reliable selection. Candidate-tree and generation–evaluation planners pair ego hypotheses with conditional predictions or learned evaluators (Huang et al. 2024; Huang et al. 2025), whereas current-only scorers do not explicitly query predicted future scene states along candidate paths. WoTE provides such evidence through one future rollout per candidate (Fig. 1(b)), repeating future BEV prediction across candidate trajectories and multiple future time steps (Li et al. 2025b).

Together, these limitations define a fixed-budget hypothesis-lifecycle problem. We therefore ask: How can a planner generate scene-relevant, mode-distinct hypotheses under a fixed budget and use current/future evidence to evaluate, refine, and select them?

To this end, we propose ManeuverFlow, a unified Hypothesize–Verify–Improve framework that preserves explicit maneuver-indexed hypotheses, as shown in Figs. 1(c) and 3. The Maneuver Gaussian Mixture Prior (M-GMP) predicts scene-conditioned weights over motion-defined components, and M3F generates base hypotheses by maneuver-routed one-step transport. Once per planning step, the world model predicts one candidate-independent future BEV field; a learned trajectory-guided probe projects each hypothesis into the current and predicted fields to form path-specific Trajectory Evidence Memory. Metric Prism pre-scores candidates through learned PDM factors. The Evidence-Coupled Frenet Refiner (ECFR) uses the same evidence to predict local Frenet residuals for selected hypotheses. Refined hypotheses replace selected bases, re-query the shared field, and compete with retained hypotheses under the same Metric Prism scoring function.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Scene-adaptive maneuver generation. We introduce a maneuver-structured generator that combines M-GMP with the maneuver-routed M3F to model motion-defined maneuver components and generate scene-adaptive, intent-conditioned trajectory hypotheses as explicit alternatives in one step.

Future-evidence verification and refinement. A learned probe projects each candidate onto a shared future BEV field to extract trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-aligned scoring and ECFR’s local Frenet refinement. Metric Prism jointly re-scores refined and retained hypotheses for final selection.

With a lightweight ResNet-34 TransFuser (TF) perception backbone, ManeuverFlow-TF achieves 90.58 PDMS and 90.14 EPDMS on NAVSIM v1/v2 navtest, respectively. Its camera-only Latent TransFuser (LTF) variant further obtains 75.19 and 74.58 PDMS∗ under replayed and reactive traffic on WorldEngine, delivering the highest listed composite planning scores across all reported benchmark and traffic settings.

2. Future-evidence verification and refinement. A learned probe projects each candidate onto a shared future BEV field to extract trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-aligned scoring and ECFR’s local Frenet refinement. Metric Prism jointly re-scores refined and retained hypotheses for final selection.

title: Robot-WATCHDOG : failure detection through object-centric graph representation
authors: Quentin Rolland,Fabrice Mayran de Chamisso,Jean-Baptiste Mouret
abstract: Reliable real-time failure detection is critical for deploying learned robotic policies, yet defining failures explicitly is infeasible in open-world settings. This motivates failure detection from nominal demonstrations alone. Existing methods, however, struggle to balance robustness to benign variations with the ability to capture semantic and interaction-level errors. We introduce Robot-WATCHDOG, a self-supervised framework that models manipulation scenes as object-centric spatio-temporal graphs. Building on this representation, we investigate two complementary failure scores: Trajectory Projection and Correlation (TPC), a non-parametric measure of geometric deviation and relational consistency, and GnnT, a Graph Attention Network with a Transformer that predicts future object states. We evaluate both on a public benchmark and on a new dataset of semantically complex manipulation tasks, across six tasks and ten random seeds. Both scores outperform image-based failure detectors, particularly on semantic and interaction-level failures. TPC provides the strongest performance in AUPR and MCC on both dataset averages, with low variance across seeds. Qualitative results are made available at https://cea-list.github.io/Robot-WATCHDOG/.
introduction:
Learned robotic policies provide no guarantees beyond the distribution induced by training demonstrations [2]. Detecting deviations from expected behavior is therefore essential for accountable deployment, and increasingly emphasized in regulation for high-risk AI systems such as the EU AI Act [18, 37]. As imitation learning and vision-language-conditioned policies increasingly enable long-horizon, closed-loop manipulation [9, 42, 6, 24, 21, 30], policies are executed autonomously in real time and without step-by-step human intervention, motivating dedicated monitoring systems that operate online, require no failure examples, and can identify anomalous behavior before errors propagate.

Explicitly enumerating all possible failures, however, is infeasible in open-world robotic settings. The standard framing therefore casts failure detection as a one-class problem [41, 32, 33]: a monitor trained exclusively on nominal demonstrations must identify, at runtime, deviations from expected behavior. Existing approaches divide broadly into two families. Visual failure detectors [35, 15, 43, 32] flag deviations in raw image space or learned visual representations. They are sensitive to benign background changes, lighting shifts, and visual clutter, producing frequent false positives that erode operational efficiency. Kinematic and action-based monitors [27, 14, 38] instead operate on trajectory or joint-space signals; they are robust to visual noise but structurally blind to the environment. They only verify whether the movement itself is familiar, failing to detect if the robot is interacting with the wrong object or operating in an environment that mismatches training.

This division points to a broader limitation. A substantial class of failures in robotic manipulation does not arise from abnormal motion or corrupted observations, but from incorrect interactions between otherwise familiar objects: grasping the wrong item, violating task-order constraints, or placing an object in an incorrect spatial relation to others [23, 8]. These failures emerge naturally in manipulation tasks whose success depends on object identity, relative placement, and sequential consistency, yet they remain difficult to capture when monitoring is restricted to either image appearance or motion trajectories alone.

The central idea of this work is to recast robotic failure detection as monitoring the evolution of object interactions over time. Rather than treating visual and kinematic signals as separate modalities, we represent the scene as a spatio-temporal graph of interacting objects, where nodes encode object states and edges encode their pairwise spatial relationships throughout execution. This object-centric formulation generalizes prior monitoring approaches: visual detectors can be interpreted as operating on node appearance, while kinematic monitors correspond to tracking motion along trajectories. By jointly modeling objects, their relations, and their temporal evolution in a unified representation, the proposed framework captures both the signals targeted by prior work and the relational structure required to detect task-relevant interaction failures.

Failure detection then becomes a well-posed problem: deviations from reference relational dynamics constitute anomalies. We instantiate this principle in Robot-WATCHDOG, a self-supervised framework that abstracts a manipulation episode into an object-centric spatio-temporal graph and scores each timestep against expert demonstrations. Within this representation we study two scoring functions. TPC (Trajectory Projection and Correlation) is non-parametric: it measures orthogonal projection distances to expert trajectories together with deviations in the pairwise correlation structure between objects. GnnT couples a Graph Attention Network with a Transformer encoder to predict future object dynamics from a sliding observation window, and flags prediction errors. Both are converted into binary decisions by conformal prediction calibrated on held-out expert demonstrations, which sets the decision threshold from a user-specified level without tuning the threshold on failure examples.

We evaluate Robot-WATCHDOG on four tasks of the public BotFails benchmark [32] and on a newly introduced dataset featuring two relationally challenging manipulation tasks: structured table setting and waste sorting on a moving conveyor belt. All results are averaged over ten seeds, each redrawing the expert partition and the network initialisation. Both object-centric scores outperform image-based detectors, and TPC is consistently the stronger of the two: averaged per dataset it reaches AUPR 0.81 and maximum MCC 0.75 (BotFails) and 0.81 / 0.72 (Watchdog), against 0.62 / 0.49 and 0.65 / 0.63 for GnnT, while the best baseline reaches only 0.44 / 0.32 and 0.35 / 0.34. After conformal calibration, TPC attains MCC 0.68 and 0.64 where the strongest baseline reaches 0.22 and 0.33. The learned score only leads in the continuously dynamic conveyor scene. Methods that perform well on simple kinematic deviations struggle with relational failures involving object identity and spatial arrangement, the very setting Robot-WATCHDOG addresses.

Our main contributions are: (i) identifying relational anomalies as a key yet underexplored failure mode in robotic manipulation, arising from dependencies on object identity, spatial arrangement, and temporal consistency; (ii) introducing two scoring functions: TPC (Trajectory Projection and Correlation) a non-parametric, geometric method and GnnT, a spatio-temporal graph formulation ; and (iii) releasing a benchmark of relationally challenging manipulation tasks with annotated relational failures.

title: EndoRSI: Physical-Evidence-Driven Recursive Improvement of Endoscopic Robot Policies
authors: Chi Kit Ng,Yidong Zhang,Tianchun Wu,Siu Hing Lui,Hanlin Zhao,Huxin Gao,Hongliang Ren
abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best-performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot-policy research.

title: PartiGen: Part-Aware Representations for Language-Conditioned Humanoid Motion Generation
authors: Chuxuan Huang,Zhanxiang Cao,Tianyue Zhan,Haoyang Li,Yang Zhang,Liyun Yan,Chenlin Ming,Keqi Zhu,Yizhi Chen,Shengcheng Fu,Zihao Zhou,Xinyi Peng,Kaixuan Zhang,Boyang Xing,Jiawei Bao,Yang Yang,Yue Gao
abstract: Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation. Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively. Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points. In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.
introduction:
Natural language offers an intuitive interface for specifying whole-body humanoid behaviors. Text-to-motion generation (Guo et al., 2022a; Tevet et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024) supports their synthesis, but visually plausible motion may violate robot joint limits, dynamics, actuator capabilities, or contact constraints. We study a system in which a language-conditioned generator specifies a whole-body reference and its temporal extent, while a tracking controller uses robot-state feedback to produce joint-level control targets. The challenge is to generate references that express the requested behavior while accounting for the robot’s motion constraints and the task’s temporal organization.

An instruction such as “walk while waving” illustrates the challenge: the arm gesture and locomotion must coexist within a single robot trajectory, with consistent root motion, joint configurations, and timing. A reference generator therefore needs to preserve the distinct roles of body parts while representing their relationships within a shared whole-body context. Part-aware modeling (Zhong et al., 2023) and physics-guided generation (Yuan et al., 2023) provide relevant foundations for addressing these requirements. We investigate how an anatomical prior can guide local feature processing within a shared robot-motion representation, together with kinematic supervision of the resulting trajectory. Its temporal extent must also reflect the instruction, with an endpoint that need not coincide with the boundary of a fixed-length motion primitive. These considerations connect body-part structure, kinematic consistency, and endpoint selection within the same robot reference-generation problem.

We propose PartiGen, integrating language-conditioned humanoid motion generation and execution. Part-aware attention builds a shared whole-body representation from anatomically masked inputs. Text- and history-conditioned latent diffusion generates motion primitives under forward-kinematics supervision, followed by frame-level endpoint selection on the complete candidate trajectory. A pretrained, frozen GRIT controller (mrzuang, 2026) tracks the references using robot-state feedback in MuJoCo and on the Unitree G1.

Our contributions are:

An anatomical input-grouping mechanism for robot motion representation learning. Fixed masks select joint-angle channels before independent Q/K/V projections, while shared motion features and a single whole-body latent retain access to global context.

A language-conditioned motion generation framework with frame-level endpoint prediction. Conditioned on text and motion history, the framework autoregressively generates motion primitives in the shared latent space under forward-kinematics supervision. A learned end-of-sequence predictor then selects an endpoint within the complete candidate trajectory.

Simulation and real-world validation. Integrated with a frozen GRIT controller, PartiGen achieves an 81.8% posture-screen pass rate over 500 simulated references. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 motions attempted on a physical Unitree G1 are judged successful by the authors.

title: Evo-RL: Iterative Robot Reinforcement Learning from Selective Experience
authors: Kai Ye,Yifan Jin,Qianhang Luo,Hongru Zhang,Jiedong Zhang,Shuyuan Hu,Song-Yuan Wu,Jihai Xu,Jie Zhao,Bo Zhao
abstract: Existing real-world reinforcement learning methods improve robot policies by combining human corrections with autonomous rollouts. However, accumulated experience varies in its value for policy improvement, and even successful trajectories can contain inefficient or redundant behavior, motivating more selective experience reuse. To this end, we propose Evo-RL, an iterative reinforcement learning method that combines human interventions with advantage-guided experience selection. Evo-RL uses human corrections and experience with positive estimated advantages from successful trajectories to iteratively refine the policy. To support learning from these different experience sources, we introduce RW-RL-Dataset, which spans over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments. On a real-world high-precision manipulation task, Evo-RL improves attempt success rate over RECAP by 30.46%. Our code, model checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions by conditioning on visual observations and language instructions [1]. Recent advances have extended their applicability to a wider range of tasks and robot embodiments [2, 3, 4] and improved deployment efficiency [5]. Yet policies trained on demonstrations can still encounter unfamiliar states during deployment, where errors can accumulate and recovery may be difficult [6]. These limitations motivate continued policy improvement using experience collected during execution.

Existing approaches support this improvement through human corrections and reinforcement learning. Human interventions supply corrective behavior at states visited by the deployed policy [7, 8], while autonomous rollouts provide feedback beyond the initial demonstrations. RECAP [9] combines demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and human interventions, using value-estimated advantages to condition policy training and iteratively update the policy with deployment data.

The value of accumulated experience for policy improvement varies across and within trajectories. Even successful trajectories may contain hesitation, repeated attempts, or other inefficient behavior, so the contribution of experience to policy improvement must be assessed at a finer level. Human corrections target deployment difficulties, but policy actions in the same trajectories may include behavior that prompted the intervention. These observations motivate Evo-RL’s selective update procedure: estimated advantages guide the selection of experience for policy updates, while only human-controlled portions of successful intervention trajectories are retained for corrective fine-tuning.

We propose Evo-RL, an iterative real-world reinforcement learning method that combines human corrections with advantage-guided experience selection. Starting from a demonstration-trained policy, Evo-RL collects human interventions and autonomous rollouts during deployment. It trains a value model on demonstrations, intervention data, and autonomous experience, using rewards that account for execution time and human takeovers, and then estimates advantages to guide experience selection. For policy fine-tuning, Evo-RL retains only the human-controlled portions of successful intervention trajectories, keeps the original demonstrations, and adds selected positive-advantage experience from demonstrations and successful autonomous rollouts. RECAP trains the policy on accumulated experience with a binary advantage label as an additional input. Evo-RL instead uses estimated advantages to select experience for policy updates and increase the sampling weight of selected experience. The updated policy is then redeployed for the next iteration.

To advance the real-world RL research, we further introduce RW-RL-Dataset which organizes demonstrations, human interventions, and autonomous experience with action-source metadata and semantic annotations. It spans over 1,000 hours across four diverse robot embodiments and includes the task-specific training experience used in our experiments.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose Evo-RL, an iterative method that combines corrective supervision with selective reuse of experience guided by positive estimated advantages. Under our evaluation protocol, first-round Evo-RL achieves an attempt success rate (ASR) 30.46% higher than RECAP on a real-world manipulation task requiring high-precision alignment.

We present RW-RL-Dataset, a collection of over 1,000 hours of real-world data from four robot embodiments, pairing synchronized camera observations with robot states and actions. Its annotations specify task instructions and scene context, execution quality and error counts, subtask intervals, and whether each frame records human or policy control.

Under our evaluation protocol, first-round Evo-RL achieves an attempt success rate (ASR) 30.46% higher than RECAP on a real-world manipulation task requiring high-precision alignment.

Its annotations specify task instructions and scene context, execution quality and error counts, subtask intervals, and whether each frame records human or policy control.

title: Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies
authors: Yang Wang,Ping Liu,Ruiyu Wang,Xuhua Chen,Lingfeng Zhang,Tao Zhang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Evaluated on 16 RoboMME tasks and 4 real-world robotic manipulation tasks
abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.
introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation can produce perceptually similar observations that require different actions, depending on prior execution or earlier visual evidence. Repeated actions require execution-stage information, whereas occlusion and target reidentification require distinguishing visual detail that may no longer be observable. These requirements motivate separate representations for evolving execution context and accessible historical evidence (Fig. Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies).

Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and instructions to robot actions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Large-scale robot data, action chunking, and generative action models broaden their capabilities [6, 7, 8, 9]. However, they do not determine which episodic information a policy should retain. Recent memory-augmented policies preserve perceptual observations, cognitive summaries, or representations at several temporal scales [10, 11, 12]. Which historical information should be compressed, and which should remain directly accessible?

Recurrent compression summarizes execution history, but a compact state need not preserve detail for later target identification. Storing historical features preserves access, but uniform sampling may miss brief evidence, and spatial pooling may discard distinguishing detail. We therefore distinguish execution context, frame relevance, and within-frame detail.

Our design combines recurrent temporal memory with selected spatial evidence (Fig. 2). We make three contributions:

We introduce a task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet (GDN) compressor supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. These objectives encourage execution context and reconstructable visual history in one temporal token.

We formulate task-conditioned evidence access as threshold retrieval with shared temporal and spatial supervision. The retained-frame count adapts to the available evidence.

We introduce linear multi-scale fusion to combine coarse context and fine spatial detail within sixteen tokens per retained frame.

title: Beyond Actions: Learning Future Operation Targets for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Min Lin,Bokai Zhou,Jianqi Lin,Kaiyuan Yang,Yicheng Chang,Junjie Yu,Xiaofan Liu,Jianhua Han,Rui Li,Shen Zhao,Xiaodan Liang
abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action–Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy’s primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves 50.97%50.97\% overall success, improving over π0.5\pi_{0.5} and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made substantial progress toward generalist robot control by mapping images, language, and robot state to continuous actions (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025). Yet the target used to train this mapping usually describes what the robot commanded, not what the command changed. An action sequence specifies motor behavior, but leaves its effects on the robot and environment implicit. In dexterous manipulation, this gap matters: contact, hand configuration, and object pose can turn similar commands into different outcomes, while different motions can achieve the same task-relevant change. The challenge is to make physical progress part of the policy’s prediction target without sacrificing the detail needed to execute an action.

Predicting the future offers one way to expose such progress. World and world-action models use future observations or latent dynamics to support control (Wu et al., 2024; Cen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). However, a complete visual future contains changes due to appearance, occlusion, and camera motion that need not determine the next control command. Conversely, a scene change alone may leave out the contact timing, finger coordination, and robot motion required to produce it. Latent-action and future-informed visuomotor methods provide more compact targets (Ye et al., 2024; Bu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026b), but compactness alone does not resolve whether a target is both predictable from the current observation and sufficient for precise action decoding.

We therefore seek a target that connects three requirements: it must be predictable before acting, retain task-relevant information about the resulting physical transition, and support recovery of executable continuous actions. We introduce AFCE (Action–Future Coupled Effect Learning), which learns a temporal Effect from synchronized demonstrations of executed actions, realized robot-state changes, and sparse world changes. Rather than specifying the Effect through hand-designed semantic labels, we let these sources interact and constrain a shared representation through joint reconstruction. The action objective retains control detail, while the robot-response and world-change objectives ground that detail in observed consequences.

Figure 1 illustrates the resulting training interface. An offline tokenizer constructs Effect targets from recorded trajectories, where future evidence is available. The VLA then learns to predict these targets using only the current images, language instruction, and robot state. At deployment, a decoder maps the predicted Effect and current state to an action chunk. Thus, future observations shape the supervision without becoming inputs to the deployed policy.

The central test of this interface is whether the Effect remains useful after prediction. Accurate reconstruction from a ground-truth Effect does not ensure that the VLA can predict that Effect, nor that decoded actions succeed under closed-loop control. We evaluate these questions separately: reconstruction tests what the representation retains; ground-truth-Effect replay tests whether it supports execution; and predicted-Effect rollout tests the complete policy against direct action supervision under the same evaluation protocol. In mixed single- and dual-arm training, AFCE improves aggregate task success, particularly on dual-arm tasks, while some fine-control tasks remain challenging.

Our contributions are:

We formulate VLA target learning around three coupled requirements: predictability from current observations, information about task-relevant future changes, and continuous-action executability.

We introduce AFCE, a temporal Effect learned by jointly reconstructing executed actions, realized robot response, and sparse world change from a shared representation.

We evaluate the representation and the complete policy through reconstruction, ground-truth-Effect replay, and predicted-Effect closed-loop control, showing aggregate gains under mixed single- and dual-arm training while identifying remaining fine-control limitations.

1. We formulate VLA target learning around three coupled requirements: predictability from current observations, information about task-relevant future changes, and continuous-action executability.

2. We introduce AFCE, a temporal Effect learned by jointly reconstructing executed actions, realized robot response, and sparse world change from a shared representation.

3. We evaluate the representation and the complete policy through reconstruction, ground-truth-Effect replay, and predicted-Effect closed-loop control, showing aggregate gains under mixed single- and dual-arm training while identifying remaining fine-control limitations.

title: PATACON: GPU-Parallel Tangent-Bundle RRT-Connect for Constrained Motion Planning
authors: Gahyun Oh,Junho An,Suhyun Jeon,Suhan Park
abstract: Fast whole-body motion planning enables continuous replanning for humanoid robots in dynamic environments while satisfying collision avoidance and kinematic constraints. However, constrained motion planning incurs substantial computational cost due to repeated constraint projection in addition to collision checking and nearest-neighbor search. Recently, GPU-based massively parallel planners have been proposed to reduce computational cost. Nevertheless, these planners still steer in the ambient configuration space, so projecting candidates that deviate from the manifold remains a significant source of overhead, particularly in highly constrained, high-dimensional problems. In this work, we introduce PATACON, a GPU-parallel bidirectional planner that explores tangent space to exploit the local manifold geometry induced by known constraint functions. Experiments on dual-arm closed-chain and humanoid whole-body constrained planning tasks show that PATACON outperforms the prior work as configuration-space dimension and constraint codimension grow, achieving up to an 11.25 times speedup. These results suggest that GPU-parallel tangent-space exploration brings constrained whole-body motion planning closer to real-time performance.
introduction:
Dual-arm closed-chain and humanoid whole-body motion require maintaining task-dependent kinematic relationships while satisfying joint limits and avoiding collisions. These kinematic requirements can be formulated as nonlinear equality constraints, which define a lower-dimensional constraint manifold embedded in a high-dimensional configuration space [1]. In sampling-based motion planning, collision checking and nearest-neighbor queries are generally major sources of computational cost[2, 3]. Planning on a constraint manifold introduces additional overhead because constraint projection is performed repeatedly throughout tree expansion. Reducing this computational burden is particularly important in scenarios that require repeated replanning as the target, obstacles, or task conditions change, where low planning latency is essential for responsive execution.

A widely used approach generates candidate motions in the ambient configuration space and projects them onto the manifold as the tree grows [1]. cpRRTC [4] brought this approach to the GPU by assigning each thread block to steer from the nearest node toward a random sample, project the waypoints of the resulting straight-line segment in parallel, and perform collision checks with early termination. This reduces constrained planning to milliseconds, but the exploration scheme is unchanged; each extension still steers in the ambient space and relies on projection to satisfy the constraints.

Ambient-space steering, however, ignores the shape of the manifold. Kim et al. [5] showed that a target sampled in the ambient space can contribute little progress along the manifold once projected, and that the resulting large number of projections degrades both computational efficiency and the Voronoi bias of RRT. Because the constraint Jacobian provides the tangent space at any configuration, displacements can instead be restricted to it: Stilman [6] observed that tangent displacements are more likely to remain within the constraint tolerance, and TB-RRT [5] grows trees on tangent spaces bounded by the local curvature, outperforming projection-based planners with larger gains on more complex problems. However, TB-RRT expands one node at a time, incurs additional preprocessing and bookkeeping for its tangent spaces, and relies on lazy projection. Therefore, the feasibility checked on tangent spaces must be re-evaluated after projection.

We propose PATACON (PArallel TAngent-bundle RRT-CONnect), a GPU-parallel bi-directional planner that brings tangent-space-guided exploration to massively parallel tree expansion, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
Unlike TB-RRT, PATACON projects and validates every candidate before tree insertion, so every node is feasible. Its efficiency has two sources: tangent-space candidates are more likely to remain within the constraint tolerance [6] and avoid ambient targets whose projections make little progress along the manifold [5], and a single sample and nearest-neighbor query yield multiple candidate edges that are validated concurrently on the GPU, which amortizes the preprocessing and bookkeeping of tangent spaces over multiple edges.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Tangent-space-guided GPU-parallel extension. PATACON replaces the ambient-space steering of existing GPU-parallel planners with extension along local tangent spaces, so that candidates follow the manifold geometry before projection.

Tangent-space-guided GPU-parallel extension. PATACON replaces the ambient-space steering of existing GPU-parallel planners with extension along local tangent spaces, so that candidates follow the manifold geometry before projection.

Shared tangent-space banks. Tangent spaces are maintained
in tree-specific banks shared across thread blocks, together with the
correspondence between projected manifold states and their tangent-space
coordinates, so that multiple blocks can explore different regions of the
manifold concurrently.

Speculative multi-edge expansion. From one sample and one nearest-neighbor query, PATACON generates consecutive candidate edges along a tangent direction, validates them concurrently, and inserts the longest valid prefix, unlike the step-by-step CONNECT heuristic of RRT-Connect [7].

We evaluate PATACON on eight benchmarks ranging from 7-DoF manipulation to 35-DoF humanoid whole-body planning. Although cpRRTC is faster on low-dimensional problems, PATACON shows increasing advantages with configuration-space dimension and constraint restrictiveness, reaching a 11.25×11.25\times speedup with a 100% success rate.

title: Prediction-Informed Landing Window Planning for UAV Landing on USV in High Sea States
authors: Kaizhen Li,Xi Zhou,Dan Zhang,Xiaowei Li
abstract: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on unmanned surface vehicle (USV) is difficult in high sea states. Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments.
introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and unmanned surface vehicle (USV) are increasingly used as a complementary robotic team in search and rescue, offshore inspection, environmental monitoring, and maritime surveillance. UAV provide rapid aerial observation and wide-area coverage, whereas USV provide endurance and direct access to the water surface. Reliable autonomous landing is therefore essential for sustained UAV-USV operation because it enables UAV recovery, recharging, and redeployment without continuous human intervention.

Landing a UAV on a moving USV is particularly challenging in high sea states [1]. Wave-induced heave, roll, and pitch continuously change the relative pose and velocity between the vehicle and the deck. During the final descent, USV attitude can vary substantially within the time required for the UAV to reach the deck, so a touchdown condition that is safe at the current instant may become unfavorable before contact. Wind, sensing uncertainty, and control delay further reduce the available touchdown margin. The landing problem therefore involves not only stabilizing the vehicle and tracking the USV, but also choosing a touchdown time that is consistent with the future motion of the deck.

This temporal decision becomes more difficult as sea conditions become more dynamic. A controller that reacts only to the current USV attitude may begin to descend when the platform is temporarily favorable but fail to anticipate the rapid closure of the corresponding landing window. Conversely, an overly conservative controller may miss short favorable intervals and increase the recovery time. These observations motivate a landing architecture that preserves reliable low-level flight control while providing the high-level decision layer with explicit information about future platform attitude.

In this paper, we develop a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework for UAV landing on USV in high sea states. A pretrained temporal model forecasts the short-term evolution of USV attitude, and the predicted attitude is used to evaluate feasible touchdown windows and guide the high-level landing decision. A conventional low-level flight controller remains responsible for vehicle stabilization and motion tracking. The framework is evaluated in a real-to-simulation setting, where USV-motion data collected under real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo landing platform.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

A prediction-informed hierarchical landing framework is developed by coupling explicit platform-attitude forecasting with high-level landing-window planning and conventional low-level flight control.

A pretrained temporal prediction model is introduced to provide future attitude information for touchdown-window assessment under rapidly varying sea states.

A real-to-simulation validation setup is established by replaying platform-motion data collected in real sea conditions on a MuJoCo platform, enabling evaluation under realistic disturbance patterns.

1. A prediction-informed hierarchical landing framework is developed by coupling explicit platform-attitude forecasting with high-level landing-window planning and conventional low-level flight control.

2. A pretrained temporal prediction model is introduced to provide future attitude information for touchdown-window assessment under rapidly varying sea states.

3. A real-to-simulation validation setup is established by replaying platform-motion data collected in real sea conditions on a MuJoCo platform, enabling evaluation under realistic disturbance patterns.
