title: Grounded-Dreamer: Robot Learning from World Model Synthetic Data with Physical Grounding
authors: Feng Jiang,Shu Chen,Yuanfei Wang,Yuan Li,Zhenhao Shen,Jiaqi Liang,Yang Chen,Lei Wei,Chen Xie,Ruihai Wu
abstract:
Scaling robot manipulation policies requires large amounts of diverse, action-labeled data, yet collecting such data in the real world remains expensive and difficult to scale.
Existing methods either depend on human teleoperation, rely on simulation with limited visual realism, or use human videos that lack embodiment-specific annotations.
In this paper, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework for synthesizing physically grounded robot manipulation data with video world models while avoiding human teleoperation demonstrations.
Grounded-Dreamer combines the visual realism of generative video models with simulator physics engines.
Starting from a small set of real images depicting robot task initial states, our method automatically reconstructs task-relevant objects and camera geometry, aligns them in simulation, and collects physically valid trajectories.
These trajectories are used to post-train both a video world model and an inverse dynamics model, enabling the generation of visually realistic robot manipulation videos and corresponding robot actions from real images.
To filter physically implausible rollouts, Grounded-Dreamer replays generated trajectories in the reconstructed simulation and retains only those that successfully complete the tasks.
The real-world robot policies are trained solely on the grounded synthetic trajectories without any human demonstrations.
Empirical results in real-world tasks demonstrate that Grounded-Dreamer can synthesize physically grounded data and substantially facilitate policy learning without requiring human teleoperation effort.
introduction:
Building general-purpose robot policies capable of performing diverse manipulation tasks across varied environments requires large-scale, high-quality data. However, robot data is difficult to scale, and existing sources present a challenging trade-off between quality and quantity. Real-world teleoperation provides high-fidelity demonstrations but is limited by intensive human labor. While UMI data collection (Chi et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025) improves efficiency, there remains a need for manual operations. Conversely, simulation data offers inexpensive, action-labeled trajectories but is hindered by the sim-to-real visual gap. Human-centric videos are abundant and diverse, yet they lack the robot action annotations essential for direct policy training. Consequently, the field remains trapped between costly manual collection and the limitations of imperfect proxy data.

This dilemma motivates the pursuit of scalable robot data synthesis. Prior efforts such as DemoGen (Xue et al., 2025) and MimicGen (Mandlekar et al., 2023) have attempted to augment existing datasets by diversifying robot demonstrations; however, these methods still rely on human-collected trajectories as initial seeds. Other approaches, including RoboGen (Wang et al., 2024b) and GenSim (Wang et al., 2024a; Hua et al., 2025), leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) and simulators to automate task generation and trajectory collection. While these frameworks significantly reduce human intervention, the resulting data remains confined to simulation, leaving the visual sim-to-real discrepancy unresolved.

Generative video world models offer a potential alternative. Trained on internet-scale data, these models capture rich visual and world dynamics priors, enabling the generation of manipulation rollouts. When paired with an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM), such videos can be converted into action-labeled trajectories. However, pretrained models like Cosmos (NVIDIA et al., 2025) are primarily trained on human-centric videos. Directly applying them to robotic tasks often results in "hallucinated" physics, such as inconsistent object motions or non-physical contacts.

In this work, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework that synthesizes high-fidelity robot manipulation data without a single human teleoperation demonstration. Our core insight is to link the visual realism of generative world models with the grounding of physics simulators. We first build an automatic real-to-sim pipeline that calibrates camera poses, reconstructs task-relevant objects, and aligns them with the scene. Within this reconstructed simulator, we automatically collect diverse trajectories by leveraging the simulator’s ground-truth states. These grounded trajectories serve as the foundation for post-training both the video world model and the IDM.

During data synthesis, the post-trained world model generates visually realistic manipulation videos from real-world initial images, while the IDM extracts the corresponding robot actions. To guarantee physical validity, we implement a closed-loop verification step: replaying the inferred trajectories within the reconstructed simulation. This process filters out physically inconsistent generations, ensuring that only successful, grounded trajectories are used for further policy training.

We evaluate Grounded-Dreamer across seven diverse real-world manipulation tasks, spanning short-to-long horizon sequences and sophisticated tool use. Our empirical results demonstrate that policies trained exclusively on grounded synthetic data achieve performance competitive with those trained on real-world human demonstrations. Furthermore, owing to the inherent visual diversity and our targeted augmentation strategies, Grounded-Dreamer significantly outperforms real-data policies in out-of-distribution scenarios, showcasing robust zero-shot generalization across novel scenarios.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose Grounded-Dreamer, a data synthesis framework that eliminates the need for human demonstrations by linking video world models with simulator physics engines.

We introduce an automated real-to-sim reconstruction and collection pipeline, enabling data synthesis that maintains both high visual fidelity and strict physical grounding.

We demonstrate through extensive real-world experiments that our grounded synthetic data effectively facilitates policy learning, achieving robust performance across diverse scenarios through purely autonomous data generation.

1. We propose Grounded-Dreamer, a data synthesis framework that eliminates the need for human demonstrations by linking video world models with simulator physics engines.

2. We introduce an automated real-to-sim reconstruction and collection pipeline, enabling data synthesis that maintains both high visual fidelity and strict physical grounding.

3. We demonstrate through extensive real-world experiments that our grounded synthetic data effectively facilitates policy learning, achieving robust performance across diverse scenarios through purely autonomous data generation.

title: Low-Latency Mapless ESDF Queries for MAV Reactive Collision Avoidance
authors: Leonard Freißmuth,Cedric Le Gentil,Helen Oleynikova,Stefan Leutenegger
abstract:
Reactive collision avoidance in unknown, cluttered environments must perceive obstacles and correct motion within milliseconds.
Existing methods rely on maps for high-rate collision queries, but their acceleration structures require pre-processing.
That cost is amortized in long-horizon planning, where a map serves millions of queries; reactive planning, however, is a near-field, short-horizon problem with potentially only hundreds of queries per measurement, where building a map may not pay off.
We propose a mapless, Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)-accelerated Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) query with negligible pre-processing that operates directly on posed depth images, with resolution set by pooling the image rather than by a voxel size.
On an embedded GPU it is simultaneously more accurate and lower in total latency than every voxel-grid configuration we measured between 2 cm and 20 cm2\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}20\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}, at one to two orders of magnitude less memory at matched resolution.
With our query integrated into a Model Predictive Controller (MPC), simulated runs in laser-scanned forests at up to 9 m/s9\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} collide in 0.4 %0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} through dense branches, against 5.9 %5.9\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} with the best voxel grid and 5.5 %5.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} with the best mapless baseline at our resolution, whose failures we attribute to voxel resolution and total latency respectively.
We deploy the system onboard at two forest sites and fly at commanded speeds of up to 4 m/s4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s}.
introduction:
For fast Micro Air Vehicle (MAV) flight in cluttered environments, reactive collision avoidance may require obstacle perception and motion correction within milliseconds.
The local planner must therefore rely on the latest sensor data for fine, near-field obstacles such as branches emerging from the occlusion of nearer geometry.
Standard approaches integrate sensor measurements into a map—such as occupancy grids [1, 2] or distance fields [3, 4]—and query that map for collision.
For a reactive safety layer, the relevant quantity is the total latency from a new depth measurement to a collision answer.
It comprises two terms: the pre-processing required to build or update the map, including any acceleration structure over it, and the query time itself, which grows with the number of queries.
A map trades constant pre-processing cost for lower per-query cost, which pays off in long-horizon planning where a measurement may be reused for millions of queries.
Reactive planning, however, is a near-field, short-horizon problem: the controller queries only its immediate neighborhood, on the order of 10210^{2} times per sensor update.
In this regime the pre-processing term, rather than the per-query term, dominates total latency, which raises the question whether a map pays off at all.

Voxel maps are a common choice for such local planning, but their fixed voxel size has to be traded off twice.
A depth camera resolves finely nearby and coarsely far away, so a fixed voxel size under-represents the near field or over-represents the far field, and finer voxels cost more compute and memory.
Prior mapless methods avoid these tradeoffs by retaining posed depth images, querying each frame through a per-frame KD-tree [5, 6] or an occlusion-aware pyramid [7].
We instead evaluate depth pixels directly in parallel on the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU), with local depth minima and maxima for pruning as the only pre-processing.
The resulting sensor-space Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) (Fig. 1) keeps the sensor’s range-dependent resolution, controlled by pooling, returns distances and gradients, handles unknown space optimistically or conservatively, and carries a covariance-based pose-uncertainty margin.
On a Jetson Orin NX it answers the 400400 queries of our reactive planner in 6.2 ms6.2\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} at full resolution, one to two orders of magnitude below KD-tree and mesh baselines, and at that setting both more accurate and lower in total latency than every voxel grid we measured, at the least memory at matched resolution (Sec. IV-B).
In closed-loop simulation through laser-scanned forests at up to 9 m/s9\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s}, runs of a Model Predictive Controller (MPC) are safer with our query than with voxel grids, which fail through resolution, or with KD-trees or meshes, which fail through total latency (Sec. IV-C).
We deploy the system in ten forest flights at commanded speeds of up to 4 m/s4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s}.

Our contributions are:

A parallel sensor-space distance query algorithm that fuses posed depth views, with pooling-controlled resolution and conservative or optimistic handling of unknown space, benchmarked on an embedded GPU for total latency, accuracy, and memory.

A covariance-based uncertainty margin that inflates obstacles by the odometry uncertainty.

A closed-loop evaluation comparing voxel-grid, KD-tree, mesh, and our representation in laser-scanned forests behind one MPC on the embedded platform, separating the effects of total latency and resolution, and a demonstration of the running system in ten real-world forest flights at commanded speeds of up to 4 m/s4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s}.

1. A parallel sensor-space distance query algorithm that fuses posed depth views, with pooling-controlled resolution and conservative or optimistic handling of unknown space, benchmarked on an embedded GPU for total latency, accuracy, and memory.

2. A covariance-based uncertainty margin that inflates obstacles by the odometry uncertainty.

3. A closed-loop evaluation comparing voxel-grid, KD-tree, mesh, and our representation in laser-scanned forests behind one MPC on the embedded platform, separating the effects of total latency and resolution, and a demonstration of the running system in ten real-world forest flights at commanded speeds of up to 4 m/s4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s}.

title: Human2Dex: Dexterous Robot Learning from Wrist-Centric Human Demonstrations
authors: Jiachen Zhang,Yuanyuan Li,Shaqi Luo
abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/.
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation policies require demonstrations that jointly capture arm motion, high-DoF hand configuration, and contact-rich task progress. Acquiring such demonstrations separately for each target hand is costly and difficult to scale. Many existing systems make data collection more compatible with robot deployment through instrumented motion capture, robot-like interfaces, or wearable hardware [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. These interfaces can reduce the correspondence burden during transfer, but they often establish robot compatibility partly through the acquisition setup, control interface, or embodiment-aware mapping. When the target embodiment changes, the corresponding conversion or embodiment-specific setup must still be established for the new hand. This motivates a higher-level question: how can a reusable human demonstration interface convert the same human manipulation episodes into executable training data for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot?

We study this question from a wrist-centric perspective. Head-mounted egocentric video provides scalable human data and broad scene context [7, 8, 9, 10, 11], whereas a wrist-mounted camera provides local hand–object observations that more closely correspond to the eye-in-hand views used for close-range dexterous control. This similarity in observation arrangement makes wrist-centric acquisition a natural starting point for demonstration reuse. However, matching the observation arrangement does not by itself establish correspondence between human and robot data. The two settings can still differ in hand appearance, articulated structure, kinematics, command spaces, and grasp-related geometry.

Even under wrist-to-eye-in-hand alignment, three linked mismatches remain. First, human and robot hands differ in appearance and articulated structure, so the same visual content does not automatically provide the same structural semantics. Prior work has addressed this issue through appearance adaptation, robot-hand rendering, and structured hand representations [12, 4, 13, 14]. Second, human motion is not itself an executable command for a target hand: Linker O6 and Wuji have different kinematic structures, degrees of freedom, joint limits, and native action spaces. Human-to-robot retargeting and embodiment-aware motion mapping therefore remain necessary for constructing target-specific supervision [1, 13, 15, 16]. Third, even after observation semantics are aligned and executable supervision is constructed, a policy must infer how the task object is positioned relative to the hand’s current grasp configuration. Image-centered object coordinates indicate where an object appears, but do not directly express its relation to the closing hand. Existing work has explored hand–object and functional grasp representations for grasp synthesis, contact modeling, and perception [17, 18, 9, 19, 20]. Thus, structural correspondence supports observation interpretation, executable supervision supports target-hand policy learning, and an explicit object–hand relation can provide a more direct interaction cue, particularly when grasp alignment matters.

We present Human2Dex, a reusable wrist-centric human demonstration interface that shares human demonstrations and their observation and motion semantics across embodiments while retaining target-hand-specific executable supervision and policy learning. To align observations, Human2Dex combines mask-guided local hand-appearance adaptation with a shared 21-point hand representation, establishing consistent structural semantics for human and robot observations. To construct executable supervision, fused human hand motion is retargeted separately to each calibrated target hand, producing native action labels for Linker O6 and Wuji. To represent interaction geometry, Human2Dex introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR), which expresses tracked task objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket defined by the thumb–index grasp center. The same human demonstration corpus is therefore converted into separate training sets for the two target hands, while action labels, normalization statistics, policy training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain specific to each hand–task pair. No task demonstrations are collected with the target robot hands.

We evaluate whether this interface supports human-data reuse across embodiments under real-world dexterous manipulation. A matched Linker O6–Croissant study examines wrist- versus head-centric observation, while the main evaluation covers Linker O6 and Wuji across six real-world tasks. Additional reference-frame and task-wise analyses examine selected design choices and the task dependence of interaction grounding.

Our contributions are:

A reusable human demonstration interface for multiple dexterous embodiments.
Human2Dex converts one wrist-centric human demonstration corpus into separate hand-specific training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, allowing each hand to learn an independent policy without collecting task demonstrations on the target robots.

A grasp-centered interaction representation for policy conditioning.
The Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation expresses tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket, complementing structural observation alignment and target-specific action supervision with an explicit object–hand relation.

A two-hand, six-task physical evaluation with targeted design analyses.
We evaluate the complete interface on two calibrated dexterous hands and six real-world tasks, complemented by controlled comparisons of observation viewpoint and object-reference coordinates and task-wise analysis of interaction-grounding behavior.

title: Forward Dynamics Models
authors: Zipei Ma,Junzhe Jiang,Jiahui Zhang,Juntong Zhang,Chun Gu,Bozhou Zhang,Jiankang Deng,Xiatian Zhu,Li Zhang
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively.
Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions.
We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm.
Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions.
At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost.
The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones.
Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
introduction:
Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs) offer two complementary foundations for robotic action learning.
Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt VLMs to map current observations and task instructions directly to actions (Kim et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026b; NVIDIA et al., 2025), following the action-imitation paradigm (Chi et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2023) (Figure 1(a)).
While effective, this paradigm learns what to do without explicit supervision on what happens next, leaving the rich signal in future world states unused.
World action models (WAMs) instead build on video backbones to model visual dynamics alongside actions (Hu et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025; Pai et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2026a).
A prevalent design first predicts future world states and then infers actions from them in an inverse-dynamics manner (Li et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026c; Ma et al., 2026b; AgiBot Research Team et al., 2026; Tian et al., 2024) (Figure 1(b)).
However, future prediction is inherently error-prone, since every visual detail matters across both space and time.
Placing it before action prediction means its errors accumulate and amplify into the actions, and future generation also adds substantial inference overhead.
Other works predict future frames and actions jointly or in parallel (Ye et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026b), align policy features with future embeddings (Zheng et al., 2025), or train an action model and an action-conditioned world model side by side (Cen et al., 2025b).
These designs motivate studying the specific contribution of future supervision through action features, beyond supervision through shared context.

We investigate whether a policy can benefit from future supervision without ever depending on predicted futures.
To this end, we introduce Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models built on an action-to-future learning paradigm.
Borrowing the classical notion of forward dynamics (Jordan & Rumelhart, 1992; Agrawal et al., 2016), the mapping from state and action to the next state, FDM connects action learning with future world state prediction:
given the current world state and task instruction, FDM jointly predicts actions and future world states with asymmetric conditioning.
Future prediction reads action features, while action prediction cannot access future information.
The model is trained end to end, so the future-prediction loss backpropagates through these action features into the policy.
Action-to-future specifies this one-way information dependency within joint prediction.

This reverses the conditioning direction of future-conditioned WAMs and brings several advantages:
(1) Robustness: action prediction does not depend on predicted future world states, so errors in those predictions cannot propagate into actions;
(2) Action-grounded supervision: ground-truth future states supervise the action features used to generate actions, complementing action imitation with supervision from observed consequences;
(3) Efficiency: action-only inference skips future generation while retaining the context processing required for action prediction;
(4) Flexibility: either a VLM or a VGM can serve as the backbone.
As shown in Figure 2, FDM w/ VLM improves real-world success at comparable latency to π0.5\pi_{0.5}, while FDM w/ VGM improves success with 1.8×1.8\times faster inference than FastWAM-Joint.
Table 1 contrasts the formulations of the three paradigms.
Our analysis further confirms that, unlike FastWAM-Joint, whose action error grows with the quality degradation of predicted futures, FDM’s action error is insensitive to future-prediction quality (Section 4.4).

Our contributions are threefold:
(i) We introduce FDM, a novel family of robotic action models that learns in an action-to-future manner during training, with future supervision flowing into the policy through its action features, and requires no future prediction at inference;
(ii) We build VLM- and VGM-based instantiations of FDM, demonstrating its backbone flexibility;
(iii) Experiments in simulation and on real robots show that FDM achieves strong or competitive performance across VLM- and VGM-based settings, and analysis shows that it avoids the error propagation of future-conditioned designs.

title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
authors: Dijia Zhan,Zhuo Li,Xuemiao Xu,Sun Zheng,Jinyi Li,Wenjun Wang,Jie Tang
abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.
introduction:
Autoregressive robot policies generate future actions by predicting discrete tokens one at a time (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). To connect this prediction process to continuous motion, action tokenizers encode future action chunks into token sequences and decode the predicted tokens back into executable actions (Mete et al., 2024; Pertsch et al., 2025). The encoded sequences provide the policy’s training targets, so the tokenizer determines how action information is distributed across tokens and how each token depends on its predecessors (Liu et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026). The question is then how to structure these targets so that each token has a clear role in reconstructing the action chunk.

Learned action tokenizers use reconstruction objectives to compress action chunks into discrete sequences for policy learning (Lee et al., 2024; Mete et al., 2024). Recent work further shows that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to characterize these representations, as token organization also affects downstream policy learning (Dong et al., 2026). Ordering constraints and prefix supervision provide additional structure by encouraging earlier tokens to preserve essential action information and later tokens to add detail (Liu et al., 2026). However, these objectives do not by themselves explicitly define each token’s contribution relative to the actions already reconstructed. That contribution can remain implicit in the learned encoder–decoder mapping, leaving an opportunity to ground successive tokens in the action information still missing from the current reconstruction.

The residual between a target action chunk and its current reconstruction provides a concrete description of this missing information. Because it is measured in the reconstructed actions, it reflects what preceding tokens have actually recovered, including the effects of quantization and decoding. Encoding this residual gives the next token an explicit target tied to the reconstruction produced so far. This motivates Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which structures action sequences as successive corrections to an evolving action draft.

ReAT implements this formulation through explicit reconstruction feedback. During tokenizer training, the encoder maps the remaining reconstruction error to a discrete token, and the decoder uses that token together with the current action draft to produce a learned correction (Figure 1). The updated draft then provides the basis for constructing the next token. Each additional token thus represents a correction to the existing action draft, with Figure 2 illustrating how reconstruction improves as tokens are added. The resulting residual tokens provide structured prediction targets for observation-conditioned autoregressive policies.

We evaluate ReAT on 19 manipulation tasks spanning LIBERO, MetaWorld, RoboCasa, and real-world bucket stacking. With 8 tokens, ReAT outperforms the evaluated action-tokenization and diffusion-policy baselines in task success on all three simulation benchmarks and the real-world task. On LIBERO, it surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines using only 4 tokens. LIBERO ablations further support the contribution of explicit reconstruction feedback to policy performance and show that prefix supervision enables effective control with shorter token sequences.

In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce ReAT, an action tokenizer that constructs each successive token from the residual left by the decoded prefix, explicitly incorporating quantization and decoding effects into token construction.

We combine a draft-conditioned recurrent decoder with prefix reconstruction supervision to turn residual tokens into successive action corrections. Each nonempty prefix reconstructs a complete action chunk, allowing a single autoregressive policy to use different token budgets without retraining.

Experiments across three simulation benchmarks and real-world bucket stacking show that 8-token ReAT outperforms the evaluated action-tokenization and diffusion-policy baselines in task success. On LIBERO, 4-token ReAT also surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines, while mechanism ablations support the contributions of reconstruction feedback and prefix supervision.

1. We introduce ReAT, an action tokenizer that constructs each successive token from the residual left by the decoded prefix, explicitly incorporating quantization and decoding effects into token construction.

2. We combine a draft-conditioned recurrent decoder with prefix reconstruction supervision to turn residual tokens into successive action corrections. Each nonempty prefix reconstructs a complete action chunk, allowing a single autoregressive policy to use different token budgets without retraining.

3. Experiments across three simulation benchmarks and real-world bucket stacking show that 8-token ReAT outperforms the evaluated action-tokenization and diffusion-policy baselines in task success. On LIBERO, 4-token ReAT also surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines, while mechanism ablations support the contributions of reconstruction feedback and prefix supervision.

title: Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion: Object-Centric Flow Replanning for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Chen Yu,Sudarshan S Harithas,Juan Borbon,Dingqi Zhang,Jiuguang Wang
abstract:
People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory
push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids
pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric
framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop,
creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way,
while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial
Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far
as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers
pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on
hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.
introduction:
People rarely commit to a way of moving an unfamiliar object before testing it; a short push reveals
whether it rolls freely, resists, or veers off line, and the plan is adjusted before the motion has
finished. We pursue this ability in humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are
unknown at the outset [3, 4, 5]. What is at stake is the path and not merely the
effort: an omnidirectional cart can be driven laterally to its goal, whereas a constrained rear axle
admits only a curved approach, so the geometry of the maneuver is settled by a property the robot
cannot observe until it is already pushing.

Our framework treats the cart, rather than the robot, as the thing being planned for. A recurrent
estimator maintains a belief over the cart’s physical properties, a conditional flow planner
generates a timed object trajectory conditioned on that belief, and a whole-body controller tracks
that trajectory while preserving grasp and balance. Because motion is what produces evidence, the
three components close a loop in which every correction arrives mid-maneuver, and that timing is the
difficulty: regenerating the plan from each new belief, on top of noisy pose estimates, perturbs the
very trajectory the controller is following, while refusing to regenerate leaves the robot committed
to a path its own measurements no longer support. Building on plan-reuse
methods [1, 6, 7], we ask:
how much should a new estimate change the robot’s plan?

Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) answers with the beliefs themselves. As the
replanning component of our framework, it partially reverses plan generation
under the old belief and reconstructs under the updated one, with the depth of reversal set by how
far the two beliefs overlap: when successive beliefs agree the plan is barely disturbed, and as they
diverge more of it is rewritten. The rule requires no per-situation tuning, and the change it
induces in the encoded plan vanishes as the overlap approaches one.

Experiments span a controlled nonlinear benchmark, where BOPI attains higher task success with
smaller cumulative plan changes, and 18 goals in G1–Dex3 simulation. Figure  shows
object-centric control across cart types (A–D), real-robot translation and
turning (E–J), and simulation replay of recorded plans and updates (K–P).

Our contributions are: (i) an object-centric estimation–planning–control framework that
adapts cart trajectories while tracking continues; (ii) BOPI, its belief-adaptive
replanning method, with an exact-integration bound under which the encoded
plan change vanishes as belief overlap approaches one; and (iii) simulation and hardware
evaluations showing lower goal error in simulation and lower final position and tracking error on
hardware.

title: VICAR: Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting for Humanoid Interactive Skills
authors: Dvij Kalaria,Bike Zhang,S. Shankar Sastry
abstract: Third-person human videos offer a scalable alternative to task-specific reward engineering, teleoperation, and manually scripted demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation. Recent video-to-humanoid systems have shown that noisy human motion, object trajectories, and contacts can be extracted from unstructured videos and refined into deployable skills. However, a key gap remains for contact-rich imitation: the task is often defined by world-frame contacts whose poses, timing, and speed must survive embodiment mismatch and runtime scene changes. Towards this, we present VICAR (Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting), a pipeline for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos. The system first recovers human motion, reconstructs task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, and then retargets the motion to a humanoid while preserving global contact poses, motion speed, and collision clearance. Unlike retargeting methods that only remove penetration or preserve local interaction geometry, our formulation represents user-specified contact poses and collision clearance as high-priority Lagrangian penalty terms and optimizes the full motion to remain smooth through contact-rich transitions. The resulting motions are used to train a contact-conditioned motion generator whose inputs include movable contact points enabling runtime adaptation to new contact positions. We demonstrate the framework on ten diverse third-person video skills, including six table-tennis serves, three object-pickup tasks, and ladder climbing, and deploy the learned skills on hardware. These results suggest that contact-preserving retargeting is a practical step toward humanoids that learn useful interactive behavior by watching humans.
introduction:
Humans routinely learn interaction skills by watching other humans. A child does not need an adult to physically guide their body through every action, in the way teleoperation is often used to train robots; they can learn by observing that a cup should be reached on the table, that the table edge can support the body while crouching, or that a tossed ball must be met at a precise point in space. For humanoid robots, however, this mode of learning remains difficult: third-person videos provide abundant motion cues, but the robot must execute them with a different morphology, different joint limits, and different contact geometry. These tasks are organized around sparse contact events: a hand must arrive at an object, a foot must land on a rung, or a racket must meet a ball at the right pose and time. A trajectory can therefore resemble the source motion yet remain unusable if those events drift in the world frame.

The embodiment gap becomes especially severe for contact-rich tasks. Consider a standing adult picking up an object from a table. For the adult, the table may be near waist height; for a shorter humanoid such as Unitree G1, the same table may be near the chest, as shown in Figure 2. A retargeted motion that only matches human joint or keypoint motion will miss the object. The same issue appears when a robot crouches to pick up an object under a table while using the other hand for support: success depends on preserving the support contact, avoiding the table, and keeping the motion dynamically trackable. Collision avoidance alone does not resolve this ambiguity: several collision-free poses may exist, but only a small subset preserves the demonstrated contact and approach speed.

Many video-imitation pipelines rely on egocentric or robot-view demonstrations, but the web and everyday recordings contain a plethora of third-person human videos that can provide strong priors for humanoid whole-body motion learning. Recent systems show that monocular videos can provide scalable skill data for humanoids. VideoMimic [1] reconstructs human-scene geometry from casual videos and uses the resulting meshes and retargeted motions for contextual control. HDMI [2] learns humanoid-object interaction policies from monocular RGB videos by co-tracking robot and object states. OmniRetarget [3] improves interaction-preserving retargeting by preserving human-object-terrain relations through an interaction mesh and hard kinematic constraints. These works make major progress, but our target setting places a different emphasis: we want the robot to preserve specific global contact poses that may move at runtime, such as the ball-hit point in a table-tennis serve or the object position in a pickup task. The challenge is thus not only to reconstruct what the human did, but also to identify which interaction quantities must remain invariant after embodiment transfer.

We introduce VICAR, a video-to-humanoid learning pipeline centered on contact-aware retargeting. Given a third-person video, VICAR extracts human motion using GENMO/GEM [4], reconstructs task-relevant obstacle geometry using monocular depth and semantic segmentation. The selected regions are unprojected into a point cloud, voxelized into collision geometry, and scaled following the human-scene alignment ideas of VideoMimic [1]. We then retarget the motion in two stages: an initial OmniRetarget-style [3] pass gives a feasible robot reference, and a second optimization uses high-priority collision and global contact-pose penalties while preserving motion speed.

Our retargeted motions are not merely static references. They seed a motion generator conditioned on movable contact points that can be adjusted online during inference: for example, the ball-hit point in a table-tennis serve can move with the perceived ball position, and object-pick motions can be adapted to different object placements. A downstream policy then tracks the generated reference using proprioception and gravity observations, allowing deployment on hardware.

This paper makes the following contributions:

We formulate contact- and speed-preserving retargeting for third-person video imitation, using high-priority global contact-pose and collision penalties derived from monocularly reconstructed obstacles.

We connect this retargeting stage to a contact-conditioned motion generator that supports dynamic contact locations and contact-point augmentation.

We evaluate the pipeline on ten diverse skills, including six table-tennis serves, object pickups above and below a table, bimanual box pickup and placement, and ladder climbing. All skills are deployed on hardware except ladder climbing.

title: Towards Safer Cities: A Design Process for Perception Datasets in Urban Driving Scenarios
authors: Alexander Kroth,Cristian Martinez,Steven Peters
comment: . Submitted to 17. Uni-DAS e.V. Workshop Fahrerassistenz und automatisiertes Fahren. For details of the conference, seethis https URL
abstract: Urban environments present significant challenges for the perception systems of automated driving due to their high complexity, characterized by dense traffic, diverse obstacles, or a wide range of possible scenarios. While numerous automotive datasets exist, few focus on urban settings, and the majority are acquired exclusively on passenger cars and overlook other transport modalities such as heavy-duty trucks, busses and trams. In contrast to passenger vehicles, these platforms operate under different geographical and operational constraints; including traversing pedestrian zones or platform-specific tasks such as movement of trailer or winter service. In this work a method is proposed for a guided dataset creation based on an analysis of existing datasets using user-generated map data. Furthermore, representative truck-specific use cases are identified and exemplified to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed methodology and to support targeted acquisition planning.
introduction:
Heavy-duty vehicles, buses and trams form the backbone of urban transportation for both goods and passengers. However, their operation is threatened by an already existing and growing shortage of qualified drivers [9, 8]. Long-haul applications such as main-line rail or trucking are facing similar problems, but are already in the focus of both research and industry [19]. To tackle this issue automation is proposed as a possible solution. In main-line rail, this is reflected by the introduction of the European Train Control System (ETCS), which is already being tested in selected projects [4]. In the trucking sector, companies such as Torc and Aurora are pursuing to solve the hub-to-hub use-case, focused on highway operation [22, 1].

In contrast, great progress has been made in the research and adoption of automated driving in passenger cars. This is illustrated by both the large amount of available datasets and research based on them in this sector [10]. Furthermore, commercial services such as Waymo currently operate autonomous taxi fleets in multiple cities in the United States and are expected to expand to London in early 2026 [23]. Datasets form the basis for the development, training, and evaluation of both modular and end-to-end trained automated driving stacks. The scope of existing datasets closely aligns with automated driving solutions we see today.

This work demonstrates that current datasets only partially cover the requirements of truck and tram automation in urban environments. Based on an analysis of existing datasets and user-generated map data, relevant truck- and tram-specific scenarios are identified and used to derive Operational Design Domains (ODDs) for both platforms. Building on these findings, a methodology for targeted data acquisition is proposed to systematically address the identified gaps and support the creation of future urban truck and tram datasets.

title: Failure-Resilient Multi-Robot Coordination with $k$-Connectivity Constrained Submodular Maximization
authors: Yoonjae Hwang,Hojune Kim,Ellen Novoseller,Guangyao Shi,Gaurav S. Sukhatme
abstract:
Multi-robot coordination is essential in applications such as coverage, target tracking, and information gathering, where robots must jointly select actions to maximize team performance. Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient kk-Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing a direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor ρ\rho. Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor

of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.
introduction:
Multi-robot systems provide scalable solutions to applications such as environmental monitoring, target tracking, search and rescue, and collaborative exploration [1, 2, 3, 4]. In many of these settings, the robots must coordinate their sensing or motion decisions to maximize a common team objective [5]. Submodular set functions provide a natural mathematical framework for such coordination by capturing the principle of diminishing returns: the marginal benefit of adding an additional robot decreases as more robots are already selected. Many commonly used objectives, including mutual information [6], area coverage [7], number of observed targets [8], and sensor-measurement entropy [9] are monotone submodular [10]. This structure enables computationally efficient greedy algorithms with well-established constant-factor performance guarantees, as reviewed in Section II.

Classical submodular maximization, however, typically assumes that the selected robots remain available throughout execution. In practice, robots may be lost due to hardware failures, communication interference, denial-of-service attacks, or other adverse events. This has motivated resilient submodular maximization, where the team is selected so that the objective remains large even after a bounded number of robots are removed [8, 11, 12]. Existing resilient formulations primarily focus on preserving
submodular objective performance
after such removals. Yet, critically, robot loss can disrupt the communication network among surviving robots. A team might therefore retain high sensing or coverage capacity after failures while becoming disconnected and rendered unable to continue coordinated operation.

Communication connectivity and resilience have both been studied extensively, but largely as separate requirements. In this work, we consider them jointly and ask how to select robot actions so that the team achieves a high submodular objective while remaining connected even after adversarial robot removals. We refer to this problem as Resilient kk-Connected Submodular Maximization (see Fig. 1). The joint treatment is substantially more challenging than simply combining two existing constraints. Resilience requires accounting for the worst-case subset of removed robots, while connectivity is a global property whose feasibility depends on which robots survive.
This interaction also breaks key structures used in existing approximation analysis. In the resilient maximization framework of Tzoumas et al. [11], robustness is achieved by constructing a sacrificial “bait” set of β\beta high-value robots together with a greedily selected remainder. Under a connectivity requirement, however, the adversary determines which robots are removed, and the worst-case removal need not coincide with the bait set. Consequently, enforcing connectivity only on the non-bait robots does not guarantee that the surviving team remains connected. Moreover, the constraint of selecting one trajectory per robot together with a global vertex-connectivity requirement does not form a matroid. As a result, classical curvature-based greedy guarantees cannot be applied directly and must be re-established for the connectivity-constrained resilient setting.

We make the following contributions:

We formulate resilient submodular maximization under a (β+1)(\beta{+}1)-vertex-connectivity constraint and show that the family of partial, connectivity-feasible selections is not a matroid (Proposition 1), identifying precisely why the classical greedy analysis fails to transfer.

We introduce a connectivity filter with a rigid-shift fallback across both bait and greedy stages, show it guarantees a feasible, (β+1)(\beta{+}1)-connected output that survives any removal of size at most β\beta regardless of composition (Proposition 2), and re-derive the curvature-greedy bound against a connectivity-respecting benchmark (Lemma 1), isolating the filter’s entire cost into a single interpretable constant ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1].

We prove a resilient, connectivity-preserving approximation guarantee (Theorem 1) and empirically corroborate the algorithm’s feasibility, the price of connectivity, and the squared resilience factor (Section V).

title: CeDR-Nav: Cross-Embodiment Mapless Navigation via Offline Demonstration Recasting
authors: Xianghui Wang,Xinming Zhang,Yiwei Qian,Siwei Cheng,Shanze Wang,Dan Zhang,Wei Zhang
abstract:
Learning-based methods have demonstrated strong performance in mapless robot navigation. However, a learned policy remains restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments
across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness
of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points
over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and
target-specific policy training completed within seconds.
introduction:
Autonomous navigation is a fundamental capability for mobile robots. In recent years, learning-based methods have emerged as effective approaches to mapless navigation in complex and cluttered environments [1, 2, 3]. However, a learned navigation policy is commonly restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. In practice, the physical dimensions and sensor configurations of mobile robots not only vary across platforms, but also change within a single platform due to task requirements. When the robot’s embodiment changes, the original policy can suffer substantial performance degradation and may cause dangerous collisions. Whether learning from collected demonstrations or from agent–environment interaction, obtaining a navigation policy demands significant effort for every new embodiment [4, 5].

Existing methods address this challenge by adapting trained policies
at deployment [6], training universal policies
across embodiment configurations
[7, 8, 9, 10],
or learning from multi-platform navigation experience
[11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. However, the conservative enclosure used by DVST can restrict
passage through otherwise traversable gaps when the target
and reference robots differ substantially in
shape [6]. Training universal policies across configurations, such as
DRL-DCLP [7], requires time-consuming online
training with carefully designed environments, while the resulting
policy can underperform a dedicated target-specific policy. These data-driven approaches rely on multi-platform datasets
or scene-geometry estimation for experience augmentation
[11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16].

In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for each target embodiment. However, the geometric dimensions and velocity limits of the source embodiment prevent these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target embodiment [17, 18, 19]. This raises the central question of this work: can source demonstrations be converted into valid target supervision without new demonstration collection, so that a dedicated navigation policy can be obtained for each target embodiment without additional online interaction?

In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a Cross-Embodiment Demonstration Recasting framework that obtains a dedicated policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online RL training. Specifically, CeDR-Nav first recasts source demonstrations into valid training data for the target embodiment through geometry-consistent scaling and validity assessment, ensuring that the recast trajectories remain geometrically consistent with the target embodiment. Subsequently, CeDR-Nav trains a target-specific policy using a Gaussian mixture model [20] to capture the multimodal action distribution in the recast demonstrations. Extensive cross-embodiment simulations and quantitative real-world experiments on multiple robot platforms demonstrate that CeDR-Nav derives effective navigation policies for diverse target embodiments from source demonstrations. The main contributions of this article are summarized as follows.

We introduce CeDR-Nav, an offline demonstration recasting framework for cross-embodiment mapless navigation that replaces target-specific online RL with offline learning from existing source demonstrations. It learns a navigation policy dedicated to each target embodiment, without requiring target-specific training-environment design.

Extensive quantitative experiments in simulators and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms and navigation tasks validate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav.

title: EgoReveal: Learning Active Vision and Object Manipulation under Partial Occlusions from Egocentric Demonstrations
authors: Hiromu Kurihara,Kazutoshi Tanaka,Masashi Hatano,Tadashi Kozuno,Hideo Saito,Mariko Isogawa
abstract:
Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations.
In contrast to resource-intensive and labor-intensive teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection.
Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments, yet prior egocentric demonstration-based methods that require no robots or specialized teaching devices do not explicitly address occlusions.
To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions.
EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts the future camera-arm pose sequence from the current view and camera-arm pose, and the other predicts the future control commands from object keypoints and a history of control commands.
EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility.
In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.
introduction:
Learning from Demonstrations (LfD), such as imitation learning (IL), enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations [1].
In LfD via teleoperation, a human operator remotely controls the robot while the system records the robot’s observations and actions, yielding directly usable action labels without requiring any mapping from the human body to the robot [2, 3].
Despite this advantage, teleoperation is resource-intensive and labor-intensive, since it requires specialized hardware and skilled operators, thereby limiting scalability to diverse, large-scale datasets.
Egocentric demonstrations are captured as first-person videos using an egocentric camera (e.g., smart glasses).
In contrast to teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection [4, 5].

Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments by the hands, surrounding objects, or clutter, obscuring task-relevant visual cues.
In this study, we focus on the common case where the target remains in view but is partially occluded at the start of the episode.
Egocentric demonstrations capture naturally changing viewpoints, with humans adjusting their viewpoint when targets become hard to see, yet many egocentric demonstration-based methods assume a fixed camera viewpoint at inference time [4, 6].
This fixed-view assumption can cause the robot to fail the task by preventing access to task-relevant visual cues under occlusions.

To ensure access to task-relevant visual cues under occlusions, recent studies use Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) and enable active vision by learning to move a robot-mounted camera from an operator’s viewpoint changes [7, 8].
These studies also rely on teleoperation or specialized teaching devices, increasing hardware costs and operational burden.

To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions.
EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts camera-arm pose trajectories from the current view and camera-arm state, and the other predicts end-effector actions from keypoints tracked in the actively moved camera view.
EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility.
In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.
L

The contributions of this paper are twofold:

Formulation: A problem setting for learning manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations without robotic teleoperation or handheld teaching devices, under partial occlusions.

EgoReveal: A framework for learning manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations that couples the Active Vision policy and the Manipulation policy via visibility-based switching to handle partial occlusions.

title: Adaptive Whole-Body MPC with Optimal Posture Planning for Humanoid Robots under Unknown Payloads
authors: Manh Cuong Nguyen,Duc Cuong Vu,Viet Anh Vu,Duc Tuan Pham,Toan Nguyen,Minh Hiep Phung,Ngo Anh Vien,Minh Nhat Vu
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 25th IEEE RAS International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids2026)
abstract:
Humanoid robots performing lifting and material-handling tasks must maintain balance despite unknown and varying payloads.
However, payload uncertainty significantly affects whole-body dynamics and may destabilize conventional controllers.
We propose an adaptive whole-body control architecture that integrates three components:
(i) a centroidal model predictive controller (MPC) that generates dynamically feasible reference motions,
(ii) an adaptive fuzzy balance controller that compensates for payload-induced model mismatch by generating corrective torques distributed across the supporting-leg joints,
and (iii) a waypoint-based optimal posture planner built on a triple-integrator model that produces smooth sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit trajectories satisfying center-of-mass (CoM) stability constraints, joint limits, and whole-body feasibility requirements.
Together, these components enable stable lowering, grasping, lifting, carrying, and placing behaviors under significant payload uncertainty.
Extensive simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework improves balance robustness and reduces tracking degradation during posture transitions and lifting tasks compared to non-adaptive baselines.
introduction:
In recent years, humanoid robots have attracted significant attention due to their versatility and potential to operate in human-centered environments [2]. Their comprehensive structure, which integrates mobility [1], manipulation [21], and perception [3], enables them to perform a wide range of complex tasks and operate in modern manufacturing systems [6]. Unlike traditional industrial robots, which are typically designed for structured, repetitive tasks, humanoid robots are inspired by human morphology and motion, enabling them to operate in environments originally designed for human workers. This anthropomorphic configuration provides remarkable advantages in industrial scenarios that require flexibility, dexterity, and whole-body coordination, particularly in tasks involving physical interaction with the environment.

Among these applications, lifting and material handling of unknown payloads represent a critical and challenging problem [25]. Such tasks frequently arise in real-world industrial environments where the object properties, including mass, shape, and inertia, are not precisely known in advance. In these situations, the robot must maintain balance while adapting its posture and control strategy to ensure stability and safety. However, despite the promising capabilities of humanoid systems, several technical bottlenecks still limit their practical deployment in industrial lifting tasks. First, the dynamic stability of humanoid robots is highly sensitive to payload variations [23], as unknown mass distributions can significantly alter system dynamics and shift the CoM, potentially leading to instability or failure. Second, posture transitions during lifting, such as squatting, grasping, and standing up, involve complex whole-body coordination and nonlinear dynamics, which remain difficult to model and control accurately [24]. Third, ensuring robustness and adaptability in the presence of uncertainties, external disturbances, and interaction forces remains a major challenge in humanoid control [20]. Therefore, developing adaptive and robust control frameworks capable of handling unknown payloads, maintaining balance, and optimizing posture during lifting remains a critical research challenge.

This paper proposes a comprehensive control architecture that integrates Centroidal MPC with a WBC framework [27]. The centroidal MPC layer generates dynamically feasible CoM motion and contact force references, while the WBC layer ensures accurate joint-space tracking under kinematic and dynamic constraints. To enhance robustness against unknown payload variations, an Adaptive Fuzzy Balance Controller is introduced to generate compensation torques for regulating the CoM and maintaining pelvic stability. The computed compensation torques are subsequently mapped into the joint space of the supporting legs through torque distribution within the whole-body control structure. This mechanism enables adaptive stabilization in the presence of external disturbances and load uncertainties. Furthermore, to ensure smooth and stable execution of sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit motions, a waypoint-based trajectory optimization formulation is proposed. The optimization problem generates dynamically consistent posture transition trajectories while explicitly satisfying CoM stability constraints and joint limits. The resulting motion guarantees stable pelvis balancing and posture transitions that are constraint-consistent.

Overall, our key contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

Firstly, this work presents a novel adaptive control structure that integrates centroidal MPC with fuzzy logic regulation, ensuring the stability of the overall system under unknown and varying payload conditions during posture and motion tasks.

Secondly, an optimization posture transition planning based on their triple-integration waypoint model is provided. This framework helps the robot change posture for the lifting task; the resulting trajectory is smooth, balancing the generated trajectory with joint limitations.

Finally, the simulation and experiment are conducted to validate the performance of the proposed method.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the related work as well as the motivation of this study. Section III introduces the adaptive balancing control framework, including the robot model, centroidal dynamics, whole-body control, and the proposed method. Section IV describes the generation of optimal posture-transition motions using the waypoint model. Section V presents the experimental implementation and results. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

2. Secondly, an optimization posture transition planning based on their triple-integration waypoint model is provided. This framework helps the robot change posture for the lifting task; the resulting trajectory is smooth, balancing the generated trajectory with joint limitations.

3. Finally, the simulation and experiment are conducted to validate the performance of the proposed method.

title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents
authors: Gangyi Li,LuYao Wang,Jingfu Sun,Jingyi Yuan,Hang Liu,Hao Zong,Yujia Hu,Tingting Gao,Jianyong Wang,Xu Yang
abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy’s parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.
introduction:
Embodied agents deployed on robotic platforms and smart hardware must translate multimodal observations and user instructions into executable behavior. Across products ranging from bipedal, quadruped, and wheeled robots to AI-enabled plush toys, the appropriate response to a given request depends on the agent’s role, capabilities, and operating constraints. Changes in user goals, new visual evidence, and execution failures can further invalidate earlier plans. We study how to train a shared multimodal policy that adapts to product specifications and revises its decisions as interactions unfold. Figure 1 presents the training framework and deployment examples.

Multimodal training has demonstrated positive transfer across tasks and robotic embodiments [1, 2], while context-aware systems use user intent and environmental feedback to guide interaction [3, 4]. However, reported failures include actions beyond device capabilities and descriptions that no longer match the user’s current scene or intent [3, 4]. These observations motivate training policies that combine transferable capabilities with adherence to product constraints and sustained alignment with the user’s current goal.

This objective imposes two requirements on training. The data must cover diverse product configurations, goal revisions, and failure recovery while preserving the correspondence between actions and observations. The learning signal must reflect reasoning quality, compliance with product constraints, and progress toward the current goal. Trajectory-level rewards summarize these criteria but do not specify how to distribute credit across tokens. Using additional evidence during training therefore requires selecting an appropriate source for each token and controlling how that evidence affects policy updates.

We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned data construction and staged policy learning. Our pipeline combines product roles, workflows, and constraints with available tools and skills to build executable environments. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories, which undergo execution checks and semantic validation. Multi-source supervised fine-tuning establishes behavior consistent with product specifications, while multi-expert on-policy distillation integrates complementary language and visual capabilities. Reinforcement learning then refines the policy using interaction-specific rewards.

To guide reinforcement learning, we combine process-quality scores from a Generative Process Reward Model (GPRM), multi-judge rankings of the same candidate trajectories, and task-queue assessments of goal alignment and cross-turn continuity. For token-level policy optimization, we introduce DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing), building on RLSD’s sign-preserving advantage modulation [5] and DOPD’s dual-source routing [6]. A frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy’s parameters score tokens along the same student-generated trajectory. DPER selects evidence based on their disagreement and support for each sampled token. The selected evidence rescales token-level advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs. Privileged information is used only during training.

We evaluate JoyInside-VLM-Agent on public tool-use benchmarks and the proprietary JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics datasets. The model achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, outperforming the evaluated baselines. Case studies on a physical quadruped robot provide qualitative evidence of visually grounded search, replanning in response to execution feedback, and honest failure reporting.

Our contributions are as follows:

Product-conditioned trajectory construction. We compose executable product configurations and generate verified multimodal trajectories covering product variation, goal revisions, and failure recovery.

DPER for policy optimization. We route token-level evidence between two privileged sources to scale token advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs.

Multi-source interaction rewards. We combine process evaluation, multi-model rankings, and task-queue consistency into a learning signal for reasoning quality, adherence to product constraints, and alignment with evolving goals.

JoyInside-VLM-Agent and its evaluation. We integrate these components into a unified training framework and assess the resulting model through public benchmarks and proprietary evaluation sets and qualitative quadruped case studies.

2. DPER for policy optimization. We route token-level evidence between two privileged sources to scale token advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs.

3. Multi-source interaction rewards. We combine process evaluation, multi-model rankings, and task-queue consistency into a learning signal for reasoning quality, adherence to product constraints, and alignment with evolving goals.

4. JoyInside-VLM-Agent and its evaluation. We integrate these components into a unified training framework and assess the resulting model through public benchmarks and proprietary evaluation sets and qualitative quadruped case studies.
