title: Evo-World: A Lightweight Vision-Language-Action Model with Future Motion Prediction via Optical-Flow Supervision
authors: Zile Zhong,Yuxin Du,Tao Lin,Haoxiao Wang,Wei Dai,Binhua Zuo,Bo Zhao
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. To address these limitations, we introduce Evo-World, a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision, thereby providing a task-relevant predictive signal focused on motion rather than appearance. We further design the training procedure to preserve these predictive representations during policy learning, regulating representation diversity while decoupling representation learning from action optimization. Across simulation benchmarks, Evo-World demonstrates strong performance, achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50 , with a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline. On real-world AgileX robots, Evo-World outperforms the evaluated baselines across single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks while using only 0.87B parameters and delivering lower GPU memory usage and higher inference efficiency. These results demonstrate that future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision provides an effective and lightweight approach to enhancing the predictive capabilities of VLA models.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control. By adapting pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to action generation, they support a broad range of manipulation behaviors (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2026). Successful manipulation also depends on anticipating how a scene should change as a task unfolds: grasping, placing, and opening require coordinated changes in the robot and its surroundings. Yet action supervision alone does not explicitly require a policy’s representations to anticipate these changes. Providing this predictive structure is therefore an opportunity to improve VLA policies beyond their understanding of the current observation.

Future-observation prediction offers temporal supervision for learning such anticipation (Wu et al., 2024; Cheang et al., 2024), but the prediction target determines which aspects of scene evolution the model must represent. Future RGB images entangle motion with appearance, including background textures and objects that remain largely unchanged. Preserving these details can support visual recognition, but it does not directly emphasize the changes needed for control. Optical flow provides a complementary target by describing image-space displacement while suppressing static texture. This motivates learning future motion representations that complement the policy’s visual and linguistic context, as illustrated in Figure 1.

We introduce Evo-World, a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision. Evo-World learns to anticipate motion from the current observation and task instruction, and uses this prediction to inform action generation. The key idea is to make scene change an effective learning target while retaining the appearance and semantics available to the vision-language backbone. Optical flow computed from demonstration videos supplies supervision during training; a compact predictive branch learns its latent representation.

For the predictive signal to remain useful, policy learning must preserve informative motion representations. We address two complementary requirements: maintaining representation diversity and preserving the motion-learning objective during action optimization. We adopt Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) from LeJEPA to discourage collapse of learned representations (Balestriero and LeCun, 2025). We also separate the gradient paths for representation learning and action optimization, allowing the policy to learn how to use the motion features while the predictive branch is trained by its own objective.

Evo-World contains only 0.87B parameters, including its predictive branch. At deployment, it uses current camera observations, the instruction, and robot state; future observations and optical-flow estimation are unnecessary. Motion prediction operates in a latent space, avoiding the need to decode future images or flow fields during action generation. This design incorporates anticipation within a compact policy suitable for deployment on a physical robot.

We evaluate Evo-World on Meta-World MT50, RoboTwin, and three real-world manipulation tasks (Yu et al., 2020)(Chen et al., 2025a). It achieves 91.1% tier-averaged success on Meta-World, a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline, and 41.8% average success across Clean2Clean and Clean2Random on RoboTwin (Table 1). On an AgileX dual-arm robot, Evo-World outperforms OpenVLA-OFT and π0\pi_{0} on all three tasks, with 63.3% average success (Table 2). These tasks cover single-arm floral arrangement and bimanual collaboration in mug hanging and microwave placement. Component ablations support the training design: regularization counters representation contraction, and both regularization and gradient separation improve aggregate success in the tested setting.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce optical-flow-supervised future motion prediction into a lightweight VLA policy, providing a strong predictive signal that complements visual understanding and language grounding.

We introduce optical-flow-supervised future motion prediction into a lightweight VLA policy, providing a strong predictive signal that complements visual understanding and language grounding.

We combine distribution regularization with separate gradient paths to preserve predictive representations during policy learning, and integrate these representations into action generation through a compact conditioning module.

We conduct comprehensive experiments across simulation and real-world robotic manipulation tasks. With a compact 0.87B-parameter model, Evo-World achieves strong task performance while retaining low computational overhead.

title: Sampling-based Kinodynamic Planning with World Models
authors: Yitian Gao,Hanlan Yang,Zachary Kingston
abstract:
Visual world models predict the consequences of actions from images, but planning with them is typically done by optimizers such as CEM and MPPI.
However, these optimizers stall on long-horizon tasks where progress requires motion the objective does not reward, such as moving around a block before pushing it.
This paper revisits kinodynamic sampling-based motion planning for world models, using the learned model as the propagator of a tree search in latent space.
Our key insight is that the sampling strategies devised for high-dimensional search in configuration space apply directly to the latent space of a world model, where they rapidly expand through intermediate states that myopic optimizers never sample.
We present two exploration strategies for the high-dimensional latent space, nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE, with GPU-native batched expansion for efficient device utilization.
We evaluate with an off-the-shelf DINO-WM on four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task.
Our approaches match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI at up to 13.8×13.8\times lower planning time in simulation, and improve the success rate by 20%20\% on the real robot.
introduction:
Visual world models learn to predict the consequences of actions from images [11].
Given a history of observations and a candidate action, the model predicts the next observation or latent state, and this prediction can stand in for a simulator when no analytical model of the task is available [12, 13, 39, 2, 1].
For example, a robot pushing a block across a table has no exact closed-form model of the contact, but a world model trained on demonstrations can predict where the block will end up (Sec. V-A5b).
The remaining question is how to search through the model’s predictions to find actions that reach a goal.

Prior works [3, 12, 14, 39, 2] typically use closed-loop planning, i.e., they repeatedly generate plans with the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) [4] or Model-Predictive Path Integral control (MPPI) [34], then execute action prefixes with receding-horizon Model Predictive Control (MPC) [23]. However, gradient-free methods like CEM and MPPI require repeated rollouts for decision-making. Combined with costly inference on large-scale world models, this requires care to balance planning quality and computational cost. Additionally, CEM and MPPI perturb around a mean, leading them to focus exploration and become trapped in local minima. Variants reshape the sampling distribution [29, 32] but keep the same search structure. With exact dynamics, tree search under a receding horizon has been shown to outperform CEM [19]; others have proposed to use search methods such as Monte Carlo tree search [18], but rely on an action prior. These gaps raise the question, are optimization-based approaches the right tools for exploring and planning in the latent space of world models?

On the other hand, classical search-based and sampling-based motion planning methods (SBMPs) excel in long-horizon planning for robotics [20], as they maintain a tree or graph that guides exploration. However, they have not been widely adopted as planning methods with world models due to the curse of dimensionality. A large body of literature tackles this problem in robotics with more efficient sampling and exploration strategies designed for high-dimensional spaces [30, 31, 7]; others use parallel hardware to speed up the planning process [27, 37, 36, 16]. These advances motivate bridging the aforementioned research gaps in world model planning with classical planning methods.

Thus, we revisit kinodynamic SBMP for planning with world models.
Our key insight is that the sampling strategies devised for high-dimensional search in robot configuration space apply directly to the latent space of a world model.
Nearest-neighbor guidance (i.e., RRT [21]) and projection-based coverage estimation (i.e., KPIECE [31]) need only a compact descriptor of each state, while the world model propagates the full latent along each branch.
Batching propagation across candidate expansions amortizes the predictor’s cost, allowing our planner to match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI at a fraction of their planning time, with a frozen, off-the-shelf world model. In this work, we present:

a kinodynamic tree planner that uses a visual world model as its propagator, with batched expansion;

a kinodynamic tree planner that uses a visual world model as its propagator, with batched expansion;

two exploration strategies for the world model’s latent space, nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based coverage guidance with KPIECE [31];

and an evaluation against CEM, MPPI, and MCTS [18] with DINO-WM on four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task, with ablations of exploration, refinement, and numerical precision.

Across the simulated domains, our planners match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI with up to 13.8×13.8\times lower median planning time and an order of magnitude fewer world-model evaluations.
On the real robot, our planner solves 29/3029/30 problems where CEM and MPPI solve 23/3023/30, and the gap is widest on tasks that require a detour before pushing, 9/109/10 versus 5/105/10.

title: LeapBot-JAC: Joint Action Chains for World Action Models
authors: Chenhao Zhu,Baibing Liu,Pei Liu,Rui Yang,Lang Zhang,Mingyue Feng,Yaonong Wang,Jun Ma
abstract: Action-chunking policies predict future controls but execute only a prefix before replanning. How should a fixed action-token budget be organized to support execution? We propose LeapBot-JAC, which allocates sparse future-control references and dense execution targets within one shared action expert. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and jointly denoised at aligned physical-time positions. Directed attention allows execution tokens to read reference tokens subject to the host’s visibility constraints. JAC adds neither action tokens nor parameters and retains the host’s world-modeling process; both chains participate in inference, while only the execution chain drives the robot. On LIBERO, JAC reaches 98.3% success with FastWAM and LeapBot-WA, up from 97.0% and 97.3%. On zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, their success rates improve from 53.5% to 70.4% and from 73.1% to 77.3%, respectively. RoboTwin and two real-world tasks provide additional deployment evaluations. Single-training-seed comparisons and FastWAM ablations support action-role organization as a practical design choice under a fixed action-token budget.
introduction:
Action-chunking policies predict a sequence of future robot controls, but closed-loop deployment often executes only a short prefix before querying the policy again. ACT and Diffusion Policy exploit sequence generation for temporally coherent behavior while using temporal ensembling or receding-horizon execution to incorporate new observations (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023). Predictions beyond the executed prefix can still influence the current output through the model’s internal dependencies. The resulting design question is how to organize those predictions: should every token have the same temporal density and deployment role?

World action models (WAMs) couple robot control with learning environment dynamics. Motus supports multiple video–action modeling modes (Bi et al., 2025); LingBot-VA uses causal video–action generation (Li et al., 2026a); Fast-WAM retains video co-training while omitting future-video generation at inference (Yuan et al., 2026). These approaches primarily organize world representations and their interaction with control. Within an existing action expert, the organization of a fixed number of control predictions remains a separate design choice.

We study action-role organization under a fixed action-token budget. Dense predictions preserve near-term control resolution, whereas sparsely sampled control targets span a longer interval using fewer tokens. Combining these roles provides a way to expose execution to a temporally extended reference without adding an action expert or expanding its token sequence. The reference consists of robot controls, not semantic subgoals or executable waypoints; its role is to condition the jointly generated execution chain.

We propose LeapBot-JAC (Joint Action Chains, JAC). A sparse reference chain RR and a dense execution chain AA share input projections, Transformer layers, an output head, and every action forward pass. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and evolve together during denoising, with independent noise samples at a common noise level. Physical-time positions align the two target sequences. A directed role mask permits AA to read RR while blocking direct access in the reverse direction, subject to the host’s legal attention edges. Only the execution prefix is sent to the robot. This construction reorganizes action prediction while preserving the host’s world-modeling process.

Prior work already explores joint generation of high-level intent and executable actions (Li et al., 2026b; Hao et al., 2025). JAC’s focus is more specific: directly supervised control references and dense execution coexist within one existing action expert at a fixed token budget. We assess task success across two hosts and examine how information-flow direction, reference weight, and reference stride affect performance.

Our contributions are threefold. (1) Action-role allocation: we formulate sparse reference and dense execution prediction within a fixed action-token budget, separating the supervision span from the executed prefix. (2) Shared-expert joint generation: we combine control-label supervision, physical-time alignment, and directed cross-chain access without adding action parameters, while retaining host visibility constraints. (3) Empirical evidence on two hosts: JAC improves LIBERO success for FastWAM and LeapBot-WA to 98.3%, and improves their LIBERO-Plus totals by 16.9 and 4.2 percentage points, respectively. Three FastWAM ablations characterize sensitivity to access direction, reference supervision, and temporal coverage.

title: TAME-Nav: Temporal Asymmetric Mixture-of-Experts Distillation for Agile and Versatile Robot Navigation
authors: Lingjie Zhang,Jun Xue,Shanze Wang,Haoyu Xi,Xinming Zhang,Xiaoyu Shen,Wei Zhang
abstract: Agile and reliable navigation is a core capability for embodied robots navigating complex spatial constraints and dynamic interactions. However, a single policy often struggles to accommodate the distinct decision-making demands of diverse scenarios. We present TAME-Nav, an asymmetric Teacher–Student navigation framework built around a temporal soft mixture of experts (Soft-MoE). The Teacher combines clean observations with causally maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks to construct privileged representations, while the Student learns complementary navigation features from corrupted observation histories through temporal encoding, soft expert routing, and latent distillation. Procedural scenario generation and parallel task-level simulation broaden training coverage, while deployment-informed asymmetric domain randomization supports sim-to-real transfer. Across in-distribution and unseen compositional scenarios, TAME-Nav achieves higher success rates, lower collision rates, and higher navigation scores than representative baselines. On a real quadruped robot, it completes all twenty trials across local-trap escape and narrow-passage navigation with sudden dynamic obstacles, with only one minor contact.
introduction:
Reliable local navigation is a prerequisite for autonomous navigation in complex environments. A local navigation policy converts onboard sensory observations and a local goal into real-time motion commands, determining whether a planned route can be executed safely and continuously [1]. A capable local navigator can also reduce the burden on upstream modules by allowing them to provide sparser subgoals at a lower decision frequency [2]. Traditional model-based planners offer interpretable motion models and geometric constraints, but their performance often depends on manually designed objectives and short-horizon environment predictions [3]. Consequently, they may become trapped near concave obstacles, oscillate in narrow passages [4], or exhibit overly conservative freezing behavior in dense, interacting crowds [5]. Learning-based methods can acquire richer interaction priors from demonstrations or environmental experience [6], yet their performance remains strongly affected by the diversity of the training distribution and the expressiveness of the observation representation [7]. Learned policies may generalize poorly to unseen cluttered or confined environments [8]. Obstacle motion must be inferred from sensory histories, while explicit object-state inputs introduce deployment-time tracking dependencies [9].

These raise two fundamental questions:

With only local observations, how can a single policy coordinate complementary navigation skills, including safe obstacle avoidance, narrow-passage traversal, and local-trap escape?

With only local observations, how can a single policy coordinate complementary navigation skills, including safe obstacle avoidance, narrow-passage traversal, and local-trap escape?

Can such coordination translate into higher task completion rates and lower collision risk in unseen compositional scenarios and real-world environments?

To address these questions, we present TAME-Nav, an asymmetric
Teacher–Student framework for agile and versatile robot navigation.
The Teacher fuses clean observation histories with causal dynamic-object
tracks, while a temporal Soft-MoE Student learns to match its privileged
navigation representation through latent distillation. Both branches
share an Actor that generates body-frame velocity commands. Using only
onboard observations and local goals, the deployed Student supports
obstacle avoidance, narrow-passage traversal, and local-trap recovery
without explicit object tracking or global-map inputs.

We further develop a massively parallel task-level simulator with
procedurally generated geometric layouts and dynamic interactions to
broaden training coverage. Deployment-informed randomization models
sensor degradation and velocity-response uncertainty: the Student
receives corrupted observations, while the Teacher and Critic retain
clean observations of the underlying simulated state.

Our evaluations demonstrate consistent gains in navigation success
and safety over SEA-Nav, NavRL, and DRL-DCLP under matched training
budgets. TAME-Nav improves in-distribution success by over 25 percentage
points over the strongest baseline and maintains its advantage across
unseen sequential and multiroom scenarios. Real-world experiments
further demonstrate its ability to escape local traps and negotiate
narrow passages with suddenly appearing obstacles: the quadruped
completes all trials in both scenarios, with only one minor contact
across the twenty trials.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows.

We propose TAME-Nav, an asymmetric Teacher–Student framework that transfers privileged navigation representations augmented with causal dynamic-obstacle tracks from a Teacher to a deployable temporal Soft-MoE Student, enabling a single policy to handle obstacle avoidance, constrained-space traversal, and local-trap escape.

We develop a massively parallel task-level simulator with procedural scene generation for diverse geometric and dynamic navigation challenges, together with deployment-informed asymmetric randomization that corrupts Student observations while preserving clean Teacher–Critic supervision.

We demonstrate improved navigation success and safety across
in-distribution and unseen compositional scenarios, and validate
reliable local-trap escape and narrow-passage navigation with
sudden dynamic obstacles on a real quadruped.

title: Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning for Long-Tailed Robotic Policies
authors: Weiwei Chen,Chenghao Xu,Meiling Yu,Xu Yang,Cheng Deng
abstract: In the practical deployment of vision–language–action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. To investigate this issue, we study the head-task action bias in shared robot policies, particularly focusing on its relationship with task-specific visual evidence. Our experimental analysis shows that, when the visual evidence required by a tail task is insufficient, the policy increasingly falls back on action patterns reinforced by data-rich head tasks, resulting in degraded performance on under-represented tasks. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning, a training framework for long-tailed robot policies. Our method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence using instruction-related and action-related signals, and constructs counterfactual observations by removing the selected evidence. The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Extensive experiments across simulated benchmarks, different VLA architectures, and real-world robot platforms demonstrate that our method robustly and consistently improves long-tailed robot policy learning, particularly for tail tasks, while maintaining reliable performance on head tasks.
introduction:
Vision–language–action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising foundation for generalist robot policies, integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation within a unified framework (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2026). Robot demonstration datasets, however, can be highly imbalanced across manipulation skills (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024). Similar to the long-tailed category distributions observed in datasets such as iNaturalist (Van Horn et al., 2018), robot task distributions can be skewed toward a few data-rich head tasks, leaving many tail tasks with limited demonstrations(Zhu et al., 2026).

Long-tailed learning addresses unequal supervision through approaches such as resampling, loss reweighting, and decoupled representation and classifier learning (Cui et al., 2019; Kang et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2022). However, most of these methods are developed for classification and are difficult to apply directly to VLAs due to differences in task formulation and model architecture.Zhu et al. (2026) propose Approaching-Phase Augmentation (APA) for long-tailed VLA learning, but it relies on additional tools, such as object detection and image inpainting, increasing the complexity of the approach.Moreover, APA primarily mitigates the problem through data augmentation, without directly constraining VLAs’ reliance on head-task action bias.

However, comparing the results of policies trained on the balanced FULL dataset and the long-tailed LT dataset (see Appendix A), we find that tail-task performance drops substantially under LT, as shown in Fig. 1(a). Interestingly, some head tasks perform worse under FULL than under LT: more complete and diverse training data do not yield uniform improvements across all tasks. This leads us to consider whether the long-tailed multi-task learning problem is related to how different tasks jointly influence a shared policy. We further visualize the model’s attention during inference. Figures 1(b) and (c) show that head tasks attend reasonably well to visual evidence associated with the target object, but may exhibit more dispersed visual attention due to cross-task interference. Tail tasks face a more severe problem: they struggle to establish reliable task-specific visual grounding. Through the toy experiment in Section 3.1, we find that when such evidence is insufficient, the model must still produce an action, and the shared policy tends to fall back on frequent action patterns in the training data, giving rise to a head-task action bias. Thus, tail tasks do not merely suffer from insufficient data exposure; during decision-making, shared action priors associated with head tasks are more likely affect the visual evidence needed for the current task.

This finding raises a new question: how can we preserve reliable decisions on head tasks while preventing tail tasks from relying excessively on head-task action bias?

Thus, we introduce Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning (ECL), Without requiring additional annotations or training data, ECL directly uses the original data and a relation-aware counterfactual branch to identify visual evidence relevant to decisions during rollouts. It constructs counterfactual samples by removing key relational tokens and strengthens the associations among task instructions, visual relations, and actions through counterfactual training. Crucially, evidence guides both counterfactual construction and supervision in ECL, which adaptively assigns weaker regularization to head tasks and stronger supervision to tail tasks according to the number of demonstrations.

Our contributions: 1)We reassess the conventional view that tail-task failures arise from data scarcity and show through a toy experiment that, when task-specific visual grounding is insufficient, tail-task predictions fall back on action bias shaped by head tasks. 2) We propose ECL, which suppresses tail tasks’ reliance on action priors via counterfactual supervised training to build their task-specific evidence, without requiring extra annotations or additional training data. 3) We evaluate ECL on two VLA policies in LIBERO-Core-LT and on two real-world robot platforms, Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, with macro-averaged gains and task-specific outcomes reported.

title: VLMs are Native Action Models: Unleashing the Manipulation Capabilities of VLMs with Explicit Action-Space Grounding
authors: Jingkun Yi,Shujie Zhang,Zirui Zhou,Haoxiao Wang,Haiyang Sun,Yuhang Dong,Xudong Xu,Xing Shen,Tao Zhang,Yong Liu,Jiangning Zhang
abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already exhibit strong visual, spatial and reasoning capabilities relevant to robotic manipulation. The key challenge in turning pretrained VLMs into generalist manipulation policies is to expose these capabilities through an appropriate action interface. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified trainable policy, but typically introduce learned action tokens, action heads, or action experts whose semantics must be learned from robot data pretraining. In contrast, modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods can exploit pretrained VLM capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but rely on external planning and control scaffolds that are not end-to-end trainable as a unified continuous-action policy. In this work, we introduce EASG, an Explicit Action-Space Grounding framework that bridges these two paradigms. By projecting a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into the wrist camera observation and expressing actions in the form of VLM’s native textual generation interface, EASG makes the semantics of a continuous robot action space directly observable in the VLM’s perceptual context. This allows pretrained VLMs to directly generate executable robot actions using their existing visual-spatial reasoning capabilities, without robot-action pretraining or additional action modules. Besides, the same action interface supports direct fine-tuning with robot trajectories, allowing the models to continuously improve beyond their manipulation capabilities unleashed by EASG. Overall, EASG enables zero-shot manipulation and generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, while supporting effective fine-tuning in the same continuous action space. These results demonstrate that, given an appropriate action interface, pretrained VLMs can themselves serve as native action models for robotic manipulation.
introduction:
Advances in large-scale multimodal pretraining have equipped vision-language
models (VLMs) with strong visual, spatial, and commonsense reasoning
capabilities [7]. Many of these capabilities are directly relevant to robotic
manipulation. Yet turning a pretrained VLM into an executable manipulation
policy requires an appropriate action interface that connects its
perceptual and reasoning capabilities to robot control. To make this, such an interface is expected to first specify to the policy how actions should be represented and generated, such as incremental end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper commands. Secondly, it’s necessary to clearly state the semantics of the action space to the VLM, including the reference frames and the physical meanings of parameterization. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models construct such an interface by extending pretrained VLMs with robot-action representations learned from robot trajectories. A common strategy treats robot actions as additional
tokens [64, 34, 48, 50], while other
approaches introduce dedicated action modules, such as flow-matching or
diffusion-based action experts [4, 44] and continuous action heads trained with regression or parallel decoding
objectives [32]. Alongside these architectural advances, VLA
training has increasingly scaled to large and diverse robot
datasets [47, 31, 55, 6]. These
approaches provide a unified and trainable action policy and have led to impressive advances in generalist robotic manipulation.

However, the semantics of these robot action spaces are generally not directly available to the pretrained VLM before robot-action training. Robot trajectories must therefore teach the model not only what action to
take, but also how that action is defined in the physical world. First, the
model must infer in which coordinate frame an action is expressed and how it
is parameterized, since these conventions are typically only implicit in the
action labels. Second, precise control requires sufficiently accurate metric
geometry. The mapping from 2D visual observations to 3D physical motion is not
uniquely determined without camera geometry [22, 61, 29]: variations in camera intrinsics
and extrinsics can make visually similar observations correspond to different
robot physical displacements. Third, the policy must learn how embodiment-specific robot states relate to end-effector motion in Cartesian space, including the
relationship between robot configurations, end-effector states, and the
resulting visual changes. Learning these geometric and kinematic
correspondences jointly with manipulation behavior places a substantial burden
on robot data and model capacity. More fundamentally, it prevents the
manipulation-relevant capabilities already present in the pretrained VLM from being directly unleashed to generate executable task-space actions. Besides, extensive robot-action training may
further alter some of the visual-semantic and reasoning capabilities inherited
from the pretrained VLM [13, 21].

An alternative line of work exposes pretrained foundation-model capabilities
through explicit intermediate representations instead of learning the entire action interface from robot trajectories. These modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods generate policy programs [38],
spatial constraints over object parts [25], composable 3D value
maps [28] or relational keypoint
constraints [27], which are subsequently converted into robot
motion by downstream planners [35, 57], optimizers [54] or controllers [15]. By formulating manipulation problems in representations that pretrained foundation models can
already reason about, these methods can perform a range of tasks zero-shot without robot-action pretraining. However, the mapping depends on intermediate representations and external planning or execution modules without a unified action policy. Consequently,
the same VLM policy cannot be trained end-to-end in the continuous action space with robot trajectories through the interface that enables its zero-shot behavior.

The two paradigms therefore expose a complementary trade-off. VLA models
provide a unified and trainable action policy, but require the action interface
to be learned from robot data before the model can act. Modular
foundation-model methods can directly exploit pretrained capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but externalize action generation across separate
representations, planners, and controllers. This raises a natural question: Given an appropriate action interface, can a pretrained VLM serve directly as a unified manipulation policy that acts zero-shot
and can be further improved through robot-data fine-tuning?

To answer this question, we introduce EASG, an
Explicit Action-Space Grounding
framework that provides a unified action interface between pretrained VLM reasoning
and continuous robot control. EASG explicitly grounds the semantics of
a continuous robot action space in the VLM’s perceptual context by projecting
a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into first-person observations in the wrist view and providing metric information for action execution. Actions are expressed through the VLM’s native textual generation interface, so the pretrained model can directly map its existing visual-spatial reasoning to continuous robot
actions without adapting to a new robot-specific output modality.
Together, these designs allow pretrained VLMs to generate executable actions
without robot-action pretraining or auxiliary learned planning modules.
Crucially, the same action space and generation interface directly support robot-data fine-tuning, allowing the VLM to continuously improve the
manipulation capabilities initially unleashed by EASG.
To ensure reliable action generation through this native interface, we
further introduce grammar-constrained decoding, which restricts autoregressive
generation to valid action formats while preserving the pretrained VLM’s
original vocabulary and generation process.
Because the pretrained VLM itself generates robot actions through the same native
generation interface both before and after fine-tuning, we refer to it as a
native action model.
To summarize, our key contributions are as follows:

We introduce EASG, an Explicit Action-Space Grounding
framework that makes robot-action semantics directly accessible to
pretrained VLMs while preserving their native textual generation interface,
enabling them to act without large-scale robot-action pretraining.

framework that makes robot-action semantics directly accessible to
pretrained VLMs while preserving their native textual generation interface,
enabling them to act without large-scale robot-action pretraining.

We show that the same action interface supports both zero-shot manipulation and robot-data fine-tuning.

We empirically demonstrate the capability of VLM-native manipulation:
a 27B-scale VLM with EASG achieves comparable zero-shot performance with
fine-tuned VLA models, while a 0.8B-scale VLM fine-tuned with EASG achieves
competitive performance with several VLA baselines.

title: Cubic Spline Interpolation for Smooth Trajectory Generation in Autonomous Motion Systems
authors: Aarush Mandayam,Sriram Aditya Gundla,Elliott Tammaro
abstract: Trajectories for robots, drones, and other autonomous vehicles must pass through a sequence of prescribed waypoints while remaining physically realizable, meaning the underlying position signal should have continuous velocity and acceleration. Piecewise-linear interpolation between waypoints violates this requirement: velocity changes discontinuously at each waypoint, implying infinite acceleration. We describe a program that fits piecewise cubic splines to a set of waypoints specified as position-time pairs (xi,ti)(x_{i},t_{i}), enforcing continuity of the function value, first derivative, and second derivative across segment boundaries. The spline coefficients are obtained by assembling the interpolation and continuity conditions into a single linear system and solving for the unknown coefficients directly, removing the need to derive the per-segment equations by hand. We demonstrate the approach on two illustrative tasks: generating smooth free-form paths from a sparse set of user-specified points, and reconstructing continuous digital traces of handwritten signatures from sampled pen positions. We discuss the computational cost of the direct linear-system approach relative to the classical tridiagonal (moment-based) formulation, and outline the extensions needed to apply this method to multi-axis robot and drone trajectories subject to velocity and acceleration limits.
introduction:
A recurring problem in robotics, computer animation, and autonomous vehicle control is generating a trajectory that passes through a specified sequence of waypoints while producing motion that is physically executable. A naive solution connects consecutive waypoints with straight line segments (piecewise linear interpolation). This is simple to compute, but it is unsuitable for actuated physical systems: at each interior waypoint, the direction and often the magnitude of the velocity vector changes instantaneously. Since acceleration is the time derivative of velocity, a discontinuous velocity implies an infinite acceleration at that instant, which no real actuator, motor, or propulsion system can produce.

This limitation motivates the use of smoother interpolants. A trajectory that is C1C^{1} continuous (continuous position and velocity) removes the infinite-acceleration problem at the position level, but a trajectory that is C2C^{2} continuous (continuous position, velocity, and acceleration) is preferable for most physical systems, since acceleration commands are what feedback controllers on robots and drones ultimately track. Piecewise cubic polynomials are the lowest-degree polynomials that can be joined together to form a globally C2C^{2} curve while still leaving enough free parameters to interpolate an arbitrary sequence of waypoints; this is the classical cubic spline [1].

In more demanding aerial robotics applications, still higher continuity (up to the fourth derivative, or “snap”) is used so that the commanded thrust and body rates vary smoothly, as in minimum-snap trajectory generation for quadrotors [2]. Cubic splines represent the simplest member of this family: they guarantee only C2C^{2} continuity, but they are correspondingly cheaper to compute and are sufficient for many ground robot, camera path, and animation applications where jerk and higher derivatives are not explicitly constrained.

In this work we describe a program that automates the construction and solution of the cubic spline interpolation problem for a set of waypoints given as (xi,ti)(x_{i},t_{i}) pairs. Rather than deriving the spline coefficients for each new set of waypoints by hand, the program assembles the full linear system of interpolation and continuity constraints, and solves for the coefficient vector directly. We apply the resulting tool to two tasks that are not typically framed as robotics problems, but which exercise exactly the same underlying interpolation machinery: (1) generating smooth free-form curves (“abstract drawings”) from a small set of user-supplied points, and (2) reconstructing a smooth digital trace of a handwritten signature from a sparse set of sampled points lying on the signature. Both tasks illustrate that once a program can turn an arbitrary list of waypoints into a C2C^{2} curve, the same machinery is directly reusable for generating feasible motion commands for physical autonomous systems.

title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
authors: Minghao Fu,Tavis Siebert,Eryk Halicki,Randall Balestriero
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3×32.3\times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.
introduction:
Visual control requires autonomous agents to complete tasks by selecting actions based on visual observations of the world. World models address this challenge by predicting the consequences of candidate actions, allowing agents to anticipate how the world will evolve before executing them. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) (LeCun, 2022) offer a compact world modeling paradigm where future world states are predicted in latent space rather than by reconstructing pixels.
Recent works such as DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2024) and LeWorldModel (LeWM) (Maes et al., 2026b) demonstrate the promise of applying action-conditioned latent world models to downstream control. These pipelines obtain visual features from pretrained encoders (Zhou et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025), or train representations from scratch with distributional regularizers such as SIGReg (Balestriero and LeCun, 2025; Maes et al., 2026b) to prevent collapse. However, these methods alone do not reliably retain control-relevant information; JEPAs can favor temporally persistent distractors (Sobal et al., 2022), while action-conditioned dynamics may retain extraneous observation information (Brandfonbrener et al., 2023).

Control with these models typically requires an online solver such as the cross-entropy method (CEM) (Rubinstein, 1999) or a separately trained action predictor. When initialized with a broad Gaussian prior over action sequences, CEM demands extensive rollouts to identify viable candidates, particularly as action dimensionality or planning horizon grows (Huang et al., 2021). Contact transitions also complicate local action optimization because the dynamics can switch between modes (Pang et al., 2023). A post-trained action predictor can provide direct control, as in GC-IDM (Nguyen et al., 2026), or guide action search, as in PRISM (Wang et al., 2026). Training these predictors on frozen JEPA embeddings leaves action supervision disconnected from visual representation learning.

We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA that jointly learns
representation, action-conditioned dynamics, and a stochastic policy
in a single training stage (Figure 1). Training combines two ingredients: a joint training objective over next-latent-state prediction and action flow matching, and SIGReg (Balestriero and LeCun, 2025)
to regularize the latent states. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) (Liang et al., 2025) predictor uses clean actions for latent dynamics prediction and noisy actions for policy learning through flow matching, so both objectives train the shared visual representation. Consequently, LeWAM supports both direct policy execution and visual planning by refining action sequences sampled from its learned policy. Our contributions are threefold:

To our knowledge, the first JEPA that jointly learns representation, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and stochastic policy, using a joint prediction objective, one weight for latent-space regularization, and approximately 17M parameters.

A planning procedure that jointly imagines the consequences of actions and how to act in the resulting states, which samples candidate action sequences from the learned action distribution and refines them with gradient descent through learned dynamics.

Across ten heterogeneous simulated environments, LeWAM improves goal-reaching success over LeWM (Maes et al., 2026b), particularly on contact-rich tasks. Four-task comparisons extend these gains to longer goal horizons and show faster planning. On goal-agnostic task completion in simulation and physical robot execution, LeWAM performs competitively with established baselines. Linear probes reveal decodable physical-state and action information, recorded-action rollouts visualize its learned dynamics, and planner ablations measure the gains from its stochastic action proposals.

title: Gamma: Grounded Multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit for Memory-Intensive Manipulation
authors: Yudong Liu,Yueqian Lin,Zijia Tang,Yuxi Zheng,Yuan Li,Shuai Zhang,Yi Li,Taotao Jing,Shuangjun Liu,Dashan Gao,Ning Bi,Jingwei Sun,Yiran Chen,Hai Helen Li
abstract:
Pretrained vision–language–action (VLA) policies fail on memory
tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the
current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and
mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle’s
grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies
entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a
single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls
far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in
noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded
context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present Gamma
(Grounded multi-Agent Memory with
Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a
collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool
(SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each
replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text
memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits
the next grounded subgoal at the oracle’s cadence, wrapped in a
propose–verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or
rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at
training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task
memory-manipulation suite Gamma recovers a large fraction of the
oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several
tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies pretrained on large manipulation
corpora (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2023) now solve a wide range of tabletop tasks
from a single language instruction. Their training data, however, is
overwhelmingly Markov: the correct action chunk is a function of
the current observation and the instruction. Robot tasks in homes and
factories are frequently not of this kind. An agent that watched a
demonstration must reproduce it after the visual evidence is gone; an
agent that saw a container shuffle must remember which container now hides
which object; an agent asked to press a button after the fourth
pass of a moving object must count. On a recent memory-manipulation
benchmark (Dai et al., 2026) instantiating sixteen such tasks, the
π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), finetuned end-to-end, succeeds on only
a small fraction of episodes (Table 1).

Two observations make this failure a well-posed problem. First,
finetuning the policy on the benchmark under the standard instruction
leaves success low even when a memory module injects past frames into
it (0.1790.179 end-to-end, 0.4450.445 for the best memory-VLA architecture;
Table 1): the mapping from a long episodic history
to an action chunk lies far from the distribution the policy was
pretrained on. Second, the benchmark (Dai et al., 2026) ships the same
policy finetuned once to condition on a privileged oracle’s
grounded-subgoal text, one grounded sentence per action chunk such as
“pick up the container at ⟨105,87⟩\langle 105,87\rangle that hides
the green cube”, and it nearly solves the suite (0.8410.841): a
grounded subgoal returns the data to the pretraining distribution,
Markov, simple and direct, since the behaviour is again a function of
the current observation and one instruction-like sentence.
Subgoal-to-action is thus solved by the pretrained VLA’s own low-level
control; learning memory-to-action directly would couple that control
with high-level memory reasoning, the hard part, whereas decomposing
the problem as

The natural candidate for this first stage is a single VLM over the
episode’s frames, as in keyframe-memory pipelines such as
MemER (Sridhar et al., 2025): select a small set of informative frames, then reason
over them to produce the next subgoal. Benchmark results show that this family
falls well short of the oracle
(Figure 1), and our tick-level analysis
(Section 5.4) explains why. (i) Keyframe selection
loses information: nothing guarantees the decisive frame survives
selection, the selector’s policy is opaque, and a dropped frame is
unrecoverable. (ii) VLMs are weak at precise spatial grounding:
grounded subgoals carry exact coordinates, and a ⟨x,y⟩\langle x,y\rangle
off by a few pixels sends the policy to the wrong one of NN identical
objects. (iii) Reasoning over raw frames is hard: the key object’s
identity and motion are buried in redundant background, and the
frame-token context grows without bound. (iv) VLMs hallucinate:
a VLM asserts what is plausible rather than what is
observed, uniquely damaging in a memory system, where one false fact
enters the record and poisons every decision downstream. The first three
failures share a root—pixels are the wrong medium for episodic
memory—and the fourth demands that whatever medium replaces them be
verifiable.

We therefore build the memory stage as Gamma, a grounded
multi-agent system rather than a single model
(Figure 2). A segmentation-based detector
(SAM-3 (Carion et al., 2025)), called as a tool on every frame, supplies the
precise coordinates a VLM produces unreliably. A VLM writer (agent-1)
runs once per replan tick and distils its window of sampled frames,
their detections, the memory so far and the planner’s expected next
subgoal into at most one grounded text line, or none when the window
shows no task-relevant change. The append-only text memory bank is the
only history carrier: faithful (every line is evidence-gated against
its own frames), compact (hundreds of steps become a handful of lines)
and transparent (every coordinate in it came from the detector). A VLM
reasoner (agent-2) reads the bank alone, without pixels, and emits the
next grounded subgoal, trained to match the oracle stream verbatim at
its cadence. Grounded text alone does not remove failure (iv): in
closed loop the finetuned writer completed actions on a learned
schedule rather than on evidence, and both agents cited coordinates
they could not know (Section 5.4). Because the bank is
symbolic and grounded, every such claim is checkable, and we therefore
wrap both agents in a propose–verify harness
(Section 4.2, Algorithm 1): every claim
the agents make (an event line proposed for memory, a completion that
would advance the plan, a cited coordinate) is checked against
mechanical visual evidence and admitted, deferred until its evidence
appears, corrected to the evidence-consistent value, or rejected. The
same contract generates the supervision (Section 4.3): a
target line exists only at the window that shows its evidence and
cites only coordinates visible in the writer’s inputs, so the agents
are trained on the verified distribution the harness enforces at
deployment; the reasoner is further trained on banks written by the
trained writer rather than on ground-truth banks, so its training
distribution matches deployment.

Across the full suite, Gamma recovers a large fraction of the
oracle ceiling with the policy fixed (0.6600.660 average success against
the oracle’s 0.8410.841, 78.5%78.5\% of the privileged ceiling,
Table 2), reaching it on several tasks. Because the memory
is readable text, every failure can be attributed to a bank line or its
absence, yielding design principles validated in closed loop
(Section 5.4, Appendix C).

Contributions.
(1) A decomposition argument, backed by a controlled end-to-end-versus-
oracle gap under one fixed policy, locating the difficulty of VLA memory
tasks in the memory-to-grounded-subgoal stage.
(2) Gamma, a grounded multi-agent memory system (detector tool, VLM
writer, append-only text bank, VLM reasoner) that replaces opaque
keyframe selection with verified symbolic memory, and whose
propose–verify harness is a general contract under which every agent
claim (event, progress or grounding) takes effect only after a
mechanical evidence check that admits, defers, corrects or rejects it,
applied identically at corpus construction and at deployment.
(3) State-of-the-art memory-task performance with a fixed policy on
RoboMME, transfer with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark, and a
tick-level diagnostic protocol that turns closed-loop failures into
attributable, fixable memory defects.

title: Tactile Sensing-based Secure and Gentle Grasping of Unknown Objects
authors: Feng Han
abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires maintaining a firm grasp while strictly avoiding both contact slip and structural damage to the object. Satisfying these inherent secure-and-gentle grasping constraints is challenging for unknown objects. We present a novel online data-driven predictive control framework for safe dynamic robotic grasping of unknown objects. The proposed system features a pair of compact, single-channel tactile-sensing modules that characterize the gripper-object dynamic interaction in real time, entirely bypassing the need for prior knowledge or offline training. A finite-state-machine-based grasping force probing mechanism is developed to establish the initial grasping force and explicitly identify grasping force constraints. Through online dynamics learning, a Gaussian Process (GP) model captures gripper-object interaction dynamics. The model uncertainties are further used to form robust grasping constraints, which are embedded into a model predictive control scheme. We demonstrate error convergence in a probabilistic sense. The proposed control framework runs at 100 Hz in real time to dynamically manipulate and handle objects rather than static holding. Extensive experimental evaluations across diverse contact surface topologies and various types of objects validate superior performance and efficiency compared to baseline strategies. The proposed method is able to manipulate objects ranging from delicate items, such as raw tofu and marshmallows, to rough objects, such as rocks.
introduction:
Robotic grasping and manipulation offer great efficiency and dexterity across a broad spectrum of automated tasks. Notable examples include automated fruit harvesting in modern agriculture [1, 2, 3], dynamic food sorting and picking in the food industry [4, 5, 6], and the delicate and ultra-precise grasping and transporting of live organs during robotic surgery [7, 8]. With prior knowledge and offline training, these grasping tasks can be achieved safely. However, reliable robotic grasping of unknown objects remains one of the most fundamental yet challenging objectives in autonomous robotics [9, 10, 11]. When a robotic gripper interacts with unseen objects, the inherent but mathematically unknown grasping force constraints must be satisfied. The grasping force should provide secure but delicate contact to avoid contact slip, damage, or breakdown [9, 12, 13]. These constraints are related to the object’s mass, material compliance, friction, and contact interface topology, etc., which are completely unknown. Even the same object under different contact interface topologies with the same gripper will result in different interaction dynamics [14]. For instance, grasping a metal cube along diagonal portions or parallel edges requires significantly different forces.

Human grasping and manipulation of unknown objects take advantage of the coordination of vision and haptic-based force feedback [15, 10, 16, 17]. The advanced biostructure of human fingers is capable of adapting to the object’s geometry, size, surface topologies, etc. When handling objects out of the line of sight, human manipulation can still achieve success by relying fundamentally on blind haptic reflexes [18, 17]. During this process, humans learn the unseen object’s mechanical properties, “feel” the interaction mechanism online, and then adjust the applied force to reach a secure-and-gentle grasp [17, 14].

For robotic grasping, accurate sensing plays a significant role in characterizing the robotic gripper-object interaction mechanism and dynamic grasping control. Sensing technology can be categorized into contactless (i.e., vision-based) and contact (i.e., tactile/haptic-based) groups. Vision-based machine learning agents can recognize and label object types and prescribe a grasping force [19, 16, 20, 9, 13, 21]. However, such pipelines heavily depend on a pre-trained network over massive object datasets [22, 23]. Vision systems inherently suffer from critical degradation in occluded spaces and an inability to monitor visually unrecognized micro-slip at the interface [24, 25, 12, 13]. Furthermore, the computational cost of vision-based grasping is usually demanding, and the real-time control frequency is relatively low [26, 9]. For instance, in [26], video processing is used to handle tactile sensing feedback, and the control frequency can only reach 11 Hz. Tactile sensing provides an alternative by perceiving physical interactions through direct contact [27, 19, 14, 28]. Nevertheless, tactile sensing requires accurate calibration, and haptic feedback is inherently susceptible to distortions caused by complex contact surface topologies, localized stress concentrations, and vibrations [29, 30]. The uncertainties in sensing propagate into interaction dynamics characterization and control design. Under dynamic grasping with a time-varying reference force, the control system design must respect secure-and-gentle grasping constraints [9, 26].

To overcome the challenges in unknown object grasping, we propose a multi-phase, vision-free interaction dynamics learning and predictive control architecture. The proposed tactile mechatronics can adapt to different contact interface topologies and detect potential object slip or yielding while preserving the fidelity of the measurement. Additionally, a Gaussian Process (GP)-based calibration model accurately captures the interaction force from raw measurements with bounded uncertainties. The case-specific interaction mechanism is characterized online through a haptic-based finite state machine (FSM). The object geometry, stiffness, and grasping force constraints are identified systematically. Through online dynamics learning, a GP-based non-parametric interaction dynamics model is constructed. Together with the identified constraints, we design a robust model predictive control (MPC) scheme by incorporating both calibration and modeling uncertainties, ensuring grasping force control convergence and strict constraint satisfaction. The proposed control is data-efficient and does not depend on prior knowledge or datasets. Compared to the low-frequency control of vision-tactile sensing, the real-time control frequency of the proposed control reaches 100100 Hz.

Robotic grasping and manipulation encompass multifaceted innovations, including advanced gripper design, sensing and perception, actuation, modeling, and control. In the following, we review the most relevant work in the literature.

Robotic grasping has been used in various applications due to its dexterity, ranging from fruit harvesting in agriculture [1, 2, 3] and food-feeding in caregiving [15, 31] to raw material picking in manufacturing. For different applications, various gripper mechanisms have been developed, including rigid [13, 14, 32] and soft grippers [27, 28]. For instance, a compliant three-finger gripper is designed with embedded strain gauges in [19], while the work in [3] designs a hybrid robotic gripper combining six soft auxetic fingers with a rigid exoskeleton. Soft grippers can provide direct lifting force, whereas parallel-jaw grippers usually apply a normal contact force, with lifting force generated indirectly through friction [14].

Emerging tactile sensing technology provides direct information about the gripper-object contact interface at the interface [33, 34, 35], which resembles advanced human grasping feedback. To provide rich contact information, multi-tactile sensing arrays have been designed and integrated into gripper systems [14, 9, 16, 35]. However, the high nonlinearity of tactile sensors requires advanced calibration to address hysteresis, dead zones, saturation, etc. A popular approach in the literature is to use machine learning-based methods to interpret raw measurements and bypass the calibration process. Tactile sensing, in principle, measures pressure and is thus sensitive to the gripper-object contact profile, area size, slip, and vibrations, leading to inherent uncertainties and case-specific feedback [29, 30]. Integrated with vision systems, visual-tactile sensing combines the advantages of both modalities, providing rich feedback information for decision-making and control design [9, 13, 26]. However, the computational costs become very demanding, resulting in a low real-time control frequency (i.e., less than 5050 Hz).

A critical component in robotic grasping is contact force design and control. Since interaction dynamics are case-specific, most existing works either ignore the hidden nonlinear gripper-object interaction dynamics or embed them implicitly into the learning process [19]. The most popular approach designs the grasping force based on prior datasets [13, 22, 23]. Empowered by machine learning techniques, robotic grasping can perceive and recognize objects, with grasping forces designed accordingly to enable object-specific strategies. In [27, 36], raw tactile feedback is used for object recognition within a neural network. However, when grasping unknown, delicate objects, failures are commonly observed. Secure-and-gentle grasping requires adequate force without aggressive contact. The boundary grasping forces vary depending on the object’s mass, compliance, surface roughness, and contact topology [17, 14, 16], and they must be identified online. Meanwhile, most works in the literature focus on object grasp-and-hold tasks [37, 14] rather than dynamic grasping force control, which is critical in the presence of environmental uncertainties.

Additionally, PID, MPC [9, 26], and machine learning-based control strategies [27, 19, 38, 39, 16] have been proposed in the literature. Physical model-based control primarily focuses on gripper kinematic movement control rather than explicit gripper-object interaction dynamics [9, 27]. The MPC approach enforces constraints on gripper movement and contact force to ensure safe and secure grasping. In [9], an MPC is designed using gripper kinematics and vision-tactile sensing feedback. However, the constraints are only imposed on the kinematic movement of the gripper. Because the interaction dynamics remain unknown, there are no constraints involving the interaction force. Machine learning-based control is also popular given the complicated gripper-object interaction dynamics. In [27], raw tactile sensing data are directly processed in a neural network without calibration. End-to-end reinforcement learning neglects interaction dynamics, and the grasping force is designed through reward shaping [19, 38]. Learning from human grasping is another alternative [39, 16]. However, these learning mechanisms rely on offline training and have low transparency and adaptation to unknown objects.

The major contributions of the proposed online grasping dynamics control framework are summarized as follows:

The proposed tactile sensing module is compact, containing only a single-channel thin-film force-sensitive resistor (FSR). The module does not require an advanced tactile sensing array design nor significant alteration of the grippers and supportive mechatronics. Through GP-based calibration, the tactile sensing provides high-fidelity measurements regardless of the tactile contact interface topologies.

The proposed novel finite-state machine safely and explicitly identifies the object’s geometry, compliance, and object-specific grasping force constraints online in real time, which lays a solid foundation for secure and gentle grasping control. During this process, no prior knowledge or vision inspections are needed.

We explicitly learn the gripper-object interaction dynamics online. An MPC-based controller ensures force control performance and robust constraint enforcement within the information-theoretic envelope of the dynamics learning uncertainties and tactile sensing uncertainties. We provide a comprehensive theoretical proof to establish probabilistic stability and convergence, bounding the true but unknown force control error within a compact residual set. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no previous work has explicitly identified and incorporated the secure-and-gentle grasping force constraints of unknown objects into control design.

We validate the framework through extensive experiments, demonstrating superior control accuracy, slip prevention, and structural protection over baseline architectures across diverse types of objects, ranging from raw tofu to metal blocks. The control system reaches a real-time 100100 Hz frequency.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II outlines the system modeling and formalizes the robust dynamic grasping problem. Sec. III details the tactile sensor mechatronics design and calibration. Sec. IV identifies the initial grasping force and inherent secure-and-gentle grasping force constraints. Sec. V formulates the online interaction dynamics learning and robust MPC scheme and delivers the analysis for error convergence. Sec. VI presents the experimental setup, sensor configurations, and performance benchmarks. Finally, limitations and future research avenues are discussed in Sec. VII, and concluding remarks are provided in Sec. VIII.
