title: Multimodal Image-based Robotic Assistance and Guidance Environment (MIRAGE): A Novel Unified Framework for Surgical Navigation and Visualization
authors: Ehsan Nasiri,Yi Zheng,Michael A. Kokko,Xiaoyao Fan,William R. Warner,Keith D. Paulsen,Ryan J. Halter
comment: Submitted to the ASME Journal of Mechanisms and Robotics; currently under review
abstract: This paper presents the computational architecture and quantitative preclinical evaluation of MIRAGE, a multimodal image-guided robotic surgery framework for real-time visualization and navigation. It integrates stereovision scene reconstruction, augmented-reality (AR) video overlay, quantified heads-up display (HUD) navigation, and intraoperative ultrasound within the da Vinci console’s TilePro display (Intuitive Surgical). Additional modules include optical/electromagnetic tracker registration, stereo calibration, fiducial rigid registration with RMSE feedback, and 3D point-cloud reconstruction. Video I/O and rendering run in a C++ backend, while a Python GUI coordinates calibration, registration, reconstruction, visualization, and user interaction through an in-process zero-copy binding layer. The framework formalizes spatial transforms, module states, and synchronization of heterogeneous video and tracking streams. Preoperative calibration uses synchronized checkerboard image pairs and optimization, with estimated intrinsics, extrinsics, and rectification reused intraoperatively. MIRAGE was validated in phantom experiments across da Vinci S,Si, Xi, and SP platforms. Across clinically relevant working distances, mean 3D reprojection error was 0.6mm, with best 0.1mm RMSE at 100mm on Xi. Results support MIRAGE as a preclinical technical-validation platform for accurate, responsive, and extensible multimodal surgical guidance.
introduction:
Robotic surgery has been shown to improve patient outcomes, with lower morbidity rates compared to traditional open surgery [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
Image-guided surgery, also known as surgical navigation, is another form of computer-assisted intervention designed to give surgeons real-time intraoperative guidance. Its purpose is to enable precise and efficient access to target regions, support surgical planning, and minimize the risk of damage to surrounding critical structures[7, 8, 9].
Imaging modalities integrated with surgical robots include fluorescence imaging, augmented-reality overlays, and navigational displays [10, 11]. In urologic surgery for example, image-guided robotic systems employing near-infrared fluorescence imaging and augmented reality overlays have enhanced visualization of tumors and critical anatomy, improving surgical decision-making and functional outcomes [12, 13]. Similarly, in transoral robotic (TORS) procedures, the introduction of intraoperative imaging and navigational augmented reality helps surgeons overcome confined operative spaces and the lack of haptic feedback, thereby increasing the accuracy of tumor resection and safety near vital structures [14]. These advances, underscore a broader trend toward more precise, image-enhanced robotic interventions that improve oncologic and functional results for patients [10].

Recent development in image-guided and robotic surgery have explored a wide spectrum of visualization strategies, ranging from integral videography (IV) autostereoscopic displays for 3D overlays without head-mounted devices [15] to goggle-based and monitor-based augmented reality (AR) systems that project preoperative models into the surgical field [16, 17]. In urology, numerous groups have applied computer vision and machine-learning techniques to automate 3D model registration during robotic partial nephrectomy [18, 19, 20], while systematic reviews highlight the broader use of extended reality (AR/VR) tools for planning, navigation, and education [21, 22].
Similar approaches have been extended to TORS to assist with tumor localization [23, 24] and to robotic prostatectomy, where AR improved anatomical orientation but remained hindered by organ motion [17]. Across these studies, the main benefits include enhanced depth perception, improved anatomical visualization, and reduced surgeon workload, whereas persistent drawbacks involve soft-tissue deformation, registration inaccuracy, high computational demands, hardware costs, and limited large-scale clinical validation.

Many image-guided robotic surgery systems are still evaluated as isolated demonstrations rather than integrated, time-synchronized navigation frameworks. This paper asks whether heterogeneous imaging, instrument tracking, modeling, reconstruction, and overlay streams can be synchronized, fused, and rendered within a unified robotic surgery framework while preserving measurable navigation accuracy and real-time responsiveness across multiple robotic platforms.

Prior multimodal guidance systems in robotic surgery (e.g., [25]) have typically addressed only subsets of the sensing/visualization stack and left key integration gaps. In robotic prostatectomy, for example, Ukimura et al. [26] reconstructed TRUS-derived, patient-specific 3D models and displayed them on the da Vinci console via TilePro, reporting favorable margin outcomes but relying on preoperative data and static alignment. Samei et al.[27] integrated preoperative MRI with intraoperative 3D TRUS and live 2D TRUS in a “partial AR” scene shown beneath the endoscope feed on the surgeon’s console, improving situational awareness yet still constrained by registration quality and without optical/EM tracking fusion. Fusing optical and EM tracking instrument provides complementary robustness and tighter, continuous pose estimation of the endoscope and TRUS probe in a common frame, improving overlay accuracy under real operative dynamics. In [28] authors registered ultrasound/photoacoustic images to the da Vinci stereo camera via an arc-to-line optimizer and achieved sub-centimeter target registration error (TRE) in simulation/bench experiments, but the workflow remains preclinical and depends on photoacoustics hardware. Meza et al.[29] fused freehand ultrasound with structured-light surface capture (optically tracked) to one frame with sub-mm inter-modality error, demonstrating fusion accuracy but outside the robotic console and without endoscopic integration, so the surgeon is not able to see/fuse the modalities natively in the binocular console view. Classic stereo-vision pipelines (e.g., Stoyanov[30]) deliver real-time 3D tissue reconstruction from robotic endoscopy but are vision-only and lack fusion with other modalities (e.g., without any alternative imaging/sensing modules). In contrast, we introduce a unified, integrated framework that fuses preoperative stereo calibration, dual optical–EM tracking within a heads-up display(HUD)-TilePro navigation-visualization interface, live 3D stereo reconstruction (point clouds), 3D AR overlay, and live ultrasound streaming. This integration supports dynamic intraoperative registration within a console workflow. Component calibration accuracy and end-to-end target accuracy are distinct endpoints, since the latter also depends on registration, tracking, motion, and temporal association.

The novelty of this work is not the individual use of stereo calibration, rigid registration, learned disparity estimation, or AR rendering, which are established in the literature. Instead, the contribution is a unified, time-aware, and quantitatively evaluated architecture that coordinates these components within a single console-attached robotic surgery workflow. By defining cross-modal states, timestamp association, transform propagation, buffer ownership, synchronization rules, and evaluation metrics, the framework enables reproducible testing of multimodal surgical guidance under realistic system-level constraints.

Recent consensus guidance recommends evaluating surgical robotics through staged translation rather than technical feasibility alone, spanning device performance, usability, patient acceptability, health-system impact, and long-term monitoring (IDEAL) [31]. This is directly relevant to multimodal image-based robotic assistance and guidance environment (MIRAGE), where value depends not only on accuracy and frame rate, but also on workflow integration, user trust, failure mitigation, and reproducible evaluation across platforms and procedures.

Prior systems that utilize C++-Python software frameworks largely follow three major patterns:
(1) Code-generated monoliths (e.g., large simulators) auto-generate both the C++ API and the pybind11 [32] glue to form a single expansive Python module; this scales to evolving engines but introduces a generator/continuous integration (CI) toolchain and is not tailored to low-latency, heterogeneous device streams [33].
(2) Custom-designed interface over a single high-performance library deliver near–C++ speed, but typically bind one math-control stack rather than multiple device-module subsystems [34].
(3) Thin Python fronts over real-time C++ processes (e.g., shared-memory or bursting-mode toolboxes) keep hard real-time loops out-of-process in C++ and expose a minimal Python API. This helps determinism but adds orchestration and deployment complexity beyond the process boundary [35].

In the proposed multi-threaded multimodal system, most high-level modalities are implemented in Python, while video acquisition, rendering, calibration support, and selected hardware-facing modules are implemented in C++ and bound in-process via a custom-developed binding interface into a single Python orchestrator and GUI. The contribution is not the use of pybind11 alone, but the surrounding integration method: explicit buffer ownership, timestamped frame exchange, mutex-protected shared state, asynchronous worker management, and a unified state machine that coordinates C++ and Python modules. This design binds multiple heterogeneous C++ subsystems alongside Python-native modalities under one event loop, prioritizes in-process frame access over out-of-process shared memory, and exposes C++ frame buffers to Python through the buffer protocol when copy-free access is possible. Long-running C++ operations are isolated from the GUI event loop through worker threads and status callbacks. The system maintains a consistent timebase and timestamping policy to support Python-side data fusion and quantitative synchronization analysis.

The binding layer connects C++ acquisition and rendering to the Python interface through timestamped image and pose exchange, shared configuration, and worker-status callbacks.

The formulation brings the spatial transforms, timestamp association, and module interfaces into a common description of the integrated workflow. Registration and calibration use established methods [36, 37, 38, 30]; the integration analysis concerns their coupled spatial, temporal, and configuration dependencies.

Compared with general-purpose robotic middleware and application frameworks such as the robot operating system (ROS/ROS2), the da Vinci research kit (dVRK) or NVIDIA Isaac, MIRAGE is deliberately implemented as a single workstation, console-attached framework focused on image guidance rather than robot actuation. In our configuration, the robot is driven entirely by its native clinical console, while MIRAGE concentrates on integrating stereo video, tracking, and multimodal visualization-navigation on the same machine. Introducing an additional middleware layer
would add serialization, inter-process communication, and dependency-management overhead without clear benefit for this tightly coupled setup.The single-process design prioritizes direct frame access and a common application state on the console workstation. Related infrastructure includes OpenIGTLink for data exchange [39], Plus for tracked-image acquisition and calibration [40], 3D Slicer for extensible medical-image computing [41], and ROS 2 for communication and component composition [42]. Table 1 compares these roles with the application scope of MIRAGE. These complementary roles motivate comparisons with equivalent tasks, hardware, data-transfer policies, and timing boundaries.

The contributions of this research paper are summarized as follows:

[1.] A novel time-synchronized multimodal robotic surgery architecture that formalizes the coupling among stereo video, optical/electromagnetic tracking, AR overlay, stereo reconstruction, ultrasound, HUD navigation, and surgeon-console visualization within one state-driven framework.

[2.] A novel cross-language real-time integration method that defines explicit function mappings, buffer ownership, synchronization invariants, thread-safety rules, and state-transition models between a C++ video/rendering backend and Python-based navigation, reconstruction, registration, and GUI modules.

[3.] A temporal association and interpolation strategy for heterogeneous surgical data streams operating at different update rates, including video frames, tracker poses, rendering loops, and GUI events.

[4.] A quantitative evaluation protocol for multimodal image-guided robotic surgery systems, including calibration/reprojection error, fiducial registration error, overlay reprojection error, stereo reconstruction error, end-to-end response time, synchronization error, and platform-specific repeatability.

[5.] A comparative system-level analysis against representative prior image-guided robotic surgery approaches, identifying which capabilities are integrated within MIRAGE and which remain limitations.

[6.] Preclinical validation with phantom experiments across the da Vinci S, Si, Xi, and SP platforms, demonstrating the feasibility of real-time multimodal guidance and defining the next evaluation steps needed for IDEAL-aligned translational assessment.

This study asks whether heterogeneous imaging, tracking, reconstruction, and rendering modules can be integrated into a time-consistent robotic surgery navigation framework while preserving geometric accuracy and real-time responsiveness.

The following hypotheses organize the evaluation of spatial accuracy, temporal association, frame access, and repeatability:

H1: A unified transform chain preserves sub-millimeter to millimeter-scale calibration and registration accuracy across platforms and working distances.

H2: Timestamped multimodal association aligns video, tracking, rendering, and GUI events across different stream rates.

H3: In-process C++/Python integration enables real-time frame access and module switching without unnecessary frame duplication.

H4: The system supports reproducible quantitative evaluation of calibration, registration, overlay accuracy, reconstruction error, synchronization error, and latency.

This study is a preclinical technical and workflow validation, not evidence of clinical superiority or improved patient outcomes. Under IDEAL robotics [31], MIRAGE aligns primarily with stages 0–1, with early stage 2a elements, based on iterative development, integration with clinical robotic platforms, and phantom testing. Accordingly, evaluation focuses on integration, accuracy, real-time performance, reproducibility, and surgeon-facing visualization; clinical outcomes, learning curves, human factors, failure modes, health economics, and long-term surveillance remain future work.

5. [5.] A comparative system-level analysis against representative prior image-guided robotic surgery approaches, identifying which capabilities are integrated within MIRAGE and which remain limitations.

6. [6.] Preclinical validation with phantom experiments across the da Vinci S, Si, Xi, and SP platforms, demonstrating the feasibility of real-time multimodal guidance and defining the next evaluation steps needed for IDEAL-aligned translational assessment.

title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
authors: Taoyang Jia,Weikai Huang,Linxin Song,Jared Darlington,Jieyu Zhao,Yue Wang,Jiafei Duan,Zhongzheng Ren,Ranjay Krishna
abstract:
Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision.
We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects.
We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable.
In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers’ success at the same distances.
introduction:
Humans routinely react to fast-moving objects with their entire body.
A goalkeeper shifts, dives, and braces for an incoming shot; a worker catches a box tossed from a truck; a person reaches for a falling cup while stepping to keep balance; another twists aside as a cart passes unexpectedly close.
These behaviors require more than tracking an object in motion. They require predicting where it will go, deciding how the body should meet or avoid it, and coordinating a whole-body response before contact, often within about a second. Humanoids have the morphology to perform such behaviors, but robust visually reactive whole-body control remains largely out of reach.

This capability couples three challenges. First, the robot must control the whole body: it must place its feet and torso, move its arms into position, absorb impact, and remain balanced. Second, it must reflexively react to fast object dynamics under latency. In our real-robot trials, a thrown box reaches the robot roughly one second after release, while camera-to-control latency alone has a median of 69 ms in our detector-based pipeline. The robot therefore cannot simply react to the latest observation; it must infer where the object is going and commit to an interception before contact.
Third, it must do so from egocentric vision. Because the camera moves with the robot, observed image motion combines object motion with self-motion, while the robot’s own arms increasingly occlude the object near contact.

We study catching thrown boxes as a representative test of all three challenges. Catching a box is more demanding than intercepting a ball with the hands: the robot must reposition its body, use the forearms and torso to form a support, absorb the box’s momentum, and retain the load without losing balance. At the same time, the box is an ordinary uninstrumented object observed only through onboard RGB-D cameras. The task is difficult even for people: across our trials, three human catchers succeed on only 28.3% of throws from 7 m.

Existing systems address only parts of this problem. Robotic manipulators can catch moving objects from fixed or wheeled bases, avoiding the challenge of whole-body balance and impact absorption [1, 2, 3]. Recent humanoid systems demonstrate dynamic interactions such as punching away a ball [4] or catching a basketball with the hands [5], but rely on motion capture or retroreflective objects rather than grounding fast object motion from onboard vision.
As a result, whole-body control, fast prediction of object dynamics, and egocentric visual grounding have rarely been combined on a real humanoid.

We present Reflex, a three-stage framework for visually reactive whole-body control (see Figure 2). Stage 1 learns whole-body catching from privileged simulator state using reinforcement learning and human motion priors. Stage 2 learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed (20–60 ms latency) and incomplete observations of its position, velocity, orientation, size, and observation age, producing a latent representation that conditions the controller to react. Stage 3 learns to recover this same dynamics representation from egocentric RGB-D history and camera ego-motion while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. Our decomposition gives each capability a direct training signal and isolates expensive visual learning from reinforcement learning.

In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is vital for good performance; removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and 0.6 m-offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes on 65% and 40% of throws at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of the human success rate at the same distances (85.0% and 68.3%). Ablations further show that camera ego-motion matters for visual grounding, that regressing the learned latent works better than regressing the full privileged box state, and that action-matching initialization outperforms weight mapping by 5.2 points on average.

More broadly, our results suggest a path toward humanoids that can react to dynamic events directly from onboard vision, rather than relying on instrumented environments or task-specific perception systems. Catching is one instance of a broader class of visually reactive whole-body skills, including interception, avoidance, handoffs, and physical assistance. These everyday tasks require predicting how the world will change and coordinating the body before contact.

title: Verifier-Mediated Multi-LLM Coordination for Multi-Robot Path Planning
authors: Vivek Khatana,Zijian Song,Naira Hovakimyan,Petros Voulgaris
abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability.
introduction:
Foundation models provide a flexible interface for semantic reasoning, task decomposition, and high-level planning in robotic systems. In multi-robot settings, however, a plan that is individually meaningful for each robot may still be jointly infeasible after geometric grounding. Independently generated routes can intersect in space and time, violate shared workspace constraints, or create execution conflicts that are not apparent at the symbolic planning level. These failures motivate an execution-aware coordination mechanism between foundation-model reasoning and physical robot motion. A key architectural question is whether multi-robot foundation-model planning should be centralized or decentralized. A centralized planner can reason over the complete team state and generate coordinated plans jointly, but its context and decision space grow with team and task complexity. In contrast, decentralized planners provide modularity and local reasoning, but they require an explicit coordination mechanism to resolve conflicts between independently generated plans. Recent multi-robot LLM frameworks coordinate robot teams through centralized or decentralized symbolic reasoning and inter-agent communication [1, 2]. However, such symbolic coordination does not by itself ensure that the resulting plans remain physically feasible after geometric grounding.

This work studies verifier-mediated multi-LLM coordination. Each robot-level LLM proposes a symbolic task plan, which is grounded into an executable trajectory by a geometric planning layer. A shared execution-level verifier evaluates the grounded trajectories for obstacle and inter-robot conflicts. When a conflict is predicted, the verifier converts the failure into structured feedback—including the affected agents, conflict location, and conflict time—and returns this information to the appropriate LLM planner for targeted replanning. This creates a closed coordination loop between foundation-model reasoning and robot execution without requiring unrestricted natural-language negotiation. The framework is illustrated in Fig. 1.

The main contributions of this work are:

We formulate centralized and decentralized LLM-based architectures for multi-robot task planning under shared execution constraints.

We introduce a verifier-mediated coordination mechanism that converts predicted geometric conflicts into structured feedback for targeted multi-LLM replanning.

We empirically study coordination and task completion performance across increasingly complex multi-robot tasks in CARLA [3] and demonstrate transfer of the planning–verification–execution framework to Crazyflie [4] aerial robots.

Relation to prior work. Recent work has explored centralized and decentralized LLM-based multi-robot symbolic reasoning and coordination [1, 2, 5], as well as feedback and constraint-guided refinement of LLM-enabled robotic behavior [6, 7, 8]. Our focus is different: we use an external execution-level verifier to evaluate grounded multi-robot trajectories, detect physical conflicts, and return structured agent-specific geometric feedback for targeted multi-LLM replanning.

1. We formulate centralized and decentralized LLM-based architectures for multi-robot task planning under shared execution constraints.

2. We introduce a verifier-mediated coordination mechanism that converts predicted geometric conflicts into structured feedback for targeted multi-LLM replanning.

3. We empirically study coordination and task completion performance across increasingly complex multi-robot tasks in CARLA [3] and demonstrate transfer of the planning–verification–execution framework to Crazyflie [4] aerial robots.

title: Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving in Road Construction Zones Using Human-in-the-Loop Driving Data
authors: Shuo Zhang,Aman Sunesh,Semiha Ergan,Kaan Ozbay
abstract:
Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones
remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation.
Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane
layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating
interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers.
These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult
to predict. To address these challenges, we collect
WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset comprising
1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers,
using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with
prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers.
Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human
participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene
information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive, achieves a mean minADE6 of 1.09 m
and minFDE6 of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark,
WZDrive reduces minADE6 by 7.18% and minFDE6 by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop
data collection with multimodal learning from human
driving signals and in the context of work-zones. A project website with code and example data is available at
https://shuo9898-zs.github.io/wzdrive/.
introduction:
Roadway work zones are essential for maintaining and upgrading
transportation and utility infrastructure, but they temporarily change the
conditions under which vehicles operate. Maintenance activities can narrow
or redirect travel lanes and require drivers to respond to surrounding
vehicles, temporary traffic-control devices, and roadway workers in
constrained spaces. These temporary changes can create safety-critical
conditions for drivers and workers. In the United States, an estimated
101,000 work-zone crashes occurred in 2023, resulting in roughly 39,000
injuries and about 900 fatalities (Work Zone Safety Information Clearinghouse, 2026; National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, ). As aging infrastructure and continuing utility work sustain the need for maintenance and rehabilitation (Ullman et al., 2014), roadway work zones will remain a recurring part of road travel and an important setting for studying how vehicles adapt to temporary road configurations.

Ego-trajectory prediction estimates a vehicle’s near-future
motion to support autonomous driving (AD) and advanced
driver-assistance systems (ADAS).
In work zones, these predictions can help AD systems
assess where the vehicle is likely to travel and plan
safer paths around workers and nearby traffic.
For ADAS, they can support hazard warnings and corrective
control when a driver’s actions may lead to unsafe motion.
However, temporary lane changes and interactions with
vehicles and workers make prediction challenging.
Limited road space in urban areas can restrict standard
traffic-control layouts, while short-term work zones
may provide less warning and protection, leaving drivers
less time to respond.

Dedicated work-zone datasets have advanced scene
understanding and navigation.
EPOSH focuses on perspective-view and bird’s-eye-view
segmentation (Dwivedi et al., 2021), while ROADWork
provides rich visual annotations and reconstructed
driving paths (Ghosh et al., 2025).
However, ROADWork’s pathway-prediction task uses
spatially sampled waypoints derived from video-based
reconstruction rather than directly recorded vehicle
states at fixed time intervals.
General driving datasets, including nuScenes,
Argoverse, and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset,
provide temporal trajectories and established forecasting
benchmarks (Caesar et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2019; Ettinger et al., 2021). Yet their collection and evaluation protocols are not
specifically organized around safety-critical work-zone
conditions. This leaves a need for dedicated trajectory data and systematic evaluation of vehicle motion under these
conditions.

Human signals offer a potential means of addressing
prediction challenges that trajectory history alone
cannot resolve.
Prior work has developed immersive platforms for
collecting human driving signals (Silvera et al., 2022)
and explored EEG-based feedback and attention-based
guidance for ADAS and autonomous driving
(Zhuang et al., 2026; Zhuang et al., 2025; Biswas et al., 2024).
These studies motivate investigating human signals
as complementary information for predicting driving
responses in complex work-zone conditions.
We therefore propose a multimodal approach that combines
historical driver-control and attention signals with
vehicle trajectories, surrounding agents, lane geometry,
and temporary work-zone context. To address ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway
work zones, we recruited 33 participants to collect
driving data across six scenarios using a CARLA–SUMO-based
driving simulator with VR-controlled workers and
prerecorded worker animations
(Dosovitskiy et al., 2017; Lopez et al., 2018).

Our contributions includes:

Dataset: We collect WZDrive-Data,
comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments with
synchronized vehicle trajectories, driver signals,
and scene context across six scenario conditions.

Benchmark: We benchmark rule-based,
sequence, and state-of-the-art models for ego-trajectory
prediction in roadway work zones.

Model: We propose WZDrive,
which combines multimodal encoding and stage-wise
refinement to improve ego-trajectory prediction
over the evaluated baselines.

1. Dataset: We collect WZDrive-Data,
comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments with
synchronized vehicle trajectories, driver signals,
and scene context across six scenario conditions.

2. Benchmark: We benchmark rule-based,
sequence, and state-of-the-art models for ego-trajectory
prediction in roadway work zones.

3. Model: We propose WZDrive,
which combines multimodal encoding and stage-wise
refinement to improve ego-trajectory prediction
over the evaluated baselines.

title: StereoEngine: Scaling Stereo Bimanual Robot Data without Stereo Cameras
authors: Jason Chen,I-Chun Arthur Liu,Gaurav Sukhatme,Daniel Seita
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Stereo vision is increasingly used for robotic manipulation with a growing body of work incorporating it into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, the scarcity of large-scale, real-world stereo datasets remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling such policies. Recent generative monocular-to-stereo methods target settings such as VR content and autonomous driving. No prior work produces realistic synthetic stereo data for robotic manipulation where stereo supervision has come predominantly from simulation. We propose StereoEngine, which introduces two complementary methods to synthesize stereo data for robotic manipulation. In the first, we warp a monocular (left) video into the right view using estimated depth and inpaint the disoccluded regions with a video diffusion model which lifts monocular demonstrations into stereo pairs without training on real stereo. In the second, we render a stereo pair in simulation and jointly generate both photorealistic views which produces consistent left–right data without any real video as input. StereoEngine outperforms existing baselines in generated stereo quality, and using its synthetic data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves downstream bimanual manipulation. Project website: https://stereoengine.github.io.
introduction:
Imitation learning from teleoperated demonstrations has enabled increasingly capable bimanual manipulation systems [1, 2, 3]. Recent stereo-conditioned policies extend this by taking stereo observations as input and exploiting binocular views to improve spatial reasoning, including challenging cases such as transparent objects [4, 5]. However, scaling these stereo-conditioned policies to the point where they can be used for large-scale general imitation learning remains difficult, as large-scale robot datasets are overwhelmingly monocular and single-arm [6, 7, 8]. The few datasets captured with stereo cameras, such as DROID [9], are single-arm which means no large-scale bimanual stereo dataset exists. Collecting stereo demonstrations at comparable scale would require expensive stereo rigs and costly re-teleoperation. This motivates scalable methods to synthesize stereo data without additional real-world collection [10, 11, 12, 13].

While monocular-to-stereo synthesis has emerged as a promising direction [14, 15, 16], existing works target domains outside of robotic manipulation, such as VR/AR content [17, 18, 19, 20].
Reconstruction-based novel-view synthesis (e.g., NeRF [21], 3D Gaussian Splatting [22]) requires multi-view datasets and per-scene optimization on static scenes, unlike our dynamic single-view setting.
Methods that train on stereo pairs draw on simulation data that suffers from domain gaps or on only a small number of real pairs [23]. To our knowledge, no prior work synthesizes realistic stereo data directly from real robot video data.

To address the data bottleneck, we present StereoEngine, a scalable framework for synthesizing photorealistic stereo data for bimanual manipulation using video diffusion. StereoEngine provides two independent methods. When a real monocular demonstration exists, we convert it into a stereo pair by warping the left view and inpaint the disoccluded regions which are the surfaces that become visible in the right view but were never observed in the left. This preserves the appearance of the real data, though every generated pair remains tied to an existing demonstration. When no real video exists, we instead generate both views from a simulated trajectory, which allows data generation for entirely new tasks and configurations. Together, the two methods lift the abundant monocular data that already exists and generate new data where none exists, without ever training on real stereo correspondences.

We evaluate StereoEngine across 480 real-world rollouts spanning five bimanual manipulation tasks. See Figure 1 for a visualization of the diverse synthetic stereo pairs produced by StereoEngine.
Using ExStereo [24] and StereoVLA [5] as our downstream policies, mid-training [24] them on StereoEngine data—an intermediate stage between a policy’s large-scale pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning—or fine-tuning them on it directly, consistently improves manipulation performance and generalization over baselines.

The contributions of StereoEngine are:

StereoEngine-L, a monocular-to-stereo pipeline whose inpainter is trained without any real stereo pairs, using warp-derived masks, partial arm masks, and disparity dropout.

StereoEngine-S, which jointly generates both left and right views from simulation, needing no real video.

A large-scale bimanual robot stereo dataset released from both methods.

Real-world experiments showing that StereoEngine data improve stereo-conditioned policies through both large-scale mid-training (StereoEngine-L) and task-specific fine-tuning (StereoEngine-S).

1. StereoEngine-L, a monocular-to-stereo pipeline whose inpainter is trained without any real stereo pairs, using warp-derived masks, partial arm masks, and disparity dropout.

2. StereoEngine-S, which jointly generates both left and right views from simulation, needing no real video.

3. A large-scale bimanual robot stereo dataset released from both methods.

4. Real-world experiments showing that StereoEngine data improve stereo-conditioned policies through both large-scale mid-training (StereoEngine-L) and task-specific fine-tuning (StereoEngine-S).

title: Visual-Wi-Fi Navigation to Signal-Emitting Devices
authors: Lihao Wang,Tianjian Xu,Tianmin Shu,Renjie Zhao
abstract:
Indoor navigation to task-relevant targets remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, or visually indistinct.
Meanwhile, smart appliances, mobile devices, and IoT tags emit Wi-Fi signals during everyday communication, providing a pervasive but underused spatial cue.
We study visual–Wi-Fi navigation, where a robot reaches a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment using onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the device, without connecting to the device or modifying infrastructure.
Realizing this requires pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations during closed-loop policy learning and reliable spatial cues from bearing measurements corrupted by indoor multipath propagation on a moving robot.
We present WiFiSpaces, which extends the Habitat embodied simulator with online ray-traced Wi-Fi sensing, rendering Wi-Fi observations for a robot-mounted antenna array at continuous poses during policy rollouts.
On top of it, we build ViFiNav, a localization-aware navigation framework: an online source-localization algorithm exploits robot motion to disambiguate and robustly aggregate bearings from multiple viewpoints into a confidence-aware source estimate, and a learned policy fuses this evolving estimate with depth observations and learns to act on it as it is refined.
Experiments show that exploiting robot motion is key to accurate source estimates, and that fine-tuning on ray-traced Wi-Fi observations in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav. The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen scene datasets, and we deploy it on a real robot with a Wi-Fi sensor built from a commodity router, without any real-world training.
introduction:
Navigation in unmapped environments often involves locating and reaching task-relevant targets, including everyday connected devices such as smart appliances and mobile devices.
While visual navigation has made substantial progress [38, 20, 19], it remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, visually indistinct, or has no direct visual manifestation [46]. A vision-only agent then lacks an explicit spatial cue and must rely on weak semantic priors or broad exploration, producing inefficient trajectories.
Meanwhile, the growing prevalence of connected devices creates a new sensing opportunity: many indoor targets already emit wireless signals as part of their normal communication, which can be overheard by a robot-mounted receiver to provide complementary spatial cues.
As shown in Fig. 1, we study visual–Wi-Fi navigation: in an unmapped environment, an embodied agent uses onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the target’s existing traffic to navigate to the physical location of a signal-emitting target device. The target is defined by the Wi-Fi source location and need not be visible.

Unlike audio cues, which require the target to actively and continuously emit informative sound and are susceptible to environmental noise [7, 8, 35], wireless signals are emitted by ordinary devices as a by-product of communication and propagate through and around obstacles [16, 29], providing spatial cues beyond visual line of sight.
Among wireless technologies, we focus on Wi-Fi because it is the most pervasive: ultra-wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) localization typically require dedicated anchors or tags to be deployed and calibrated [15, 48, 47], whereas most household and personal devices, including IoT tags, already communicate over Wi-Fi (Fig. 1), and their packets can be overheard by a commodity Wi-Fi router without connecting to the device or its network [14, 16].
Wi-Fi is a deployment choice, not a requirement: the same setting arises for any wireless modality that carries spatial cues beyond line of sight.
However, autonomous navigation with Wi-Fi signals raises two key challenges.

The first challenge is to obtain pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations at scale for learning-based embodied navigation: during rollouts they must track the agent’s continuous pose, including heading, while reflecting the source location and the 3D geometry that shapes propagation, reflection, and blockage.
Precomputed radio maps do not fit: they tabulate the signal on a discrete grid and would have to be rebuilt every episode as the source moves, over poses that are policy-dependent and unknown in advance.
To address this, we propose WiFiSpaces, to our knowledge the first embodied navigation simulator to provide online Wi-Fi observations at the agent’s current pose, by extending Habitat with a Wi-Fi sensor built on physics-based ray tracing [1]; synchronizing agent state with the wireless scene at every step and reusing scene geometry across episodes makes online ray tracing practical for closed-loop policy learning.

The second challenge is to turn noisy Wi-Fi measurements into reliable spatial cues on a moving robot. Each overheard packet yields channel state information (CSI) at the router, from which a bearing to the source can be estimated [23, 16], but indoor multipath makes single-vantage bearings heavy-tailed: in WiFiSpaces, about 10%10\% of raw bearings are off by more than 30∘30^{\circ} (Fig. 7(a)), consistent with real deployments [23, 40, 11], and acting on such an estimate commits the robot to the wrong part of the scene.
To address this, we present ViFiNav, a localization-aware visual–Wi-Fi navigation framework: an online Wi-Fi source localization algorithm resolves the directional ambiguity of the small antenna array using the robot’s natural motion and robustly aggregates multi-view bearings into a confidence-aware source estimate, and, rather than heuristically following each intermediate estimate, a learned multimodal policy fuses this evolving cue with visual observations and learns to act on it in closed loop.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

A complete system for visual–Wi-Fi navigation, which we formulate as reaching a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment from visual observations, odometry, and Wi-Fi packets overheard from its existing traffic, without modifying the target device or infrastructure.

WiFiSpaces, an embodied navigation simulator that provides online ray-traced Wi-Fi observations synchronized with continuous agent poses during policy rollouts.

An online Wi-Fi source localization algorithm coupled with a reinforcement-learned policy that learns to act on its evolving estimates.

Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment: fine-tuning in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav over the same policy without Wi-Fi fine-tuning, and the policy generalizes zero-shot across indoor scene datasets; the same policy is further deployed on a real robot with a commodity-router Wi-Fi sensor [14, 16], without any real-world training.

1. A complete system for visual–Wi-Fi navigation, which we formulate as reaching a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment from visual observations, odometry, and Wi-Fi packets overheard from its existing traffic, without modifying the target device or infrastructure.

2. WiFiSpaces, an embodied navigation simulator that provides online ray-traced Wi-Fi observations synchronized with continuous agent poses during policy rollouts.

3. An online Wi-Fi source localization algorithm coupled with a reinforcement-learned policy that learns to act on its evolving estimates.

title: REMM: Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation
authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran,Ruwan Wickramarachchi,Alessandro Oltramari,Jonathan Francis
abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with π0.5\pi_{0.5}-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.
introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation requires more than executing a sequence of independent skills. Each action changes the world in which subsequent decisions are made, and information needed later may no longer be directly observable: which object was handled first, what remains inside a container, or where an object was placed before becoming occluded. Such tasks therefore require decisions that depend on interaction history under partial observability [1, 2]. Yet retaining history alone is insufficient. A previously valid relation may cease to hold after a slip, human intervention, or environmental rearrangement. A robot must therefore preserve what happened while revising what is currently supported by the available evidence.

Generalist robot policies have substantially improved the execution of individual manipulation skills [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Recent models further extend language-conditioned control to long-horizon settings; in particular, G0.5 provides an autoregressive interface that interleaves reasoning and action generation within a single policy [7]. However, a capable executor does not by itself determine what should happen next when the relevant evidence is old, hidden, or contradicted by a subsequent physical intervention.

Recent work equips manipulation systems with temporal context through learned memory banks, sparse visual events, or retrieved keyframes  [2, 8, 9]. Hierarchical systems instead place memory and reasoning above the motor policy: HiMe  [10] maintains editable multimodal memory, while HyMeS  [11] and BATON [12] steer reusable or frozen skills using external verification and transition-aware memory. These methods establish that memory can extend a policy beyond its immediate observation. They also sharpen a different question: after evidence changes, which earlier conclusions should change with it?

Closed-loop planners can incorporate success, scene, or human feedback into subsequent decisions [13]; structured world representations encode relational scene state [14]; and dynamic memories can add, delete, or modify stored relations as new evidence arrives [15]. Yet these capabilities do not explicitly track which physical relations support previously completed task conditions. If such a relation changes without revising its downstream consequences, the controller can retain an internally coherent but physically stale task state. We therefore consider an intervention-grounded process memory in which physical relations, derived scene state, and completed task conditions are connected through explicit support dependencies. When verified evidence changes an upstream relation, its affected consequences can be selectively withdrawn. These dependencies are supplied by task and physical semantics rather than learned through causal discovery; their use as recorded justifications is related to truth maintenance [16], while remaining distinct from causal world models that learn or probabilistically infer manipulation outcomes [17, 18].

We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory layer around a frozen G0.5 executor. REMM preserves an append-only evidence history while maintaining a separate projection of currently supported state. It records causal dependency links from physical relations to derived and completed task conditions; when verified evidence supersedes a parent relation, REMM invalidates affected descendants, identifies the broken task obligation, and schedules a bounded recovery instruction at the next verified stationary skill boundary. This produces an inspectable path from physical intervention to memory revision and changed control without REMM-specific parameter training.

We evaluate REMM on real-robot tasks involving transport disruptions, delayed sequence recall, and hidden-object rearrangement. The evaluation separates retention from revision: sequence and hidden-object tasks test whether decision-relevant history persists through delay and occlusion, while transport interventions test whether previously valid task state is correctly withdrawn and repaired after the world changes. Beyond end-to-end task success, we measure change acceptance, dependency revision, recovery timing and destination, physical repair, and the observed memory-to-control trace. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall, while completing all four of its hidden-object trials.

Our contributions are threefold:

a formulation of revisable embodied memory that separates recorded execution history from currently supported task state and represents intervention-sensitive dependencies from physical relations to derived and completed task conditions;

REMM, a supervisory system that propagates dependency invalidation and dispatches nominal or recovery instructions to a frozen G0.5 policy without REMM-specific parameter training; and

a controlled real-robot evaluation that traces observed changes through memory revision to subsequent control decisions across transport, sequence-recall, and hidden-object manipulation tasks.

1. a formulation of revisable embodied memory that separates recorded execution history from currently supported task state and represents intervention-sensitive dependencies from physical relations to derived and completed task conditions;

2. REMM, a supervisory system that propagates dependency invalidation and dispatches nominal or recovery instructions to a frozen G0.5 policy without REMM-specific parameter training; and

3. a controlled real-robot evaluation that traces observed changes through memory revision to subsequent control decisions across transport, sequence-recall, and hidden-object manipulation tasks.

title: FallGown: A Soft Pneumatic Wearable Device for Fall Prevention
authors: Megan C. Coram,Haoran Lei,Steven H. Collins,Steve B. Cousins,Michelle Baldonado,Cynthia Sung,Allison M. Okamura
abstract: Concerns about falling and potential resulting injuries prevent many older adults from participating in forms of health-improving exercise such as walking, dance, and tai chi. Existing passive devices like walkers require use of the arms for support, and active devices like exoskeletons and robotic frames are often rigid, bulky, and stigmatized, which limits their use. The FallGown is a soft wearable support structure consisting of pressurized pneumatic pouches within a fabric shell; it can support the full weight of a user’s body and aims to prevent falls. It is portable (6.9 kg and 0.051 m3 when stored), minimally burdensome (7.24-20.8 N drag force depending on floor type and whether an optional rolling base frame is used), and convenient (less than 2.5 minutes on average to don and less than 0.5 minutes on average to doff). The optional rolling base lowers friction with the floor, but reduces portability and skirt deformation (which can be useful to fit through doors and other tight spaces). Fall prevention testing with a single user revealed a tradeoff between device size and stability against tipping; a skirt with 12 pneumatic pouches and a floor diameter of 1.4 meters with a base frame prevented all falls except in one case with a mechanical failure. On-board pressure sensors can sense the user’s weight distribution, providing an opportunity for monitored exercise and adaptive support.
introduction:
Wheelchairs and walkers are traditional passive devices that support mobility for adults with weakness, poor balance, and other movement challenges. Robotic versions include autonomous wheelchairs [1], frames [2], and handles [3]. Exoskeletons reduce footprint and provide more versatile locomotor assistance in unstructured environments [4]. However, the rigidity of traditional robotic mechanisms can create discomfort, and their bulkiness can limit portability. In a recent review of the state-of-the-art of robotics to assist mobility, physiotherapists and patients highlighted the following needs: safety, a one-size-fits-all approach, ease of device use, weight and placement of the device, cost of the device, and appearance of the device [5]. Negative perceptions of the appearance of an assistive device can result in stigma and reduce adoption, even for occupational scenarios [6]. Another recent survey found that fall prevention was the most (according to clinicians) or second-most (according to older adults) important feature that a wearable assistive device could offer [7].

Approaches using techniques from the field of soft robotics aim to make exoskeletons easier to wear and use, and potentially less noticeable. However, they can still be difficult to don and doff, and they are usually not able to support the user’s full body weight. Exosuits are one form of “soft” support; they have no rigid frame to bear compressive loads, rather they use fabrics and tensile elements, usually cables, anchored to the body to apply forces in parallel with the wearer’s own muscles [8, 9, 10]. Some exosuits pass applied loads through the user’s own joints, which could lead to painful changes in the magnitude and direction of joint loading. Inflatable support devices (sometimes referred to as exomuscles) have been designed to support a single joint in research projects [11, 12, 13] and commercial products like the torsional air-driven bladder used for knee support by Roam Robotics, Inc. The authors are not aware of any portable inflatable lower-body device that attempts full body-weight support.

We were inspired to create a new form of mobility support device based on the following challenge presented to our research team by a local older adult day care center: During individual or group low-impact exercises, such as dance and tai chi, older adults’ fear of falling will often cause them to opt out of physical activities or, if they choose to participate, keep them in a wheelchair or grasping a walker. Avoiding activity altogether for fear of falling can have negative impacts on long-term health [14], but reliance on current assistive devices prevents users from performing whole body movements, which are important to maintain strength and coordination and key to the aesthetics of the performance. Hands-free walkers such as the LifeGlider and Merry Walker permit arm movement, but they may still encounter the same stigma as traditional walkers, which limits their adoption. To address this challenge, we aimed to combine features of existing passive mobility support devices with soft wearable robotics. We created FallGown (Fig. 1), an inflatable skirt that is donned via a conventional climbing harness and zippers, can support a user’s weight, and has a conical shape wide enough to resist falls for a variety of user movements. As a fashion statement, FallGown evokes a ball gown and is very noticeable; it counters the clinical aesthetic of prior assistive device designs.

The primary contribution of this work is a new inflated assistive wearable device that aims to support hands-free exercise for people with weakness, poor balance, and other movement challenges that limit beneficial exercise. A secondary contribution is a series of evaluation methods that address key assistive technology needs identified by patients and physiotherapists.

title: Spa-Bench: A Real-Robot Benchmark for Spatial Grounding in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Justin Tien-Smith,Matthew Pidden,Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State, Relative Size, Referential Description, Relational Placement, Ordinal Position, and Counting. Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5–73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7–52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3–40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot learning. By connecting pretrained vision-language representations to robot actions, these models can transfer semantic knowledge acquired from internet-scale data into language-conditioned control [1, 4, 10, 12]. This transfer promises robots that can respond to new objects, instructions, and environments without requiring a separately trained policy for every behavior.

Policies evaluated on existing benchmarks have demonstrated increasingly broad manipulation capabilities, including generalization across objects, instructions, visual conditions, and task sequences [5, 6, 20]. Nevertheless, completing a manipulation task does not by itself establish that a policy has correctly interpreted the spatial structure of its environment. Spatial understanding in existing benchmarks is typically embedded within an overall task-success metric and is consequently entangled with object recognition, language interpretation, and motor execution. If a policy fails to place a green pen to the left of a red block, for example, the failure could arise from incorrect spatial grounding, failure to identify the objects, an unsuccessful grasp, or an inability to execute the required placement due to an inadequate number of demonstrations spanning the full workspace. Furthermore, benchmarks that introduce a fixed scene to mitigate some of these issues introduce a different problem: Success may result from memorizing recurring object locations or action patterns rather than from grounding the instructed spatial relation.

In this work, we use spatial grounding to describe the ability to map language about properties, positions, quantities, and relations in the current physical scene to an appropriate target, goal configuration, or decision not to act. We study this capability through the following question:

How reliably can current VLAs ground spatial descriptions into appropriate actions in the real world?

Answering this question requires more than measuring success on an ordinary held-out task. A test task that simultaneously introduces an unfamiliar object, instruction, spatial concept, or physical behavior cannot reveal which of these changes caused a failure. A diagnostic spatial benchmark should instead establish familiarity with the constituent objects, concepts, and manipulation behaviors before evaluating whether the policy can use the relevant spatial information in a different physical configuration.

We introduce the Spatial Grounding Benchmark (Spa-Bench), a controlled real-robot benchmark designed around this principle. Spa-Bench comprises six tabletop tasks evaluating the grounding of Object State, Relative Size, Relational Placement, Referential Description, Ordinal Position, and Counting. All tasks use the same robot embodiment, workspace, receptacle, and broad pick-and-place action family. The principal source of variation is therefore the scene-grounded rule that determines which object should be manipulated, where it should be placed, or whether movement is even required.

Spa-Bench evaluates policies in ID and OOD spatial configurations. ID configurations measure whether a policy has acquired the spatially grounded behaviors represented in its demonstrations. OOD configurations change the association between a spatial concept and its task argument while preserving training support for the relevant objects, physical actions, and spatial concepts. We implement this controlled split through a withheld-cell design: each component of an OOD evaluation configuration appears elsewhere in training, but their particular combination is reserved for evaluation (see Fig. 3). The purpose of this construction is to reduce object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure.

To characterize spatially grounded performance beyond the primary ID–OOD comparison, Spa-Bench includes four additional diagnostic conditions that probe complementary aspects of policy behavior. Direct-manipulation controls remove the need for spatial inference while preserving the requested robot motion. Prompt-paraphrase trials restate both OOD spatial and direct-manipulation instructions on the same scenes, testing whether their performance gap depends on exact wording. Cross-task-object rollouts vary the usual association between an object and task. Finally, no-intervention scenes test whether a policy can recognize when no action is required.

Spa-Bench contains 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations, with 200 demonstrations for each task. We evaluate five fine-tuned state-of-the-art policies that are drawn from four different VLA architectures: VLA-0, MolmoAct2, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, GR00T-N1.7 Frozen LLM (GR00T-N1.7 F-LLM), and GR00T-N1.7 Full Fine-Tune (GR00T-N1.7 F-FT). Three policies complete the full 900-rollout evaluation protocol, producing 2,700 evaluation episodes, while two partial baselines contribute 192 episodes. In total, we release 4,092 SO-101 episodes, including the demonstrations, rollout videos, task specifications, and documented scene layouts.

Across the three fully evaluated policies, ID spatial-configuration success ranges from 67.5% to 73.3%, but success decreases to 40.7%–52.0% in OOD spatial configurations. On the OOD spatial configuration matched scene subset, direct-manipulation instructions achieve 81.7%–89.2% success, showing that many of the physical behaviors are executable even when the policy fails under a spatially grounded instruction. Performance is strongly task dependent: all three policies fail every OOD Counting trial, almost always without acting; other tasks are dominated by target-selection or spatial-outcome errors. The direct manipulation advantage also persists when both instruction types are paraphrased, revealing that the state-of-the-art VLAs we evaluate do not exhibit robust spatial grounding. In summary, our core contributions are:

We introduce Spa-Bench, a six-task real-robot benchmark for evaluating spatial grounding across ID and OOD physical configurations.

We introduce Spa-Bench, a six-task real-robot benchmark for evaluating spatial grounding across ID and OOD physical configurations.

We develop a controlled evaluation protocol that combines a withheld-cell split with four diagnostics that probe physical execution, wording sensitivity, object context, and action gating.

We evaluate five fine-tuned VLA policies and release 4,092 SO-101 episodes, including 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 evaluation rollouts, together with task specifications and scene layouts.

2. We develop a controlled evaluation protocol that combines a withheld-cell split with four diagnostics that probe physical execution, wording sensitivity, object context, and action gating.

3. We evaluate five fine-tuned VLA policies and release 4,092 SO-101 episodes, including 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 evaluation rollouts, together with task specifications and scene layouts.

title: Non-Prehensile Multi-Object Placement with Mobile Robots via Diffusion-Based Trajectory Planning
authors: Lance Pharand,Megnath Ramesh,Mark Chiu,Yash Vardhan Pant,Stephen L. Smith
abstract: Non-prehensile manipulation with mobile robots has primarily targeted placement in coarse goal regions. Precision placement has been studied with manipulators on benchmarks such as Push-T, where an omnidirectional end effector can readily re-approach an object from any side. For a mobile robot, correcting the same placement errors may require wide repositioning maneuvers around the object. We formalize multi-object pushing with a mobile robot as a multi-target assignment problem at tight tolerances. We propose a diffusion planner with a causal factorization: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. This factorization allows us to sample multiple object outcomes for a single robot plan, capturing the multi-modality of pushing. We also design a set of pushing-specific costs for mobile robots, used for both guidance and best-of-NN sampling at inference. On Push-T, our planner attains the highest success rate of the methods we compare, while having the lowest rate of implausible object motion. Across three multi-box pushing environments resembling warehouse scenarios, it raises the fraction of boxes placed by 21.521.5 percentage points over an unguided baseline, and replans 1.8×1.8\times faster than a planner that denoises the two trajectories together. Lastly, we deploy the guided planner on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with object shapes absent from the training data, where it places 85.0%85.0\% of objects within tolerance against Diffusion Policy’s 37.5%37.5\%.
introduction:
In this work, we focus on the problem of multi-object pushing with a mobile robot. Formally, this is a multi-target assignment problem, where each object must be placed inside a tight target configuration (Fig. 1). Successfully solving this problem would make mobile robots viable for warehouse tasks where they must push boxes or pallets to precise positions for downstream automation to take over. Precision pushing has been studied in the manipulator setting, where Push-T [1, 2] is a popular benchmark [3, 4]. Here, a robot with a circular end-effector must push a T-shaped block onto a goal pose, with success requiring near-complete overlap. In contrast, existing non-prehensile manipulation (NPM) work with mobile robots [5, 6, 7] only requires the object to land inside a target zone much larger than the object itself.

Two properties of the mobile robot setting make pushing an object to within a small tolerance of a target harder than it is in the manipulator setting. First, mobile robots typically have non-holonomic dynamics and cannot move sideways. Second, the robot’s contact face is typically a non-prehensile bumper fixed to the front, so changing the side of the object being pushed requires a wide reposition. Both aspects make it difficult to perform the small corrections needed to bring an object within a tight tolerance of its target. In contrast, the end effector in Push-T can move sideways, is omnidirectional, and can re-approach the object from any side. Planners and policies for the studied setting must account for the difficulty of these corrections, but existing mobile robot NPM methods are evaluated in settings where this is not necessary.

Diffusion-based planners have shown promise in solving difficult pushing problems [3, 4]. Diffusion planners that predict object motion typically denoise the robot and object trajectories simultaneously [8], which can yield object motion that is implausible given the robot’s actions. We instead factorize the joint trajectory distribution into a robot trajectory prior and an object trajectory conditional. Each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate (Fig. 2). As a result, guidance can be evaluated on a predicted object outcome that is a response to the current robot plan, and its gradient is backpropagated through that response to improve the robot plan. The Causal factorization also lets us sample several object outcomes for a single robot plan, which is beneficial as pushing is multimodal [9]. Our main contributions are:

We formulate and evaluate multi-object placement by a mobile robot under tight spatial tolerances, requiring each object’s footprint to lie within its target region and previously completed placements to remain undisturbed. We assess how placement tolerance affects execution success across multiple environments.

We formulate and evaluate multi-object placement by a mobile robot under tight spatial tolerances, requiring each object’s footprint to lie within its target region and previously completed placements to remain undisturbed. We assess how placement tolerance affects execution success across multiple environments.

We propose a diffusion-based planner that uses a Causal factorization of trajectory denoising for non-prehensile pushing. With this, each robot denoising step is followed by an object step that is conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. We also propose a guidance formulation for this factorization, together with a set of differentiable cost terms tailored to mobile robot pushing.

In this work, our evaluation spans the Push-T task, three unseen mobile robot pushing environments, and a hardware deployment on a TurtleBot 3 Burger, with analysis of the planner’s capabilities and limitations.

Diffusion-based trajectory planners have been applied to both short and long-horizon tasks, both of which arise in NPM. At short horizons, the planner samples a trajectory, executes a portion of it, and then replans [1, 3]. Long horizon settings instead tend to rely on trajectory stitching, where a full plan is composed from sub-trajectories already present in the training distribution [8, 10]. Closest to our proposed factorization is MBA [11], which also splits robot and object denoising into two phases. However, MBA fully denoises the object trajectory first and conditions the robot denoising on that finished prediction, whereas our phases alternate within each denoising step. Diffusion Forcing [12] also orders denoising, but through per-token noise levels rather than separate phases, resolving lower-noise tokens first. Unlike our method, most of these planners do not apply guidance at inference, which can limit their ability to adapt to task settings outside their training distribution at deployment.

Guidance is applied to diffusion models across many domains such as image generation [13, 14, 15], autonomous driving, and robotics. Diffuser [16] steers plans by nudging the denoising process along the gradient of a learned return predictor. However, the performance of this learned model on novel scenes is dependent on its training distribution. Diffusion-ES [17] skips gradient-based guidance entirely. Instead, it samples trajectories from an unconditional diffusion model, scores them with a reward function, and projects elites back onto the data manifold. This keeps the trajectory distribution broader and improves robustness, but the search across iterations is expensive. Diffusion Planner [18] is a transformer-based driving planner that relies on hand-designed energy functions at inference, eliminating the need for an auxiliary model. Our work builds upon this concept in two ways. First, we extend these energy functions to have asymmetric penalties for precision pushing tasks. Second, we add a per-term gradient rescaling that lets each term’s contribution be tuned independent of its native scale and units.

Diffusion-based trajectory planners have been applied to pushing in non-precision settings, beyond just Push-T. CompDiffuser [8] reports encouraging results on AntSoccer, where a quadruped agent pushes a ball to a goal location, and HeRD [7] demonstrates similar gains in a multi-object box environment. Precision has instead been pursued through reinforcement learning by [19], who train a recurrent policy that pushes single objects to within 1 cm of the goal. To the best of our knowledge, no diffusion-based planner targets multi-object NPM with a mobile robot at tight tolerances.
