title: Robust and Scalable UAV-UGV Planning for Aerial Monitoring under Energy and Precedence Constraints
authors: Cahit Ikbal Er,Yasin Yazicioglu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: We consider planning for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) teams in aerial monitoring missions with ordering requirements on the monitoring points to be visited by the UAV. The system consists of multiple UAV-UGV teams, each comprising one UAV and one UGV. UAV energy limitations are modeled through endurance, defined as the maximum flight time on a full battery. The UGVs serve as mobile charging stations and transport the UAVs between consecutive aerial tours. Given a set of monitoring points subject to ordering constraints and the teams’ initial and terminal positions, the objective is to minimize mission completion time while satisfying UAV energy limits and the required visit order under bounded travel-time disturbances that may arise during execution. Unlike prior work, the plan jointly determines vehicle routes and their timing, allowing teams to slow down as needed to satisfy the ordering constraints. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm that generates efficient solutions to the underlying NP-hard planning problem. We establish feasibility guarantees, characterize the algorithm’s computational complexity, and evaluate its performance via numerical comparisons.
introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are used in various domains such as agriculture and environmental monitoring (e.g., [1, 2]). However, their limited energy restricts missions defined over large areas or long time-horizons. Using unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) as mobile charging stations addresses this limitation by providing a flexible alternative to fixed recharging infrastructure.
Recently, energy-constrained planning of UAV-UGV teams has gained significant attention (e.g., [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]). However, these methods generally assume that points of interest may be visited in any order.

In practice, aerial monitoring missions may require some locations to be visited before others. In multi-robot task allocation, such ordering requirements are formalized as cross-schedule dependencies [10]. Exact methods have addressed vehicle-routing problems with temporal synchronization [11], while polynomial-time sequencers handle task allocation under temporal and spatial constraints [12]; however, these approaches generally do not model vehicle energy. Similarly, [13] schedules cooperative tasks using greedy construction and local search, but focuses on task scheduling rather than energy-constrained spatial planning. More recently, [14] computes optimal precedence-constrained plans for heterogeneous UAV teams under energy limits, though its computational complexity grows significantly with team size and recharging relies on static infrastructure.

In this paper, we propose a heuristic algorithm for robust UAV-UGV planning in aerial monitoring missions with precedence constraints. The goal is to minimize the overall mission completion time while respecting the energy constraints and the required visit order under bounded travel-time disturbances. We formulate this planning problem as a mixed-integer program, which is NP-hard. Our main contribution is an efficient heuristic (Alg. 1) that jointly determines vehicle routes and their timing, with formal guarantees on feasibility and worst-case time complexity (Theorem 1). We validate our approach via numerical comparisons against branch-and-cut, simulated annealing, and a heuristic baseline that assigns all locations that are weakly connected by precedence constraints to the same team.

title: PriMoRetarget: Humanoid Motion Transfer Through Prioritized Motion Retargeting
authors: Nicholas Ioannidis,Dun Yang,Max Smith,Tue Vu,Ziyu Zhang,Shayegan Omidshafiei,Xue Bin Peng
abstract:
Motion retargeting is a critical preprocessing step for transferring human motion data to humanoid robots.
While existing methods are effective for single-character motions, interactions involving multiple characters and objects introduce additional contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved.
Retargeting is commonly formulated as a weighted multi-objective optimization problem, where conflicting objectives can require careful tuning of relative weights and can still compromise important motion characteristics.
We introduce PriMoRetarget, a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces relative objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy.
Lower-priority updates are constrained to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical characteristics such as foot placement and interaction contacts to take precedence over lower-priority pose objectives.
The method is evaluated on four datasets spanning single-character motion, character–object manipulation, and character–character interactions.
The resulting motions better preserve task-relevant interactions and provide reference trajectories that can be tracked more reliably than those produced by widely used retargeting methods.
introduction:
For humanoid robots, human motion-capture data provides a rich source of reference behaviors despite morphological differences between humans and robots.
Motion retargeting bridges this embodiment gap by transferring motion across embodiments while preserving the defining characteristics of the source motion.
A long line of prior work has studied retargeting single-character motions [1, 2, 3].
However, motions involving interactions with objects or other characters remain substantially more challenging, as successful retargeting must preserve not only individual body poses but also the contacts, spatial relationships, and coordinated movements that define the interaction.
Errors in these relationships can produce physically infeasible reference motions and increase the burden on downstream learning and control.

Many commonly used retargeting methods formulate these requirements as a multi-objective optimization problem, where each objective captures a characteristic of the source motion to preserve in the target motion [1, 4, 2, 5].
Such objectives may include matching source keypoints, preserving foot placement and interaction contacts, and respecting the robot’s joint limits.
Jointly optimizing these objectives is nontrivial because they can conflict: improving pose fidelity, for example, may degrade contact preservation or foot placement.
These conflicts become increasingly pronounced as additional characters and objects introduce more contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved.
To resolve these conflicts, retargeting methods typically rely on carefully tuned objective weights that reflect task- and morphology-specific priorities [1, 4, 2, 5].
However, weighted objectives encode only relative preferences: improving a lower-weighted objective may still come at the expense of a higher-weighted objective.
Consequently, these weights do not guarantee that desired priority relationships between objectives are preserved.
Achieving the desired priority relationships therefore often requires careful manual tuning of the objective weights.

Two broad classes of methods address conflicting objectives without weight tuning:
(1) prioritized optimization methods, which organize objectives into a hierarchy [6, 7, 8, 9], and
(2) gradient-surgery methods, which modify interfering gradients across objectives [10, 11].
Our approach draws on both, using an explicit priority hierarchy to specify which objectives should take precedence and gradient projection to enforce these priorities during optimization.

In this work, we propose PriMoRetarget, a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces soft objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy.
Lower-priority updates are restricted to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical requirements to take precedence over lower-priority preferences.
We show that our method is compatible with commonly used motion-retargeting objectives and apply our framework to four datasets spanning multi-character and object interactions. We evaluate the resulting motions using a range of kinematic metrics and assess their effectiveness as reference trajectories for training reinforcement learning (RL) policies.
Our method substantially reduces common retargeting artifacts that compromise physical feasibility, including foot sliding and contact errors. The code and retargeted motion data will be publicly released upon publication.

title: Distributed Harmonic-Covariance Feedback for Hole Closure in Planar Robot Swarms
authors: Jitian Liu,Subhrajit Bhattacharya
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: We consider hole closure in a planar multi-agent system whose sensing disks form a time-varying Čech complex. We propose a harmonic-covariance feedback that uses harmonic edge signals to locate holes and converts those signals into agent forces. For distributed evaluation, we use a fixed-degree polynomial of the regularized Hodge Laplacian. This polynomial is evaluated through local operator applications. The closed loop has a unique global trajectory from every safe initial state. The model data and initial state are supplied with procedures for approximation to any requested accuracy with explicit error bounds. We assume that hole area is measurable and bounded, holes evolve continuously without splitting or merging, and only finitely many temporary new holes appear. Under these conditions, offline finite calculations produce rational lower bounds for the cumulative hole area on the time horizon without querying trajectory data. These bounds converge to that cumulative area, whether finite or infinite. If it is finite, holes close in the time-averaged sense: the average normalized hole area over every fixed-length time window tends to zero as time tends to infinity. In a 15-second numerical demo, all holes close by 9.9s and remain closed through the end.
introduction:
In nature, among groups of animals such as bird flocks and fish schools, local interaction
rules can generate collective motions
[1, 2]. The same principle motivates
groups of mobile robots known as swarms. For multi-robot systems,
sensor coverage is a basic problem: each robot senses
a disk around its position, and together the robots should cover their
operating region. As the robots move, the covered set can develop holes: regions enclosed by the
sensing disks that receive no coverage at all. These holes are exactly the holes of the Čech complex built from the
current robot positions [3, 4].
The holes of a
moving cover are detected by persistent homology
[3, 4, 5]
and verified without localization or with switched higher-order
Laplacians [6, 7].

Related work on repair and coverage includes simplicial coverage repair for robot teams [8], gradient descent on weighted
combinatorial Laplacians [9], homology-based
repair of agricultural coverage [10], conformal
mapping of domains with holes onto multi-hole disks [11],
and diffusive coverage of bounded domains
[12]. Related tools include cellular sheaves, which generalize weighted
Laplacians for distributed coordination
[13, 14]; simplicial filters for
processing on complexes [15, 16]; and
occupation-measure relaxations, which express dynamical constraints
and integral costs through measures and lead to linear optimization
problems over measures
[17, 18].
The coverage-repair methods above do not provide a criterion for hole
closure based solely on the model and initial state. We derive such a
criterion for our distributed harmonic-covariance controller.
The contributions of this paper are as follows:

A feedback controller that converts the swarm Čech complex’s harmonic edge flows, which localize the holes, into locally Lipschitz force laws on the agents (such that the controlled trajectory is unique), together with a distributed realization of the controller (Sections III and IV).

Under this paper’s controlled dynamics and assumptions, we construct an offline sequence of rational lower bounds {cT}T\{c_{T}\}_{T}. Each bound is produced by explicit finite calculations without querying trajectory data. The sequence converges to the cumulative hole area over the infinite time horizon. If its limit is finite, the hole area averaged over any fixed time window tends to zero as the window moves forward (Section IV).

A numerical demo in which two holes close within 10 seconds under the regularized harmonic feedback controller (Section V).

The paper is organized as follows. Section II sets up the task and model. Section III designs the controller and its distributed realization. Section IV proves uniqueness of the state space trajectory under the regularized controller, and constructs {cT}T\{c_{T}\}_{T} from the swarm’s initial state. Section V reports the numerical simulation. Appendix A records details to approximate the normalized hole areas in the swarm and the vector field yielded by the control law, whereas Appendix B supplies proofs to main theoretical results in this paper.

title: Selectively Actuated Fiberbots for High-precision Minimally Invasive Surgery
authors: Jinshi Zhao,Libaihe Tian,Alex Ranne,Qindong Zheng,Yue Li,Xiaotong Guo,Ziqi Yang,Ali Anil Demircali,Mohamed E. M. K. Abdelaziz,Bruno Gil Rosa,Ferdinando Rodriguez y Baena,Burak Temelkuran
abstract: Long, slender instruments are essential for minimally invasive surgery (MIS), but achieving precise distal manipulation becomes increasingly difficult when actuation extends along the entire instrument. Here, we present an electrothermally actuated fiber-based robot designed for MIS procedures, in which Joule heating is concentrated in the distal active segment. The fiber is fabricated using a thermal drawing process and uses embedded metallic wires for thermal actuation. This robotic fiber, 1.9 mm in diameter and 1.2 m in length, can precisely manipulate surgical laser fibers with positional precision below 100 μ\mum. The compact size of the fiber robot allows it to pass through the working channel of a flexible endoscope, while keeping both devices mechanically uncoupled to allow independent motion. A phantom demonstration combining the robotic fiber with a da Vinci instrument conceptually demonstrated its compatibility with existing endoscopic systems for clinical applications. Our robotic fiber enables precise distal motion and holds the potential to improve clinical outcomes by enhancing precision in MIS procedures.
introduction:
Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has reduced the need for large surgical incisions by enabling diagnostic and therapeutic procedures through small access ports or natural anatomical pathways. Laparoscopic, endoscopic, and catheter-based procedures have consequently expanded the range of lesions that can be reached with reduced damage to surrounding tissues. Robotic technologies can further enhance these procedures by improving instrument dexterity, motion precision, and operator control within confined anatomical environments [1, 2].

Many minimally invasive procedures require long and slender instruments to pass through access ports, flexible endoscopes, or tortuous anatomical pathways before reaching the target site. Although this geometry facilitates access to deep anatomical regions, it makes precise distal manipulation challenging. Conventional instruments are commonly controlled from their proximal ends, and their distal response can be affected by shaft deformation, friction, backlash, and interactions with the surrounding anatomy or the working channel of an endoscope. These effects become more pronounced as the instrument length and pathway complexity increase, limiting the ability to position or scan a small distal end-effector accurately. Miniaturized continuum and soft robotic instruments offer a promising means of introducing active steering and fine manipulation at the surgical site while retaining the flexibility required for minimally invasive access [3].

In this paper, we present the next generation of electrothermally actuated fiber robots (Fiberbots). These robots take the form of a long (1.2 m in length) and slender (1.9 mm in diameter) catheter, with an electrothermally actuated tip capable of achieving sub-millimeter precision motion. A selective actuation mechanism was developed by localizing the high-resistance heating element to the distal active section. The fiberbot avoids dissipating substantial electrical power along mechanically passive portions of the shaft. Fiberbots are designed to fit through the working channels of off-the-shelf endoscopes, enabling seamless integration into an operating theater. In Sect. II, we begin by investigating common existing designs for laparoscopic robots used in MIS surgery, while highlighting their limitations that need to be addressed. Then in Sect. III, we present a new fiberbot design, highlighting its novelty in selective actuation. Using thermal fiber drawing technology, a bespoke polymer multi-lumen fiber was fabricated. This technique provides the capabilities to rapidly prototype devices with complex cross-sectional designs, while mitigating the difficulties faced by conventional extrusion or molding techniques. This section is followed by a summary of circuit assembly. Finally, in Sect. IV, we performed motion characterization to evaluate the fiberbot’s precision, repeatability, and reachable workspace. We also conducted temperature characterization to examine the temperature profile under different current levels and validate the efficiency and clinical viability of the selective actuation mechanism. To demonstrate system-level feasibility, we integrated the fiberbot with a da Vinci surgical instrument and used it to perform a moving task in an endoluminal phantom. The proposed selective-actuation architecture addresses a fundamental scaling limitation of electrothermally actuated fiberbots [4]. By localizing the high-resistance heating element to the distal active section, the fiberbot avoids dissipating substantial electrical power along mechanically passive portions of the shaft, thereby improving its suitability for high-precision minimally invasive surgery.

title: CASTER: Formalizing Zero-Shot Manipulation from Synthetic Videos as Constrained Optimization
authors: Yinlong Dai,Homanga Bharadhwaj,Dylan P. Losey
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Prior research on learning from humans often requires real human demonstrations.
But advances in video generation models offer a new paradigm: we can now prompt these generators to make synthetic videos of the task.
On the plus side, these synthetic videos take place in the robot’s current environment, and do not require actual human teaching.
However, while the generated videos appear to show plausible motions, they lack both physical consistency and robot grounding, and thus the robot cannot directly roll out the trajectory shown by the video.
In this paper we seek to formalize the process of going from synthetic video generation to real-world robot trajectories for zero-shot manipulation tasks.
We recognize that this problem is an instance of constrained optimization.
The object trajectories extracted from the synthetic video provide an initial guess at the correct motion, and the robot must refine these trajectories (for instance, within a digital twin) while enforcing physical feasibility and semantic consistency.
Our optimization-based formalism provides insights into the video generation properties necessary for success.
Specifically, we show that the video generation must probabilistically seed the search within a semantic basin of attraction where the trajectory can be locally modified without losing its task alignment.
Our analysis further reveals that state-of-the-art approaches can be viewed as instances of our unified formalism with key simplifications.
In our experiments we remove these simplifications to more closely match the underlying optimization, leading to more robust zero-shot trajectories from synthetic videos and improving average task success by 34.1% compared to the best-performing baseline.
See videos at our project website: https://collab.me.vt.edu/CASTER
introduction:
Collecting robot-centric data is expensive [1, 2].
Videos of humans completing tasks are widely available, but these in-the-wild videos are often unstructured, and occur in settings that are unlike the robot’s context.
Video generation techniques can help bridge this gap.
By prompting video generators to create synthetic videos, we gather “human” data without actually requiring human demonstrations — plus, the resulting videos are set in the robot’s current environment.

Consider the example in Figure 1.
The user prompts the system with a desired task.
Given this prompt and an initial image, recent video generation models can output a synthetic video of the task being performed by a human.
Ideally, the robot would be able to directly apply this video to guide its own motion.
But there are two key limitations.
First, while the synthetic video may appear visually plausible, it is not necessarily physically feasible.
Second, the generated video features a human doing the task, introducing kinematic and visual discrepancies between what the video shows and what the robot arm can actually do.

Our work focuses specifically on using pretrained video generation models at inference time to guide robot behavior.
That is, rather than using generated videos as offline data for policy training or fine-tuning a video generator on robot-specific data, we consider a setting where a general-purpose, frozen video generator produces task demonstrations during deployment.
Existing research searches for ways to address the above problems and unlock the promise of video generation models in this setting.
Common approaches typically fall along a spectrum in how much they post-process the video data.
At one extreme, the system simply learns to project the object’s motion in the synthetic video to real-world robot trajectories [3].
At the other extreme, robots construct a digital twin to physically test and refine the proposed video behavior before applying the results in the real world [4].
We view these methods as effective ad hoc solutions, but it remains unclear how to define the underlying problem.
For example: what should the robot optimize for when trying to map the synthetic video to real-world task performance?
And what characteristics does the video generation model need to have in order for this zero-shot transfer to be possible?

In this paper we seek to formalize the process of converting synthetic videos to real-world robot trajectories for zero-shot manipulation tasks.
Our key insight is that:

Formalizing this optimization provides three fundamental benefits.
First, we can unify existing approaches as instances of our optimization problem under different simplifying assumptions.
Second, we can use the optimization structure to define the characteristics of the video generation that are necessary for success.
Finally, we can develop new methods for zero-shot manipulation using video generation models by more closely approximating the underlying problem.
Overall, we make the following contributions:

Defining a Unified Formalism.
We define a constrained optimization problem that inputs synthetic task videos and outputs trajectories for real-world execution.
This optimization must satisfy physical feasibility (i.e., the motion must be executable without accidental collisions) and semantic consistency (i.e., the motion must be aligned with the task).

Characterizing Video Generation.
Building on our theoretical framework, we derive the properties and requirements for the video generation model.
We show that simultaneously enforcing feasibility and semantic constraints depends on generating videos that can be locally modified without losing their semantic meaning.
Intuitively, tasks with a larger basin of attraction around feasible motions (i.e., many initial guesses converge towards the same equilibrium) are more suitable for synthetic video frameworks.

Developing Approximate Solutions.
We demonstrate that state-of-the-art approaches can be viewed as instances of our unified framework.
We then derive a new approach that more closely matches the underlying optimization problem by weighting trajectory features instead of matching every waypoint.
Our experiments show the pros and cons of these different solution methods.

title: What Should Embodied Agents Remember? Benchmarking and Evaluating Memory Modality for Embodied Agents
authors: Junxiang Wang,Yuchen Liu,Yi Wu,Guofei Chen,Nir Pechuk,Tao Chen,Zackory Erickson,Yuzhe Qin,Tianyu Li
abstract: Memory allows large language model (LLM) agents to use past experience, often stored as textual records, when responding to requests. For embodied agents that control robots, visual and spatial observations introduce a broader choice of memory modalities, affecting both the information available for subsequent tasks and the model inference costs of constructing and using memory. We introduce MeMoREval, a benchmark for studying this problem through a controlled experience-request protocol. Agents first experience a sequence of events without knowing the subsequent tasks, and subsequently they use memory to respond to information and action requests without receiving new observations. The benchmark comprises 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments and measures task success alongside the inference costs of memory construction and use. Our reference evaluations reveal that storing frames outperforms storing generated descriptions at lower write-time inference cost for the primary model, while storing frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success for every tested model. Extensions to accumulated experience, selective frame retention, and visual input to memory writers demonstrate how the benchmark accommodates further memory-design investigations. Two physical-robot demonstrations establish the feasibility of applying its protocol beyond simulation.
introduction:
A coding agent investigating a bug may uncover facts about a codebase that remain useful long after the immediate fix. Memory systems preserve such findings beyond the model’s current context (Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Packer et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b). For large language model (LLM) agents that control robots, what is worth preserving extends to camera frames, object locations, and whether physical actions succeeded. This experience can be retained as textual descriptions, raw images, structured spatial records, or combinations of these forms, and the choice affects both what survives and what memory costs.

A textual record might note that several mugs were on a counter while omitting the colors needed to later retrieve a particular mug. Generating a description requires selecting what to mention before the future task is known, and task-relevant details may be discarded. A stored camera frame retains visual details for interpretation once the task is known, while a structured spatial record makes object locations and relations directly available.

Decisions to remember certain information are particularly important for embodied agents because recovering forgotten information can require considerable physical action. A coding agent can often rediscover a fact by inspecting an available codebase again or inspecting an earlier version of the codebase, which incurs additional computation and latency, but the memory lapse is largely invisible to the user. For a robot, recovering missing information may require navigating between rooms, opening containers, or manipulating objects. Such recovery makes memory failures apparent through repeated searches and unnecessary physical actions, delaying task completion. Moreover, changes to the environment can make forgotten information irrecoverable: once objects have been moved or removed, their earlier spatial relationships may no longer be observable.

To study which forms of retained evidence best support subsequent recall and action, we introduce MeMoREval, a controlled Evaluation protocol and benchmark for studying Memory Modalities of Robotic embodied agents. We distinguish the memory modality, which determines the form of retained evidence, from the memory backend, which organizes that evidence and makes it available to the agent. Our study addresses three questions: (RQ1) How do memory modalities affect success on information and action requests across task categories and models? (RQ2) How do these modalities trade off task success against write-time and read-time inference cost? (RQ3) How can MeMoREval inform memory-design decisions for deploying embodied agents?

Our evaluation protocol constructs each task from two phases. In the experience phase, the robot follows a scripted sequence of events while the memory module records its observations. In the request phase, the agent starts from a fresh context and uses memory to answer information requests and plan action requests, as a robot would when a user poses a request. Plans are executed without returning new observations, so the agent cannot compensate for missing memory by searching again, which would reward exploration ability rather than memory. Experience phases can also be stacked to evaluate memory over longer histories.

We instantiate this protocol in 53 simulated tasks across four simulated indoor environments and seven categories of remembered information. MeMoREval supports textual records, generated image descriptions, camera frames, scene graphs, and their combinations. Using common recorded observations and a fixed agent implementation, we compare different memory configurations on task success as well as model inference costs, as both write-time and read-time costs are candidates to be optimized in embodied agent design.

Our reference evaluations show that storing camera frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success for every tested model. For the primary model, archiving frames achieves higher success and lower write-time inference cost than generating descriptions, while also yielding the lowest read-time inference cost per successful request. The benefits of individual modalities vary across models and task categories, demonstrating the value of evaluating representations together with the models that use them.

We further examine deployment-oriented variants that accumulate experience across tasks, let writers select which frames to retain, or provide images to writers during memory construction. These variants preserve the benchmark’s evaluation structure while extending the design choices under study. The resulting differences in task success, retention rates, and inference costs illustrate how MeMoREval can support investigations of memory organization, evidence selection, and writer inputs. Two demonstrations on a physical robot further establish that the protocol and memory interfaces can be instantiated using camera observations and an annotated spatial map.

We situate the memory-modality question within prior work on LLM and embodied agents and their evaluation (§ 2), then establish the agent model and memory terminology needed to study it (§ 3). We then introduce the design of our evaluation protocol and its instantiation in MeMoREval (§ 4). Our experiments address the three research questions and demonstrate the protocol on a physical robot (§ 5).

Our contributions are:

A controlled memory evaluation protocol for embodied agents that separates experience from subsequent information and action requests, supports accumulated histories, and measures write-time and read-time inference costs.

MeMoREval, a benchmark of 53 tasks across four simulated environments, with configurable memory modalities and backends and complementary demonstrations on a physical robot.

Reference evaluations across memory modalities, models, and backends that characterize trade-offs between task success and inference cost and identify opportunities for improving evidence retention and access in deployed embodied agents.

1. A controlled memory evaluation protocol for embodied agents that separates experience from subsequent information and action requests, supports accumulated histories, and measures write-time and read-time inference costs.

2. MeMoREval, a benchmark of 53 tasks across four simulated environments, with configurable memory modalities and backends and complementary demonstrations on a physical robot.

3. Reference evaluations across memory modalities, models, and backends that characterize trade-offs between task success and inference cost and identify opportunities for improving evidence retention and access in deployed embodied agents.

title: PanTact: Teaching Whole-Body Dexterity with a Wearable Contact Interface
authors: Xiaomeng Xu,Han Zhang,Zhian Ruan,Xiaofeng Guo,Jinkun Cao,Ruihan Yang,Carmelo Sferrazza,Shuran Song,Guanya Shi
abstract:
Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment.
To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact11
1
          
          
          
        The name PanTact combines pan- (all) with tact- (contact, tactile), reflecting a humanoid that manipulates with any body surface., a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity, the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing.
Website: https://pantact.github.io.
introduction:
When humans interact with the physical world, we use more than just our hands: our arms and torso embrace bulky objects, our forearms sweep multiple items or brace against surfaces, and our knees push objects when our hands are full.
We call this capability whole-body dexterity (Xu et al., 2025a): the ability to accomplish manipulation tasks using any suitable surface of the body.
Humanoid robots share the human body’s overall morphology, with dozens of actuated degrees of freedom and potential contact surfaces distributed across the body. Yet much of loco-manipulation research limits manipulation to the hands, reserving the rest of the body for locomotion and balance and typically avoiding other body contact with the environment. This leaves much of the humanoid body’s potential for manipulation unused.

Realizing this potential requires coordinating whole-body motion with contact sequences across body surfaces.
Human demonstrations provide natural examples of this coordination. We therefore ask:
how can a humanoid learn whole-body dexterity directly from human demonstrations?

Advances in imitation learning and demonstration interfaces (Wu et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2026) have made learning manipulation from humans increasingly scalable.
However, these pipelines capture and imitate either end-effector (EEF) or joint trajectories,
and do not explicitly carry body-contact information from demonstration through policy prediction to robot execution. Extending these pipelines to whole-body dexterity introduces three connected challenges:

Capturing body contact in human demonstrations. Existing interfaces record only EEF motions or joint angles and do not directly measure where and when body contact occurs.

Preserving contact in human-to-robot policy transfer.
EEF targets leave body contacts unspecified, while retargeting whole-body joints can alter contact locations because humans and robots differ in shape and proportions.

Executing contact with whole-body control. Controllers designed to track motion references or EEF targets lack an explicit objective for achieving contact goals on the body.
They must incorporate contact goals while maintaining motion tracking and balance.

To address the above challenges, our key observation is that contact provides manipulation-centric information
that can be separated from embodiment-specific motion. Contact location and timing describe the task-level physical interaction, whereas the body surface and joint configuration used to produce it depend on the robot embodiment.
Contact also identifies which parts of the demonstrated body motion need to be preserved during transfer, allowing the robot to learn task-critical contacts without necessarily matching free-space body motions.
We therefore use contact as a cross-embodiment interface: measuring contacts on the human, predicting their desired states and locations with the policy, and tracking active contact goals with the controller.
Tracking only active contact goals without assigning them to particular robot links allows the controller to choose a body configuration suited to the robot to make contacts and maintain balance.

We present PanTact, a system that learns whole-body dexterity from robot-free human demonstrations and deploys it on an off-the-shelf humanoid through three components:

Contact-complete, robot-free data collection system. We augment egocentric sensing and bimanual UMI grippers with modular contact patches, reconfigurable force-sensing tiles covering the demonstrator’s forearms and knees that provide contact timing, intensity and location.

Contact-predictive whole-body manipulation policy.
The policy observes embodiment agnostic observations with body portions geometrically masked out from the egocentric view, and jointly predicts EEF trajectories and per-sensor contact goals, each specifying a contact state and position.

Contact-aware whole-body controller. We propose three formulations to achieve active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces under physical constraints: upper-body contact-aware IK, whole-body IK executed by a dense tracker, and direct sparse contact tracking.

We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without adding body contact sensors. Our tasks combine grasping and body support to move differently sized objects simultaneously, sweeping objects with arm surfaces, using the legs for non-prehensile manipulation and locomotion at the same time, and sequentially switching contact across different body parts. Result videos are best viewed on https://pantact.github.io.

2. Preserving contact in human-to-robot policy transfer.
EEF targets leave body contacts unspecified, while retargeting whole-body joints can alter contact locations because humans and robots differ in shape and proportions.

3. Executing contact with whole-body control. Controllers designed to track motion references or EEF targets lack an explicit objective for achieving contact goals on the body.
They must incorporate contact goals while maintaining motion tracking and balance.

title: Fly-by-Code: Embodied Coding Agents for Aerial Manipulation with Active Visual and Physical Feedback
authors: Jaewoo Lee,Jeongyeon Seo,Sihyun Cho,Gyeongrak Choe,Yutong Wang,Bavin Saravanan,Jia-Bin Huang,Furong Huang,Sebastian Scherer,Guanya Shi,H. Jin Kim,Seungjae Lee,Dongjae Lee
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Embodied coding agents construct robot policies from natural-language instructions by generating executable programs and refining them from execution feedback. This refinement assumes that execution feedback reveals whether the task succeeded and, after a failure, provides sufficient evidence to guide program revision.
Aerial manipulation violates this assumption in two ways. Payload constraints restrict onboard camera coverage and leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot’s view (partial observability), while strong dynamic coupling and limited control margins make physical interactions fragile (limited interaction robustness) and leave failure causes unresolved. Re-examining the same feedback cannot recover observations that were never collected or separate failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. To acquire this missing evidence, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an active “View and Probe” framework. When execution feedback leaves unresolved questions, the agent synthesizes a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints (View) or test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions (Probe).
Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, AF reduces false completion declarations from 25 to 5 and raises final task success from 31.7% to 75% compared with terminal feedback under the same coding-agent configuration and task-execution limit. Using shared robot APIs, task programs refined with AF in simulation run on a physical aerial manipulator without task-program source-code modification and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world. These results show that executable diagnosis fills gaps in execution feedback for embodied coding agents, improving both completion assessment and program refinement in aerial manipulation.
Project Page:
https://fly-by-code.github.io/
introduction:
Embodied coding agents provide a promising approach to task-level coordination by translating natural-language instructions into executable programs that combine general control flow and computation with calls to robot perception and action APIs (Liang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2026). In an iterative refinement loop, the agent executes a program, examines execution feedback, and revises it until it determines the task is complete. This refinement implicitly assumes that execution feedback provides sufficient evidence to assess the task outcome and, when execution fails, to identify how to revise the program.

This assumption breaks down under two challenging conditions: partial observability and limited interaction robustness. Partial observability can leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot’s observations, while failures arising from physical interaction limitations can be difficult to distinguish from perception or manipulation errors. We refer to these two gaps in execution feedback as missing outcome observations and unresolved failure causes, respectively. Re-examining the same feedback cannot supply observations that were never collected or resolve failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. Effective refinement therefore requires the agent to identify what additional evidence is needed and how to acquire it.

Aerial manipulation amplifies both limitations of execution feedback. An aerial robot equipped with a manipulator must physically interact with the environment while maintaining flight (Ollero et al., 2022). Spatially extended tasks can exceed the coverage of a fixed external camera, leaving the agent dependent on egocentric onboard sensing whose viewpoint changes with robot motion. At the same time, limited control margin and disturbances from manipulator motion and interaction wrenches can produce failures (Yadav et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2025) that are difficult to distinguish from perception or manipulation errors. For example, an empty gripper after a placement attempt does not reveal whether the object reached the target, while a failed door-opening attempt may not reveal whether the grasp failed, the commanded motion was inappropriate, or the platform lacked sufficient physical capability.

Resolving these gaps requires new evidence: choosing a viewpoint that reveals an unseen outcome or performing a targeted physical interaction that tests a specific failure hypothesis. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an explicit post-execution diagnostic stage. Rather than immediately revising the task program based on existing execution feedback, AF first lets the agent generate and execute a separate diagnostic program to gather evidence for unresolved questions. Using the same robot APIs as the task program, the diagnostic program can move to informative viewpoints to acquire missing outcome observations (View) or perform targeted physical interactions in simulation to test hypotheses about unresolved failure causes related to interaction behavior or embodiment constraints (Probe). The resulting observations and measurements are returned to the same agent, providing additional evidence for both completion assessment and subsequent program revision.

Existing coding-agent systems obtain evidence through multimodal execution feedback (Fu et al., 2026), per-primitive traces (Lu et al., 2026), task-specific verification procedures (Xiao et al., 2026), or information-gathering actions embedded within task execution (Fu et al., 2026). AF instead synthesizes an attempt-specific diagnostic procedure after execution, separately from task evaluation. AF uses the same prompt across tasks, while the agent generates a diagnostic program for each attempt to investigate unresolved questions. By decoupling diagnosis from task progress, AF gives the agent freedom to select actions for their information value rather than their immediate contribution to task completion. Task outcomes are evaluated before diagnosis, and the environment resets before the next task attempt, so diagnostic actions contribute evidence without earning task credit.

Across six aerial manipulation tasks in two simulated environments, AF achieves 75% final task success, outperforming terminal (31.7%) and execution-trace (48.3%) feedback under the same agent configurations and execution limits. These results show that additional observations and interaction evidence improve program synthesis beyond existing execution-feedback baselines. We analyze task progress across refinement iterations, evaluate AF across models and interfaces, and examine how diagnostics inform program revisions.

Finally, we investigate the real-world transferability of our approach by deploying the synthesized programs on a physical aerial manipulator. Because simulation and hardware share task-level APIs, these programs run on our custom hardware without source-code changes, even though the underlying sensing and control implementations differ. The resulting programs repeatedly complete two multi-stage tasks, 2-Objects Pick-and-place and Cabinet, despite differences between the simulated and physical scenes and variations in initial robot position and heading across trials (Figure 1).

In summary, our work makes the following key contributions:

We characterize two limitations of execution feedback for embodied coding agents: missing outcome observations and unresolved failure causes, which hinder completion assessment and program revision.

We introduce Active Feedback (AF), a post-execution diagnostic stage within a simulation-based program-refinement loop. At this stage, the agent synthesizes an attempt-specific executable program to acquire evidence through informative viewpoints that supply missing outcome observations (View) and targeted physical interactions that test hypotheses about unresolved failure causes (Probe).

We evaluate AF in aerial manipulation. Across six simulated tasks, AF improves final task success to 75%, compared with 31.7% for terminal feedback and 48.3% for execution-trace feedback, while also improving completion assessment. We further demonstrate repeated physical execution of simulation-synthesized task programs through shared robot APIs without task-program source-code modification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of embodied coding agents for aerial manipulation.

title: Beyond the Snowflakes: Disentangling Weather Effects from Confounding Meta-Factors in LiDAR Object Detection
authors: Yiming Yang,Jeremy P. Bos
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) is critical for autonomous perception, yet its performance is known to degrade in adverse weather. While existing literature models snow as atmospheric noise that degrades performance, our granular evaluation on the WADS-3D and CADC datasets reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: detection accuracy consistently improves as snow intensity increases. Through ablation study and meta-information analysis, we reconcile this by confirming that while falling snow acts as noise, its negative impact is outweighed by a dominant, concurrent factor: significantly increased object point count. We hypothesize that this object point count boost acts as a geometric enhancement, driven by snow accumulation increasing vehicle surface area and a shift from specular to diffuse reflectance. Our findings demonstrate that evaluating perception systems using broad weather-severity bins without accounting for correlated object-level data can lead to misleading conclusions about detector robustness. We conclude that accurate evaluation requires decoupling atmospheric noise from surface accumulation effects and outline future research to validate these physical models. The WADS-3D dataset is available at: https://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/wads-3d/.
introduction:
Lidar sensors are a cornerstone of perception for robotics and autonomous vehicles due to their high-resolution 3D measurement capabilities. In these systems, LiDAR enables critical tasks such as localization [1], obstacle avoidance [2], and object detection [3], providing precise depth information where vision-only systems may struggle.

However, adverse weather conditions including rain, fog, and snow degrade LiDAR performance by introducing noise, occlusion, and false returns [4]. Snowfall, in particular, presents unique challenges: snowflakes act as scatterers that obscure objects and create transient noise points. For autonomous systems, these errors can propagate to downstream modules [5, 6, 7], potentially leading to safety-critical failures.

Despite these risks, many perception algorithms are developed under ideal weather conditions, leaving a significant reliability gap in real-world, dynamic environments. While recent studies have begun investigating LiDAR performance in fog [8], rain [9], and snow [10], snowfall research remains comparatively limited. Investigating snow is difficult due to its complex spatiotemporal characteristics [11], the lack of controlled test environments [12], and the high cost of data acquisition. Consequently, many studies rely on theoretical scattering models [13] or qualitative observations, leaving a gap in systematic, quantitative analysis across varying snowfall intensities.

To bridge these gaps, we introduce the WADS 3D Object Detection Dataset (WADS-3D), an extension of the Winter Adverse Driving Dataset (WADS) [14]. Leveraging multi-year data from Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, WADS captures snowfall intensities significantly higher than those typically reported in existing literature [15], providing a unique benchmark for the most severe winter conditions. To ensure our findings generalize across different environments and sensor specifications, we further evaluate our results against the established Canadian Adverse Driving Conditions Dataset (CADC) [16]. By utilizing WADS-3D for extreme-case analysis alongside CADC for broader validation, we present a comprehensive evaluation of 3D object detection performance across a wide spectrum of winter severity. Our analysis reveals a counter-intuitive key finding: detection performance can improve with heavier snowfall. To explain this, we conduct
an ablation study, error matrix analysis, and a three-stage meta information analysis,
which demonstrates that the improvement is not a direct result
of the falling snow, but rather an artifact of confounding
variables. The model’s performance is mainly governed by
the object complexity rather than environmental complexity.

title: Tracking the Invisible: Self-Supervised Wheel Track Detection with Thermal-RGB Fusion
authors: Yiming Yang,Jeremy P. Bos
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Accurate detection of drivable area is essential for autonomous driving and advanced driver assistance systems. While state-of-the-art methods focus on general traversability estimation, they prove inadequate for snow-covered roads where following existing wheel tracks offers crucial advantages: improved traction, predictable vehicle dynamics, and verified path stability. To address this, we propose a low-cost, self-supervised approach detecting safety-critical wheel tracks using synchronized RGB-I (RGB + Long-Wave Infrared) imagery. Our method automatically generates training labels by projecting future wheel trajectories from recorded GNSS data. A neural network is designed to identify wheel tracks with the 4-channel RGB-I images from challenging, white-out road surfaces. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in visually monotonous and featureless adverse environment, offering a robust and cost-effective alternative for winter autonomy. The newly introduced ThermalTrack dataset is available at: https://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/thermaltrack/.
introduction:
Autonomous driving in cold regions faces significant challenges on snow-covered roads, where lane lines and road structures are often obscured by snow. For traditional navigation systems, Ruotsalainen et al.[1] show that existing fusion and map-matching algorithms for vehicle localization are inadequate for navigation in Arctic environments. LiDAR and HD map-based perception systems also experience localization loss under snow-covered road conditions[2]. Furthermore, HD maps struggle in these conditions due to altered driving dynamics: vehicles carving new paths in the snow shift lane centers and modifying lane widths beyond their original boundaries, making pre-mapped data unreliable. Similarly, the dynamic nature of adverse environments, where features change or disappear, disrupts map consistency and localization. Vision-based navigation struggles also in colorless and featureless environments due to challenges in visual feature extraction, leading to failures in visual odometry and navigation[3]. Fig. 1 shows a white-out frame from Winter Adverse Driving dataSet (WADS)[4], with the corresponding wheel-track probability map predicted by our method. LiDAR SLAM encounters difficulties in distinguishing between snow-covered surfaces and actual road features, leading to unstable localization and navigation errors[5]. These challenges highlight the need for robust perception systems capable of adapting to dynamic and unstructured environments.

In such unstructured environments, wheel tracks carved into the snow offer a viable alternative for navigation. Unlike obscured lane markings or transient visual features, wheel tracks provide physical guidance that persists even in heavy snow. Research has shown that aligning a vehicle’s wheels with existing ruts during off-road driving offers multiple advantages[6]. First, it enhances safety by reducing lateral slippage during turns, as the ruts provide extra lateral force to guide the vehicle along its path. It also prevents the ruts from acting as obstacles, which reduces undesirable vibrations and instability. It increases traction, particularly when traversing loose terrains such as mud, sand, and snow. This strategy also saves energy by reducing the energy wasted on compacting the ground.

Traversability estimation[7], a critical component of indoor/outdoor navigation, has gained considerable attention and made significant progress, both in urban[8] and rural[9] environments. These methods typically focus on identifying drivable areas by classifying terrain as traversable or non-traversable, leveraging advances in machine learning, sensor fusion, and traveling experience. While they excel at detecting general drivable regions, they fall short in snow-covered driving scenarios: they fail to account for the unique driving behavior in snow, where drivers tend to follow existing wheel tracks for safer and more stable travel. This gap highlights the need for a more specialized approach that focuses on wheel track detection over generic drivable area estimation, ensuring more robust navigation in adverse conditions.

In this work, we propose a novel method for detecting wheel tracks on snow-covered roads by fusing RGB and thermal images. While wheel tracks are often indistinct in RGB images, thermal imaging reveals critical temperature differentials between compacted wheel tracks (higher thermal inertia, emitting more radiation) and loose snow (higher reflectivity, emitting less radiation). To overcome the lack of clear visual features, we introduce a RGB-thermal fusion based self-supervised learning framework that mitigates manual labeling by projecting recorded wheel track trajectories onto image frames.

We validate our approach using the WADS dataset, with experiments demonstrating robust wheel track detection under extreme visual degradation (snow occlusion, low contrast, and homogeneous textures). Our method shows consistent improvements across standard evaluation metrics compared to baseline approaches. This work advances winter autonomy by leveraging thermal sensing and integrating wheel track detection with state-of-the-art traversability estimation technology.

title: MARGoS: A Configuration-Driven Platform for Reproducible MARL Experiments in ARGoS
authors: Tom Philipp Backert,Mohammad D. Soorati,Javad Ghofrani
comment: Submitted version (prior to peer review) of a paper published in the VARIABILITY 2026 Satellite Events proceedings (Project Showcase Track), LNCS 17104, Springer.
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has become a prominent research direction, particularly within collective robotics, where the ARGoS simulator is widely used to study emergent swarm behavior. Yet despite this growth, systematic support for reuse and reproducibility in MARL-based swarm robotics remains limited and insufficiently standardized: a single experiment is assembled from manually aligned simulator files, training scripts, configuration values, paths, seeds, and environment details, so reuse and reproduction stay fragile even within one research group. To address this gap, we introduce MARGoS, a lightweight, configuration-driven platform developed in this project that elevates these experiment-defining inputs to first-class, platform-managed artifacts. MARGoS enables reproducible experimentation through configuration hashing, end-to-end seed propagation, frozen (immutable) configurations, structured logging, environment fingerprinting, and exportable experiment bundles that facilitate sharing, replay, and verification of results across machines and over time. A five-dimension evaluation (architecture, efficiency, reproducibility, usability, and collaboration) supports our claim that managing experiment variation as a platform responsibility makes ARGoS+MARL experiments easier to reuse, reproduce, and hand off. Our code is available at https://github.com/tombackert/margos.
introduction:
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a prominent paradigm for training collective robot behavior, in which large numbers of simple, embodied agents produce group-level behavior through decentralized local interaction rather than through a central controller [16, 6]. Because experimenting with physical swarms is costly and slow, this training is simulation-first, and ARGoS is a widely used modular simulator for exactly this setting [15, 1]. Running MARL training on ARGoS, which we refer to as ARGoS+MARL, is therefore a natural and increasingly common way to study learned swarm behavior. Its experiment workflow, however, is largely manual: a single run is assembled by hand from separately edited scenario files, training code, parameters, seeds, output paths, and environment assumptions, so small drifts can silently redefine the experiment and reuse or reproduction stays fragile even within one research group. We present MARGoS, a small, configuration-driven platform built in this project to make reuse and reproduction of ARGoS+MARL experiments a managed property of the platform rather than a matter of user discipline.

The recurring inputs above are variant-bearing experiment artifacts: some define a run, while others capture the state needed to rerun and compare it. When they vary independently, configuration, reproduction, and handoff become manual coordination tasks rather than managed properties. MARGoS treats these experiment-defining inputs as first-class, platform-managed artifacts through configuration hashing, end-to-end seed propagation, frozen configurations, structured logging, environment fingerprinting, and exportable experiment bundles. It thereby turns unmanaged artifact variation into platform-owned managed variation and frames ARGoS+MARL experimentation as a configuration and reuse problem rather than an algorithmic one: the contribution is the platform and its integration of variation-control responsibilities, not a new learning algorithm or swarm behavior.

The gap this addresses is deliberately bounded. Among the adjacent platforms surveyed in Section 2, none is both ARGoS-native and covers configuration →\,\to\, orchestration →\,\to\, logging →\,\to\, analysis →\,\to\, export and import as a single pipeline. MARGoS explores integrated experiment-lifecycle support for this stack by centralizing the variant-bearing artifacts, and it was completed as a small-scale university research project sized for meaningful evaluation rather than as a general-purpose product: enough infrastructure to measure workflow efficiency, self-reproducibility, analytical usability, and handoff. Section 2 positions the platform against those adjacent systems, Section 3 defines the evaluation it enables, and Section 4 reports the lessons it produced.

To show that this problem is real and that MARGoS addresses it correctly, we evaluate the platform along the five dimensions summarized in Table 1, which states each guiding question and the evidence type. RQ1 is enablement-only, validated by whether the platform executes the RQ2-RQ5 evaluation protocols, while RQ2-RQ5 are the four empirically tested dimensions that recur in the evaluation design (Section 3) and the consolidated results (Section 4). Throughout, the evaluation is supporting evidence for the platform contribution, not the contribution itself.

The scope is deliberately narrow: collaboration means asynchronous bundle handoff between prepared environments, not cloud workspaces, shared state, or live co-editing. The project also excludes algorithmic contributions, unrestricted cross-lab portability, and new experiments for this paper, reusing the executed project evaluation only. Each exclusion keeps the evidence tied to managed variation rather than product breadth. The next section turns the variant-bearing artifacts introduced here into platform-owned managed variation.

title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang,Peidong Liu,Mingyang Li,Jiawei Li,Wenhow Li,Wenbo Ding,Xiang Deng
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting
embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich
alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation
methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse
manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent
action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM
learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions
in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while
LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action
pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific
post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a
continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction
dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment
signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on
23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action
supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and
improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video
scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen
visual conditions.
introduction:
Scaling data drives progress in vision and language, but embodied intelligence
faces a sharper bottleneck: interaction data requires physical robots or
simulators, making it far more expensive than text or static images. Large-scale
human videos, especially egocentric ones, offer a promising way to relieve this
bottleneck [1]. They naturally record diverse everyday
interactions at a scale beyond robot-collected trajectories, and transforming
such videos into action-like supervision could complement robot-only
datasets such as Open X-Embodiment [2].

The central challenge is that human videos lack robot action labels, and human
motion cannot be directly mapped to robot control spaces. Existing methods,
such as VITRA [3], often convert human videos into pseudo-actions
through explicit motion estimation, where estimation errors can lead to noisy
action annotations;
simply adding more human video does not necessarily improve policies. Latent
Action Models (LAMs) offer an alternative: they infer implicit actions between
consecutive frames end-to-end, without predefined robot action
labels [4, 5, 6, 7].
Because these implicit actions are optimized to explain visual transitions, they
provide compact supervision for unlabeled videos.

Despite this potential, existing LAMs are limited by their architectural priors
and alignment signals. Many recent methods use Vector Quantized (VQ) latent
spaces [8, 5, 6]. While compact, a fixed
discrete codebook can over-compress the continuous changes that define
egocentric manipulation, weakening the supervision needed for fine-grained
policy learning. In addition, pixel-wise reconstruction signals such as MSE
are often dominated by large static regions, providing weak signals for small
but important hand-object interactions. As a result, learned latent actions may
miss transition-relevant structure needed for downstream embodied policies.

To address these limitations, we introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable
latent action pre-training paradigm for embodied policy learning. LAPT-Scale
contains two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM, which constructs
human-derived supervision with a continuous Latent Action Model trained on
large-scale human videos, and LAPT-Scale-Policy, which uses this
supervision to train a VLA policy. The policy training follows three stages:
human-video latent-action pre-training, embodiment alignment with target-robot
data, and task-specific post-training in simulation and the real world. Unlike
discrete LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM parameterizes implicit actions in a continuous
space to preserve fine-grained transition dynamics. To make this space
perceptually grounded and temporally consistent, we train the LAM with
alignment signals beyond pixel reconstruction: perceptual alignment for local contact
fidelity [9], semantic
alignment with self-supervised features for hand-object structure [10],
and optical-flow alignment for observed dynamics [11].

We train LAPT-Scale-LAM on 23.3K hours of diverse egocentric videos and use
it to annotate a 5.1K-hour cleaned human-video subset for policy pre-training.
With 250 hours of self-collected robot data for embodiment alignment,
LAPT-Scale reaches 90.0%/89.3% success on RoboTwin Easy/Hard, 64.8% on
RoboCasa-GR1. Scaling LAM-annotated human video from 1K to 5K hours further
improves real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0%, suggesting that continuous
latent action annotation is a promising route for benefiting from larger
human-video corpora. On four harder real-robot tasks, it retains 70.0–75.0%
success under unseen position, illumination, and background shifts.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

LAPT-Scale-LAM: a continuous latent action model with perceptual,
self-supervised feature, and optical-flow alignment signals for learning a more
expressive latent action space from human videos.

LAPT-Scale-Policy: a three-stage framework for human-video
latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and downstream
post-training.

Real-robot scaling: increasing only Stage-1 human-video
pre-training data improves downstream real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0%.

1. LAPT-Scale-LAM: a continuous latent action model with perceptual,
self-supervised feature, and optical-flow alignment signals for learning a more
expressive latent action space from human videos.

2. LAPT-Scale-Policy: a three-stage framework for human-video
latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and downstream
post-training.

3. Real-robot scaling: increasing only Stage-1 human-video
pre-training data improves downstream real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0%.

title: Probabilistic Ship Trajectory Forecasting using Transformer Models on AIS Data
authors: Frederik E. T. Schöller
abstract:
Anticipation of vessel trajectories is an essential task when navigating at sea. This applies to both human navigators and autonomous surface vessels. Trajectory forecasting enables sub-routines such as collision avoidance to assess the situation and react accordingly in time. This paper investigates Transformer and Performer models for trajectory prediction of surface vessels in confined waters. Using widely available position data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), candidate models are trained and evaluated. Historical information on how other vessels have moved in the local area surrounding each agent is conveyed using positional heat maps. The heat maps are generated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and encoded with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) before entering the Transformer models. The models are trained with quantile loss to efficiently obtain a model-aware prediction interval, as this is crucial for timely collision avoidance.
The proposed model architectures are shown to greatly outperform previous work while the inclusion of local heat maps enables the prediction of vessel movement that is not otherwise indicated from the previous positions.
introduction:
Recently, autonomous surface vessels have gained notable research interest. Services such as decision support or full autonomy are envisaged to be a crucial part of the future of shipping. This, however, requires excellent situational awareness [1, 2].

Situational awareness is obtained through three main steps: perception, understanding of the environment, and anticipation of how the situation develops [3]. While nearby vessels can be detected on both radar and cameras [4], estimation of future trajectories is needed if a short term path should be planned. A human navigator will use information about surrounding waters from the Electronic Chart Display and Information System (ECDIS) together with the past motion of vessels to assess the current situation. The past motion of nearby ships can be obtained e.g. by detection and tracking using radar [5, 6] or tracking camera detections [7, 8]. Commercial vessels and some large leisure crafts use Automatic Identification System (AIS) to broadcast current position, speed and heading among others.

Trajectory forecasting is a widely researched area, especially for pedestrian motion prediction. Many methods use Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks for motion prediction such as [9, 10, 11]. While Recurrent neural networks (RNN) are commonly used for tasks such as time series forecasting and Natural Language Processing (NLP), Transformer networks, first described in [12], have recently had immense success, especially for NLP, where models such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [13], BART [14] and GPT-3 [15] outperformed previous LSTM models. Transformer networks have also shown their strengths in pedestrian trajectory forecasting [16], where they were shown to outperform the previous LSTM state of the art. One drawback of Transformers is that the computational burden increases quadratically with input sequence length. Multiple recent studies have investigated methods to introduce Transformer models with linear complexity [17, 18], though these often do not match the performance of the original Transformer. One study introduced the Performer [19] that incorporates Fast Attention Via Positive Orthogonal Random Features (FAVOR+) and obtains linear complexity. Their Performer-ReLU model showed to outperform a similar Transformer configuration with quadratic complexity while being more efficient.

If a trajectory forecast is to be used for risk assessment in the area of short term path planning for autonomous vessels, it is crucial not to obtain a single prediction, but to produce a prediction interval in which the observed vessel could go. A prediction interval can be obtained in numerous ways. For example by using Monte Carlo dropout [20], using Bayesian neural networks with probabilistic layer weights [21] or training the model as a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) [22]. Common for these methods is that a prediction interval is not obtained directly from the network, but by running the network multiple times to approximate a prediction interval. This might result in a misleading prediction interval, as the network is trained to output a prediction close to the mean prediction and the prediction interval is approximated by drawing from a distribution. To circumvent these problems, this work utilizes quantile loss [23] to estimate prediction quantiles during training, which generates a model that is both aware of its prediction interval and can supply this in a single forward pass.
