title: A Local Agentic AI Framework to Generate Edge Case Scenarios for Safety Assurance
authors: Victoria J. Hodge,Colin Paterson,Rob Alexander
abstract: Generating edge case scenarios is crucial for training, testing and safety assuring autonomous systems. This identifies hazardous failures to increase system reliability and robustness, ensures the system can still function safely on the boundaries of its operational design domain and learns the expected system behaviour for these edge cases. The rapid advancement in the generation and analysis capabilities of language models (LMs) has expanded their applicability and recent work has investigated LM scenario generation. However, many recent approaches rely on human-in-the-loop or rule-based strategies. This restricts the LM’s ability to generate diverse and edge case scenarios; the long tail of the distribution. Our work uses local LMs in a laptop-based agentic AI framework for adaptive scenario generation. This is cheap, fully-controlled, ensures data privacy and security. It uses think, act, observe, update, and continue loops with lightweight JSON encoding to generate scenarios. We use the system requirements, system description and environment description as knowledge bases in contextual prompts for an LM to ensure scenario realism. A second, independent LM critiques each scenario using domain specific criteria so it can be refined. The refined scenarios are run in simulation and evaluation metrics collected. These metric scores are analysed and similar scenarios are created for edge cases (exploitation) or novel scenarios are generated to explore the scenario space. Post-hoc clustering using metric scores and thematic-type analysis of the rich-text scenario descriptions produced by the LM pinpoints functional gaps and their triggering conditions. This creates traceable evidence for the safety assurance case. Our work highlights the potential of a flexible and adaptive local agentic AI framework for automating edge case generation and producing traceable safety assurance evidence.
introduction:
The impact of recent innovations in AI systems has changed how businesses and even economies function and changed how people interact with their environment. The emergence of AI-based autonomous systems is a major part of this innovation. An autonomous system is: “a system involving software applications, machines, and people, that is able to take actions with little or no human supervision’’11
1
            
            
            
          https://tas.ac.uk/our-definitions/ (accessed 27 Sept 2026). These systems have the potential to revolutionise daily life and their use is expanding rapidly, in particular in safety-critical domains. Safety-critical domains include autonomous road vehicles; medical, assistive, manufacturing and delivery robots; aerial vehicles; marine vehicles; underwater vehicles; wireless sensor networks used for monitoring; and components within systems such as an autopilot system in an aircraft [1].

The development of autonomous systems that operate in safety-critical domains remains complex. Failures in such systems can cause harm to the environment, harm to people, or substantial economic loss [2]. As systems become more autonomous, the level of human oversight decreases [3]. Replacing humans with AI in these systems means that we can no longer rely on a suitably qualified human to respond to unusual situations in a safe manner. Instead, we are required to argue that, throughout its operational lifetime, the system will, autonomously, meet operational, safety, and regulatory standards under all anticipated operating conditions. However, such safety assurance requires rigorous and often expensive through-life safety assurance processes to ensure safety standards and regulations are met, and that the system is free from unacceptable risks. Autonomous systems that operate in open-world environments shift the focus of safe development and operation from guaranteeing against known operational parameters to effectively anticipating and mitigating novel inputs, unexpected situations and uncertainty. Furthermore, the system’s operational environment may be underspecified at design time [3], or even unknown, which further increases the likelihood of unknown and unsafe scenarios. Arguing that the system is free from unacceptable risk is a complex and multifaceted process.

The required safety guarantees on the autonomous system that must be evidenced to argue its safety can be represented as g⁡(𝐀𝐒)g(\mathbf{AS}) and include requirements such as minimum obstacle clearance, minimum safe lighting level, or task completion time limits. An operational design
domain (ODD) specifies this operational environment within which an autonomous system is intended
to operate reliably and safely. The ODD effectively defines the parameters for system testing [4]. Systematic and comprehensive testing throughout development and operation is vital for ensuring the system will operate reliably and safely within its ODD. Scenario-based testing tests systems against meaningful scenarios and can be used during training and verification and validation of AI models to ensure robustness and provide evidence that g⁡(𝐀𝐒)g(\mathbf{AS}) will be met. There are three levels of scenarios for safety assurance testing in decreasing level of abstraction: functional (linguistic description), logical (range and distribution of parameters), and concrete [5, 6]. Concrete scenarios θ\theta are sampled from the logical scenario distribution Θ\Theta and specify a value for each parameter. These concrete scenarios can then be sub-divided into typical, critical (safety risk present) and edge-cases [6]. Edge cases are statistical outliers [7] that are rarely encountered in normal operational activities and lie on the boundaries of the ODD. We do not consider these three classes to be mutually exclusive as typical scenarios may be critical and edge cases may be critical. Typical scenarios can be rapidly generated using methods such as random generation where ensuring coverage is the key. Critical scenarios can be targeted by random generation in conjunction with approaches such as fuzzy logic [8] and could fall under typical or edge case.

Modern safety standards for autonomous systems such as ISO 21448: safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF) [5] and PAS 8800 [9] require specification of spatial edge case scenarios. The wide operating context of autonomous systems means the parameter space of Θ\Theta is vast and the parameters have complex, non-linear relationships. Identifying the parameters θ\theta to describe realistic edge case is complex and challenging. For example, placing an obstacle in a specific location may only cause a hazard if other obstacles are placed in specific locations. ISO 21448 clause 7 requires us to identify triggering conditions such as specific environmental layouts that expose functional gaps and lead to hazardous events. Clause 8 considers residual risk and introduces principles such as ALARP (as low as reasonably practicable) to reduce risk until any further reduction would cost far more than the safety benefit. Clause 9 mandates developing a verification strategy so we can find and mitigate issues and clause 10 mandates verification of the known scenario space to argue that known hazards are handled cleanly. We need to consider clause 11 which mandates validation of the unknown scenario space using testing approaches such as simulation and randomized scenario scaling. As the operational design domain of autonomous systems is vast, testing is limited by the resources available so needs to be focused where it is most useful and the ODD specification, whether specified by text or as a model, may not fully capture every scenario possible. Humans can provide linguistic descriptions and specify parameters ranges and distributions but producing a comprehensive set of concrete edge case scenarios by hand is infeasible due to this vast parameter space. Classical scenario generation for autonomous navigation such as Monte Carlo sampling struggles with high-dimensionality and does not target edge cases. For safety assurance, we are particularly interested in finding critical edge cases so we can mitigate the risks. Finding these safety-critical edge cases and testing them can lead to design, ODD or algorithm refinements and demonstrates that functional gaps have been considered and any found have been mitigated.

To address the issues highlighted above we propose the use of a language model (LM) supported scenario generation and testing environment able to identify edge cases for autonomous systems testing in complex environments.
Figure 1 illustrates the proposed solution which uses agentic AI running on the laptop to programmatically convert safety requirements into structured JSON, hierarchical text-based encodings of scenarios, for stress-testing autonomous systems in simulation. JSON is lightweight and human-readable and is often used for data storage and exchange. The simulation outputs metrics in JSON format to describe how effective each scenario is for uncovering functional gaps in the system’s algorithm(s). These scenarios and metric analyses provide traceable evidence for safety assurance.

A programmatic mapping framework translating formal ISO 21448 and PAS 8800 safety specifications into JSON-based spatial coordinate schemas.

A programmatic mapping framework translating formal ISO 21448 and PAS 8800 safety specifications into JSON-based spatial coordinate schemas.

An iterative and closed loop scenario generation framework capable of dynamic improvement of edge case scenario quality.

Empirical validation in simulation demonstrating higher edge-case yield and hazard discovery rates compared to baseline generation techniques.

Integration of simulation outputs as verifiable evidence artefacts for safety assurance cases.

The agentic AI framework demonstrates that such technology is feasible for smaller companies and ordinary users as it can operate on consumer-grade hardware (laptop).

The remainder of this paper reviews relevant safety standards and the scenario-based testing literature in Section 2, details and motivates the architecture of our framework in Section 3, describes how the framework relates to formal safety requirements in Section 4, describes our empirical analyses in Section 5, with the results in Section 6. We evaluate and discuss the analyses in Section 7 along with identified limitations, and Section 8 draws conclusions and identifies relevant future work to further validate and improve the system.

1. A programmatic mapping framework translating formal ISO 21448 and PAS 8800 safety specifications into JSON-based spatial coordinate schemas.

2. An iterative and closed loop scenario generation framework capable of dynamic improvement of edge case scenario quality.

3. Empirical validation in simulation demonstrating higher edge-case yield and hazard discovery rates compared to baseline generation techniques.

4. Integration of simulation outputs as verifiable evidence artefacts for safety assurance cases.

5. The agentic AI framework demonstrates that such technology is feasible for smaller companies and ordinary users as it can operate on consumer-grade hardware (laptop).

title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards
authors: Octi Zhang,Iretiayo Akinola,Rosario Scalise,Mateo Guaman Castro,Patrick Yin,Tobias Widmer,Miles Macklin,Chris Amevor,Dylan Turpin,Dirk Van Gelder,Jan Carius,Ankur Handa,Gavriel State,Yunrong Guo,Yashraj Narang
abstract:
The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based methods in robotic manipulation.
Over short horizons, it demands precise, contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts.
Over long horizons, it requires recovery and coordination across extended action sequences.
Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have enabled research advances by providing guidance on how to assemble.
But how much of the strategy must be specified?
The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that RL at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win.
AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward and task diversity admitted by this task-agnostic reward can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble.
In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1, reaching 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning.
The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, with task success rewarded only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete.
The learned policies discover dexterous and planning-like behaviors: choosing grasps for later assembly, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and preparing one part, assembling another, then returning to finish the first without an explicit planner.
For videos, see our website: https://alpha-nist.github.io/
introduction:
Robotic assembly is a longstanding challenge, and the NIST Assembly Task Boards are a persistent benchmark [1]; to the best of our knowledge, no learning-based approaches have solved all tasks on any of the boards. Assembly Task Board #1 (ATB1) consists of 20 assembly pair tasks (a part and its fixed mating geometry on the board) that are relevant for manufacturing, including peg insertion, gear meshing, electrical connector insertion, and nut threading.
Solving this task board is exceptionally challenging for three key reasons:
(1) The sequence for solving the tasks might be unspecified, and not all sequences may be efficient or valid (e.g., solving task N may obstruct the robot from accessing the parts in task N + 1).
(2) Each task is long-horizon, encompassing grasping, transport, and
contact-rich assembly [2].
Parts may begin in a wide range of poses and require multiple
reorientations before grasping.
During transport, parts may need further reorientation in-hand or
through extrinsic contact.
During assembly, parts may slip, become misaligned, or
jam during insertion or threading [2], requiring
robust recovery and reexecution.
(3) Solving the tasks requires precise control during complex contact interactions. The parts themselves are small (as small as 4 mm in diameter), have high geometric detail (e.g., helical threads), and have tight clearances between mating surfaces (as low as zero).
Tasks such as nut threading involve learning helical motion during frictional contact between multiple mating surfaces, during which a nut can tilt, cross-thread, or jam instead of advancing along the bolt [2].

Learning-free approaches typically rely on planning and strong human priors:
assembly sequence planning [3]; customized fixtures,
adapters, and tooling [1, 4]; engineered
motion and force primitives [5]; and tuned admittance,
impedance, or force-motion controllers [4, 5].

Learning-based approaches, on the other hand, can relax some of these constraints, but have shown progress only within a limited scope.
Most efforts have assumed a fixed assembly sequence, heavily constrained the initial poses of parts (e.g., beginning in an already-grasped state) [6], assumed access to accurate pose estimates, learned specialist rather than multi-task policies [2], addressed only a subset of tasks on the board [6], and/or achieved only low-to-moderate success rates by industrial standards.
Success-Guided Sampling (SGS) [7], for example, solves tasks one at a time, but requires a separate policy per task and is considerably less compute-efficient.

We draw inspiration from the landmark AlphaGo series in reinforcement
learning, which surpassed the strongest human Go players.
The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero
showed that learning from a terminal task objective
could encourage superhuman decision-making over long horizons without human demonstrations [8, 9].
In this paper, we ask whether a similar approach is possible for robotics: can sparse binary task rewards, combined with appropriate training strategies, enable a robot to solve sequences of long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation tasks, perhaps leveraging dexterous behaviors that no human could feasibly specify or demonstrate?
To make learning from sparse task rewards more tractable, we take a seemingly
counterintuitive step: train jointly across heterogeneous assembly pairs differing in geometries, tolerances, and assembly requirements (a nut and its bolt, a gear and its gearshaft, a peg and its hole) from a broad coverage of
initial states, converting MDP diversity into a resource rather than a burden.

Guided by this insight, we develop AlphaNIST, a learning framework that
trains a single policy under sparse binary task rewards across all 20 tasks
on the NIST Assembly Task Board 1 (Fig. 2).
The policy handles an exceptional range of initial part poses, learns
from point-cloud inputs without first training specialist policies,
and achieves a 98.2% overall success rate.
Furthermore, the same framework can train policies to complete 10 assembly pairs in
sequence, with a task reward issued only when all pairs are assembled with
no prescribed order.
In other words, the policy exhibits planning-like behavior.

Our contributions are the following:

A highly-effective multi-task RL framework consisting of a novel combination of the following components: A) generation of a cache of assembly-relevant reset states [10] over heterogeneous assembly pairs, B) success-guided sampling within the cache [7], C) a unified sparse binary task reward, D) multi-GPU training at scale. These components are supported by careful ablations. All tasks share one training configuration, without per-task tuning or demonstrations.

The first multi-task RL policy capable of solving all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board 1. The policy takes point clouds as input; initial part poses are sampled from a wide range, including adverse conditions (e.g., upside-down); and each task can be solved with near-perfect success rates. Positive transfer is observed, where multi-task policies can solve the 20 tasks with higher success rate than individual specialists, including three tasks that the specialists struggle to solve.

The first assembly policy capable of solving up to 10 diverse assembly pairs in sequence, without an explicit hierarchy or prescribed task order. Thus, this work demonstrates that sequencing behavior can emerge within a single low-level assembly policy.

We observe a repertoire of unique emergent behaviors including dexterous skills such as pushing and sliding (to singulate parts), in-hand pivoting, multiple sequential regrasps, extrinsic contact (to reorient parts prior to insertion), and single-gripper nut threading.
The single policy also exhibits long-horizon planning-like behavior such as bringing parts into reach, moving obstructing parts aside, and leaving a task partially-finished and then returning to it later. None of these skills and behaviors were specified.
We encourage readers to watch our supplementary videos 11
1
            
            
            
          https://alpha-nist.github.io/ for additional examples of these emergent behaviors.
We plan to release our code following the review and revision period.

title: NovaSplat: Model-Free 6D Object Pose Estimation via 3D Gaussian Splatting Onboarding and Refinement
authors: Georgios Floros,Evangelos Sartinas,Orestis Vangelis,Maria Pateraki
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: 6D pose estimation of novel objects without CAD models remains an open challenge: model-free methods must build the object representation from scratch during onboarding and have long trailed their model-based counterparts. We present NovaSplat, a model-free pipeline that closes this gap. From a short smartphone video captured at onboarding, we train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model that serves both as a template source for detection and coarse pose estimation and as a differentiable backbone for pose refinement. Our refiner optimizes the object-to-camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses under a continuous rotation parametrization free of gradient singularities. On a household-object benchmark, NovaSplat surpasses all model-based methods. On a challenging industrial benchmark with textureless and specular surfaces, it outperforms all model-free competitors while substantially narrowing the gap to model-based ones. We further introduce NovaSplat-Lite, an inference variant that is 3.1×3.1\times faster at negligible accuracy cost. Code will be made available at https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat.
introduction:
6D object pose estimation, recovering the full position and orientation of an object relative to a camera, is a core capability for robotic manipulation, augmented reality, and industrial inspection. The highest-performing methods rely on a 3D CAD model of the object: they render templates at many viewpoints and extract geometric point clouds, which are then matched against the query image using powerful frozen foundation models [35, 5]. In practice, however, CAD models are rarely available outside controlled environments, making these approaches impractical for real-world deployment. This motivates the model-free setting: given only a short video of a novel object captured during an onboarding phase, estimate its 6D pose in new scenes without any 3D model.

Model-free methods face a fundamental reconstruction problem. Where model-based methods receive the object geometry by definition, model-free methods must recover it from video, a noisier and less complete substitute that degrades every downstream stage, from template rendering to correspondence matching. As illustrated in Figure 1, this has historically resulted in a substantial performance gap between the two paradigms, limiting the practical utility of model-free approaches.

We propose NovaSplat, a complete model-free pipeline that closes this gap and in some cases reverses it. During onboarding, we reconstruct a dense 3D representation of the object from video and train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. This representation serves two roles simultaneously: rendering high-quality templates for object detection and coarse pose estimation and acting as a differentiable backbone for gradient-based pose refinement. Our 3DGS refiner freezes the learned scene representation and directly optimizes the object-to-camera pose by jointly minimizing appearance and geometric losses, using a continuous rotation parameterization that avoids singularities. This joint optimization proves considerably more robust than geometry-only refinement under the noisy reconstructions typical of video-based onboarding.

We make the following contributions:

A complete model-free onboarding pipeline that produces a high-quality 3DGS object representation from a short video, enabling model-based pose estimation methods to operate without a CAD model.

A complete model-free onboarding pipeline that produces a high-quality 3DGS object representation from a short video, enabling model-based pose estimation methods to operate without a CAD model.

A novel 3DGS-based pose refiner that jointly optimizes appearance and geometry, advancing model-free pose refinement.

State-of-the-art results on two benchmarks spanning household and industrial objects, demonstrating that model-free methods can match and exceed model-based performance without CAD models.

1. A complete model-free onboarding pipeline that produces a high-quality 3DGS object representation from a short video, enabling model-based pose estimation methods to operate without a CAD model.

2. A novel 3DGS-based pose refiner that jointly optimizes appearance and geometry, advancing model-free pose refinement.

3. State-of-the-art results on two benchmarks spanning household and industrial objects, demonstrating that model-free methods can match and exceed model-based performance without CAD models.

title: Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion Generation from Spatial Audio
authors: Jingcheng Ni,Zekun Li,Zhiyang Dou,Xiaoyan Cong,Ziyao Zeng,Hongyang Du,Randall Balestriero,Taku Komura,Srinath Sridhar
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO); Sound (cs.SD)
abstract:
Modeling human reactions to spatial audio requires understanding both what is heard and where it comes from.
Prior work generates motion offline from complete acoustic and spatial input sequences.
Humans, however, react to sounds without knowing what they will hear next.
We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from spatial audio.
The model encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens.
Conditioned on these tokens, a causal transformer with a flow head generates continuous motion latents, from which a causal decoder reconstructs motion segments.
Standard teacher-forced training derives motion histories and body-relative source locations from ground-truth motion, whereas streaming inference relies on generated motion for both, resulting in a training–inference mismatch. To reduce this history discrepancy, we introduce rehearsal training, which combines full-sequence teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction along short autoregressive self-rollouts.
To keep spatial conditioning consistent with generated motion, we propose spatial feedback, which recomputes body-relative source locations from generated root poses during both rehearsal training and inference.
On SAM, Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision.
It further supports real-time online generation of coherent reactions across sound events and source locations.
Project page: https://jingchengni.com/sonic-amg/.
introduction:
Sound provides information about events beyond the visual field, making it an important cue for embodied interaction (Chen et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021).
Human reactions to sound depend on both its content and the source’s location relative to the body.
For example, hearing a voice from behind may prompt a listener to turn toward the speaker before the utterance ends and adjust the movement as new acoustic information arrives.
As the listener turns, the source’s direction relative to the body changes. Generating such reactions therefore requires responding as audio arrives and updating spatial conditions as the body moves.

Recent work  (Xu et al., 2025) synthesizes complete motion sequences within predefined temporal windows, conditioned on fully observed acoustic and spatial inputs.
Requiring the full input window prevents it from responding causally to an incoming audio stream.
Autoregressive motion models provide a basis for streaming generation by predicting successive motion segments from preceding movements (Shi et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025).
Extending autoregressive learning to spatial audio requires representations that capture both acoustic content and spatial cues.
Furthermore, streaming generation requires each motion prediction to incorporate the acoustic and spatial information currently available as the input evolves.

We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from continuous spatial audio (Table 1).
Motion is represented in the continuous latent space of a pretrained causal temporal VAE (Xiao et al., 2025). Given a binaural audio stream and the world-space sound source location (SSL), the model
encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens.
At each step, a causal transformer processes the incoming acoustic and spatial conditions together with preceding motion latents.
Its output conditions a flow-matching head that samples the next motion latent, and a causal decoder reconstructs the corresponding motion segment.
Repeating this process extends the motion as audio arrives, without requiring the full audio in advance or revising previously generated frames.

We treat acoustic content and spatial cues as distinct modalities of spatial-audio conditioning.
We hypothesize that early fusion introduces interference between them.
Sonic-AMG therefore encodes them as dedicated what and where tokens, respectively, and learns their interactions within the causal transformer.
With sound source geometry supplied separately, the acoustic branch can focus on sound content rather than a comprehensive description of the binaural signal.
For instance, simple log-mel features in our model yield better results than MOSPA’s 2,272-dimensional audio features (Xu et al., 2025).
To design the where token, we examine perceptual research to understand how body-relative SSL influences human reactions.
We develop an 11-dimensional spatial event representation inspired by studies of nearby auditory space (Graziano et al., 1999), sound-source motion (Warren et al., 2002), and looming (Neuhoff, 1998).

With acoustic and spatial representations in place, learning the causal generator further requires addressing two sources of training–inference mismatch.
The first concerns motion history: teacher-forced training uses ground-truth histories, whereas autoregressive inference relies on the model’s own predictions.
To reduce this mismatch, two-forward training replaces selected ground-truth inputs with predictions from a preliminary teacher-forced pass (Mihaylova and Martins, 2019; Xiao et al., 2025).
However, these replacements are still predicted under ground-truth histories, where later replacements do not depend on earlier sampled outputs.
We introduce rehearsal training, which combines teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction on short histories generated autoregressively by the model.
Training on self-rollouts improves robustness to accumulated prediction errors, while teacher-forced supervision provides a stable learning signal across the full sequence.

The second mismatch arises in spatial conditioning. While acoustic content is directly supplied by the incoming audio stream, body-relative SSL depends on the root position and orientation.
MOSPA uses complete SSL sequences precomputed from recorded motion, which encode information about future ground-truth root motion.
Such conditioning is incompatible with causal streaming generation, which requires SSL to be updated from the generated root.
Training with SSL derived from ground-truth motion therefore creates a mismatch with the spatial conditions encountered at inference.
Our experiments show that this mismatch substantially degrades generation quality.
We therefore introduce spatial feedback, which recomputes body-relative source coordinates after each generated segment during both rehearsal training and inference.
The updated coordinates condition the next prediction, keeping spatial conditions consistent with the generated motion history.

On SAM (Xu et al., 2025), Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision.
It further supports causal and online motion generation from streaming spatial audio in real time.
Although trained on individual audio–motion clips, Sonic-AMG can generate coherent motion across successive sound events with varying content and source locations (Fig. Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion
Generation from Spatial Audio), demonstrating robust streaming generation.
Our contributions are:

• We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for causal human motion generation from streaming spatial audio, with dedicated what and where tokens for acoustic content and spatial cues.

• We introduce rehearsal training to address the history mismatch between training and inference, combining teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction from histories constructed through short autoregressive self-rollouts.

• We propose spatial feedback to address the mismatch in spatial conditioning, updating body-relative source coordinates from generated motion during both rehearsal training and inference.

title: What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
authors: Kai Liu,Jiangran Lyu,Tingyu Deng,Yixin Zheng,Jingtian Wan,Wenbo Cui,Mi Yan,Yizhou Zhou,Haoran Li,Dongbin Zhao,Zhizheng Zhang,He Wang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. Recent studies show that external visual representations improve manipulation performance and robustness. However, these methods select representations based on presumed capability gaps and use different integration mechanisms, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of representation choice and integration. To better understand how external representations strengthen WAMs, we conduct a systematic study through controlled comparisons of multiple visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert’s effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R2-WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.
introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generation models to robot control by jointly predicting future video and actions. This allows robot policies to draw on the visual structure and temporal dynamics learned through large-scale video pretraining, as demonstrated by DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026b), LingBot-VA (Li et al., 2026a), and Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026). Along with these priors, WAMs inherit the latent space of their variational autoencoders (VAEs).

The inherited VAE is optimized for visual reconstruction (Wan Team et al., 2025), but how well its representations support robot manipulation remains unclear. Its reconstruction objective does not explicitly prioritize manipulation-relevant information, such as object semantics and spatial relationships. Recent studies augment WAMs with external visual features and report improvements in manipulation performance and robustness (Qiu et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026a). However, these methods select different representations based on prior assumptions about which visual capabilities WAMs lack. Systematic comparisons across representation types remain limited, leaving unclear which visual representations best support robot manipulation in WAMs.

Beyond representation choice, WAM performance also depends on the mechanism used to integrate external features into the model (Yang et al., 2026). A further question is whether combining more representations leads to continued performance gains. External features can be integrated through representation alignment (Yu et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2026), action conditioning (Wang et al., 2026c), or joint prediction (Yan et al., 2026a). Existing studies often couple selected representations with specific integration designs (Qiu et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a), making the effects of representation choice and integration mechanism difficult to disentangle across methods. Besides, the diverse demands of manipulation—including semantics, geometry, object extent, motion, and interaction—suggest that different representations may be needed. Yet additional sources may also introduce redundant information or interference during optimization. Whether and when different feature combinations improve WAM performance therefore remains an empirical question.

To address these questions, we systematically study visual representations in WAMs, focusing on capabilities, integration mechanisms, and composition. Using a common WAM backbone built on a pretrained video generation model, we compare diverse visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and multiple source combinations under a shared training protocol. Our study addresses three research questions (RQs):

Which visual representations improve WAM performance?

Which feature injection mechanism yields the greatest performance gains from external features?

Does combining more feature sources consistently improve WAM performance?

Our controlled comparisons yield three findings that guide the selection, integration, and composition of external visual representations for WAMs. (1) General-purpose visual representations should be the default choice for augmenting WAMs. They can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities—even under perturbations relevant to those capabilities—while providing broader robustness gains. (2) Channel-wise joint prediction yields the largest average gains across matched sources. Our analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and effective use of the added visual information by the action expert contribute to these gains and should guide future integration designs. (3) Additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they add beyond the existing representations. The same source can improve one combination but provide little benefit or even reduce performance in another. Although feature composition can provide further gains, these are limited compared with the initial improvement. Feature composition should therefore serve as a supplementary route to improvement.

Our contributions are threefold:

A controlled study of visual representations in WAMs. We systematically compare representation sources, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations within a common WAM backbone and shared training protocol, enabling controlled comparisons of their effects on manipulation performance and robustness.

Empirical guidance for WAM representation design. We derive practical recommendations for selecting, integrating, and combining external visual representations. These findings motivate future research on stronger general-purpose visual foundation models and more efficient and effective mechanisms for integrating their representations into WAMs.

R2-WAM and validation beyond the controlled study. We instantiate these findings as a Representation Recipe for WAMs, termed R2-WAM. We validate the effectiveness of the recipe across different WAM formulations on LIBERO-Plus, and further demonstrate improvements over the corresponding VAE-only baselines on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop and RoboTwin 2.0, as well as in real-world robot experiments.

1. A controlled study of visual representations in WAMs. We systematically compare representation sources, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations within a common WAM backbone and shared training protocol, enabling controlled comparisons of their effects on manipulation performance and robustness.

2. Empirical guidance for WAM representation design. We derive practical recommendations for selecting, integrating, and combining external visual representations. These findings motivate future research on stronger general-purpose visual foundation models and more efficient and effective mechanisms for integrating their representations into WAMs.

3. R2-WAM and validation beyond the controlled study. We instantiate these findings as a Representation Recipe for WAMs, termed R2-WAM. We validate the effectiveness of the recipe across different WAM formulations on LIBERO-Plus, and further demonstrate improvements over the corresponding VAE-only baselines on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop and RoboTwin 2.0, as well as in real-world robot experiments.

title: Reinforcement Learning via Fixed-point Flow Matching
authors: Denis Blessing,Onur Celik,Gerhard Neumann
abstract: In maximum entropy and behavior-constrained reinforcement learning (RL), the optimal policy is given by a Boltzmann distribution. Generating samples from this distribution can be challenging, as it is often complex and multimodal. While flow policies trained with flow matching provide a powerful framework for representing such distributions, they traditionally rely on access to training data, which is generally unavailable in online RL. To address this limitation, we propose fixed-point flow matching (FFM), a data-free procedure for training and fine-tuning flow policies in RL. FFM leverages the target flow identity to formulate the actor update as a fixed-point iteration, utilizing a flow-matching-style regression objective where the critic’s action gradients serve as regression targets. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FFM effectively fine-tunes pretrained flow policies in the offline-to-online setting and enables efficient and accurate training of flow policies from scratch in online RL. These results establish fixed-point flow matching as a principled approach for learning expressive flow-based policies without requiring training data.
introduction:
Across a range of reinforcement learning (RL) formulations, the improved policy is available in closed form as a Boltzmann distribution of the current critic. In maximum entropy RL, π⋆​(x∣s)∝exp⁡(Q⁡(s,x)/λ)\pi^{\star}(x\mid s)\propto\exp(Q(s,x)/\lambda) is optimal for the policy improvement step of soft policy iteration (Ziebart et al., 2008; Haarnoja et al., 2017; Haarnoja et al., 2018); in KL-regularized and behavior-constrained RL, which includes offline-to-online fine-tuning, the same expression appears tilted by a reference policy (Peters et al., 2010; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2019; Nair et al., 2020). This target distribution can be complex and multimodal whenever several distinct action choices are viable, but the classical actor–critic recipe projects it onto a Gaussian due to the simplicity of the resulting optimization problem and the tractability of the policy’s log-likelihood (Haarnoja et al., 2018). Flow and diffusion models (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021) remove this representational restriction and have become the policy class of choice wherever a dataset is available (Chi et al., 2023; Reuss et al., 2023; Janner et al., 2022; Park et al., 2025b). Yet, the stable training objectives that are used to train these models are not directly usable for online RL due to a lack of samples from π⋆\pi^{\star}.
Existing methods for training flow and diffusion models in the on-policy RL setting often require backpropagating the critic through the integrator (Wang et al., 2023; Ding & Jin, 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Celik et al., 2025; Le et al., 2026), whose memory cost grows with every integration step and quickly becomes prohibitive, or rely on importance-weighted regression (Ding et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025), whose exponential critic weights have high variance and lead to unstable training updates. Moreover, methods for fine-tuning flow models typically use stochastic optimal control, which requires converting the flow into a diffusion model in order to use the adjoint method (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025; Li & Levine, 2026; Dong et al., 2026b). The adjoint method stores each sampled trajectory and integrates an adjoint state backward along it, leading to complex and expensive update schemes.

In this work we ask whether a flow policy can be trained against a Boltzmann target with the same simple regression that makes flow matching stable, but without samples from the target. Our starting point is the target flow identity: for a Boltzmann target, the velocity field that generates the noised target is, up to a rescaling of the noisy action, a conditional average of the critic’s action gradients ∇xQ​(s,x)\nabla_{x}Q(s,x) at clean actions. It replaces the data-derived regression target of flow matching by a critic-derived one, and the resulting objective, target flow matching, has the same minimizer as flow matching while reading its targets off the critic instead of a dataset. Since the objective still averages over samples of the target, we evaluate it with samples of the current policy and iterate. The resulting fixed-point flow matching (FFM) update, illustrated in Figure 1, generates actions with the current flow, labels them with critic gradients, noises them, and regresses the velocity field onto the labels. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. The whole procedure is conceptually simple, easy to implement and requires neither backpropagation through the integrator nor importance weights or conversion into a diffusion model.

The target flow identity and target flow matching (Section 4). We derive an identity that expresses the velocity field of a Boltzmann target as a conditional expectation of the gradient of its log-density, and turn it into target flow matching, an alternative training objective to flow matching that shares its population minimizer but regresses onto the gradient of the target rather than onto the displacement of the data.

The target flow identity and target flow matching (Section 4). We derive an identity that expresses the velocity field of a Boltzmann target as a conditional expectation of the gradient of its log-density, and turn it into target flow matching, an alternative training objective to flow matching that shares its population minimizer but regresses onto the gradient of the target rather than onto the displacement of the data.

Fixed-point flow matching (Section 4). We propose a fixed-point iteration that evaluates the target flow matching objective with samples of the current policy instead of the optimal one, and prove that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration (Theorem 3).

Extensions (Section 5). We further introduce several extensions for flow policies: a trust-region loss in velocity space, a loss for behavior-constrained fine-tuning that reads the reference score off the pretrained flow, and correlated exploration through temporally correlated prior draws.

Two RL instantiations (Section 5). We instantiate FFM for maximum entropy RL and for offline-to-online fine-tuning. We validate both across 5050 offline-to-online tasks and 2424 online tasks (Section 6), where FFM is competitive with or better than the strongest available baselines.

1. The target flow identity and target flow matching (Section 4). We derive an identity that expresses the velocity field of a Boltzmann target as a conditional expectation of the gradient of its log-density, and turn it into target flow matching, an alternative training objective to flow matching that shares its population minimizer but regresses onto the gradient of the target rather than onto the displacement of the data.

2. Fixed-point flow matching (Section 4). We propose a fixed-point iteration that evaluates the target flow matching objective with samples of the current policy instead of the optimal one, and prove that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration (Theorem 3).

3. Extensions (Section 5). We further introduce several extensions for flow policies: a trust-region loss in velocity space, a loss for behavior-constrained fine-tuning that reads the reference score off the pretrained flow, and correlated exploration through temporally correlated prior draws.

4. Two RL instantiations (Section 5). We instantiate FFM for maximum entropy RL and for offline-to-online fine-tuning. We validate both across 5050 offline-to-online tasks and 2424 online tasks (Section 6), where FFM is competitive with or better than the strongest available baselines.

title: Distributionally Robust Adaptive Iterative Covariance Steering for Small-Body Proximity Operations
authors: Vivek Khatana,Aditya Gahlawat,Naira Hovakimyan,Petros Voulgaris
subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY); Robotics (cs.RO); Functional Analysis (math.FA); Optimization and Control (math.OC); Probability (math.PR)
abstract: Autonomous small-body proximity operations require continuous-thrust guidance under uncertain gravity, solar-radiation pressure (SRP), and stochastic disturbances. We combine iterative covariance steering (iCS) with ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} distributionally robust adaptive control (ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}-DRAC) to provide risk-aware collision avoidance despite mismatch between the nominal planning model and the true dynamics. Iterative covariance steering plans a nominal feedback policy satisfying distributionally robust conditional value-at-risk keep-out constraints, while ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}-DRAC compensates for dynamics uncertainty and bounds the residual distributional mismatch through a Wasserstein radius used by the planner. In 𝟏𝟎𝟎𝟎\mathbf{1000} paired Monte Carlo trials with gravity, SRP, and diffusion mismatch, ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}-DRAC adaptive control reduces the keep-out violation rate from 32.7%\mathbf{32.7\%} to 0.2%\mathbf{0.2\%} and the physical collision rate from 16.4%\mathbf{16.4\%} to zero, without actuator saturation.
introduction:
Small-body proximity guidance must accommodate weak nonlinear gravity, uncertain solar-radiation pressure (SRP), and strict collision-avoidance requirements. Covariance-steering methods have addressed stochastic small-body guidance using chance constraints and impulsive control [1, 2, 3], while sequential covariance steering has enabled continuous low-thrust guidance in cislunar dynamics [4]. These approaches, however, rely on a specified planning model and can lose their safety guarantees under persistent dynamics mismatch. To maintain collision safety when the true dynamics differ from the
nominal planning model, we develop a risk-aware continuous-thrust
guidance framework combining iterative covariance steering (iCS),
ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} distributionally robust adaptive control
(ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}-DRAC), and Wasserstein distributionally robust
CVaR keep-out constraints [5]. Unlike existing nominal covariance-steering
approaches that rely on a prescribed planning model, the proposed
architecture uses ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}-DRAC to compensate for uncertain dynamics and to bound the residual state-distribution
mismatch. This bound directly defines the Wasserstein ambiguity
radius used to robustify the iCS safety constraint.

title: Mind the Temporal Gap: Evaluating Video Models for Temporal Understanding in Driving
authors: Shiva Sreeram,Erfan Aasi,Tsun-Hsuan Wang,Alaa Maalouf,Daniela Rus
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Modern video-language models are increasingly treated as general-purpose video reasoners, yet it remains unclear whether they robustly capture temporal dynamics in safety-critical settings such as driving. We study this question through controlled ego-motion tasks that require identifying actions from driving videos. Across video-language models, we find that standard prompting, visual prompting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought prompting remain unreliable and highly task- and model-dependent, with persistent class biases, although newer models show substantial task-specific few-shot gains. In contrast, lightweight LoRA finetuning and simple probes trained on intermediate visual features recover strong motion-discriminative performance, indicating that motion-relevant cues are often present inside the models but are not reliably used by the final video-to-language pathway. These results suggest that, in driving, current video-language models remain unreliable temporal reasoners and often behave more like frame-level, bias-driven recognizers than dependable temporal world models.
introduction:
Video models have undergone a rapid transformation in the last few years: from task-specific action recognizers to large-scale, spatiotemporal encoders trained with increasingly general objectives [1, 2, 3]. This evolution mirrors a central trend in modern machine learning: replacing narrowly engineered pipelines with large-scale models that can transfer across tasks, data regimes, and forms of supervision [4, 5]. In the video domain, early progress established that attention-based architectures over space and time can rival, and in some cases outperform, classical 3D convolutional approaches for visual understanding [6, 7]. Later, self-supervised pretraining, made video representations more data-efficient and transferable [2], and more recent “video foundation” efforts aim to provide general-purpose spatiotemporal representations across diverse downstream tasks [3]. In parallel, aligning visual representations with language has produced large video-language models (VidLLMs) that can caption, answer questions, and follow instructions over video inputs in a largely open-ended manner [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15], leading to a direct trend of video understanding inherited applications [16, 17, 18, 19].

This progress has fueled a natural hypothesis: if VidLLMs can describe what happens in a video, do they serve as world models, i.e., internal predictive representations that capture how the world evolves over time [20, 21].
Indeed, benchmark suites such as MVBench, Video-MME, and MMBench-Video report steady improvements and have become standard instruments for measuring video-language understanding [22, 23, 24].
However, a missing (and practically consequential) question remains: do today’s VidLLMs genuinely reason about temporal dynamics, or do they behave primarily as strong frame-based models whose outputs are only weakly constrained by time?
Recent evidence suggests that commonly used video QA benchmarks can contain substantial spatial and textual shortcuts, where single frames, shuffled frames, or language priors can explain a surprising fraction of performance [25].
Concurrently, new benchmarks targeting spatio-temporal grounded reasoning indicate that even strong models may fail to reliably align their reasoning with when and where evidence occurs [22, 26, 27].

Autonomous driving makes this gap especially stark.
Driving scenes are fundamentally dynamic: safe behavior depends on inferring ego-motion (forward/backward, left/right), as well as acceleration and deceleration, from temporally evolving cues.
Large-scale driving datasets (e.g., nuScenes and Waymo Open Dataset) therefore emphasize sequential, time-synchronized sensing precisely because motion and interaction are central to the task [28, 29].
Motivated by the promise of natural-language interfaces for driving agents, recent work has begun integrating vision-language models into driving-centric reasoning and interaction pipelines [18, 30].
Yet, despite this momentum, it is still unclear whether general-purpose VidLLMs can robustly infer even basic ego-vehicle dynamics from videos—a prerequisite for treating them as reliable video reasoning engines in the loop.

This paper provides an experimental study of temporal motion reasoning in driving-focused video understanding.
We design controlled prompts and evaluations that isolate basic ego-dynamics and ask whether VidLLMs can infer them from video segments. We then probe a spectrum of intervention levels—from basic prompting to adaptation (fine-tuning)—and complement behavioral evaluation with representation-level diagnostics.

Driving-focused temporal reasoning protocol. We propose a targeted evaluation suite for ego-motion primitives (forward/backward, left/right) and longitudinal dynamics (acceleration/deceleration) from third-person car video.

Multi-level probing of VidLLMs. We systematically test (1) standard prompting, (2) visually grounded/guided prompting, (3) text-vision fusion guided prompting, (4) chain-of-thoughts, (5) a combination of chain-of-thoughts with visual prompting, and (6) we further study lightweight parameter adaptation (e.g., LoRA) under comparable supervision. Finally, (7) we train small probing models on features extracted from different layers of the VidLLM as detailed next.

Where is motion information preserved or lost? We probe intermediate visual features and find that motion cues may be preserved, strengthened, or degraded across architectures. Several models retain highly discriminative representations immediately before the language model despite poor prompted predictions, pointing to a downstream reasoning and generation bottleneck.

A glimpse into our findings.
Our main contribution is a striking set of empirical observations. Across the tested VidLLMs, we see a consistent pattern:

a. VidLLM ego-motion predictions remain highly model- and task-dependent under prompting, with persistent class biases and poor forward/backward discrimination.

b. More elaborate/sophisticated prompting including structured guided templates and step-by-step reasoning instructions, typically improves fluency (outputs become more coherent and confident) but does not universally improve temporal correctness, where some newer models can be elicited into much better performance, but the gain fails to transfer consistently across ego-motion categories.

c. Adaptation can unlock motion reasoning:
lightweight LoRA fine-tuning can reliably turn these models into robust motion reasoners, suggesting that the underlying architectures can represent temporal cues and that a key bottleneck is the availability/quality of supervision (used data and training procedure) for dynamics.

d. Finally, layer-wise probing shows that motion information remains strongly decodable before the language model, yet is not reliably reflected in final predictions, indicating a gap between visual representation and language-based reasoning.

Together, these caution against treating off-the-shelf VidLLMs as reliable video world models for driving without explicit temporal grounding and dynamics-aware training.

1. Driving-focused temporal reasoning protocol. We propose a targeted evaluation suite for ego-motion primitives (forward/backward, left/right) and longitudinal dynamics (acceleration/deceleration) from third-person car video.

2. Multi-level probing of VidLLMs. We systematically test (1) standard prompting, (2) visually grounded/guided prompting, (3) text-vision fusion guided prompting, (4) chain-of-thoughts, (5) a combination of chain-of-thoughts with visual prompting, and (6) we further study lightweight parameter adaptation (e.g., LoRA) under comparable supervision. Finally, (7) we train small probing models on features extracted from different layers of the VidLLM as detailed next.

3. Where is motion information preserved or lost? We probe intermediate visual features and find that motion cues may be preserved, strengthened, or degraded across architectures. Several models retain highly discriminative representations immediately before the language model despite poor prompted predictions, pointing to a downstream reasoning and generation bottleneck.

title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
authors: Shenglan Li,Zhendong Mi,Hengyi Zhu,Jingwu Luo,Chun Kit Chan,Geng Yuan,Yanzhi Wang,Pu Zhao,Shaoyi Huang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene–behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38×6.38\times speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1,081 ms to 169.5 ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable general-purpose robotic manipulation by mapping multimodal observations and language instructions to actions
Guan et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025a); Li et al. (2025b); Sapkota et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025).
However, learning an effective end-to-end mapping from multimodal perception to robotic actions requires extensive, high-quality demonstration data
Liu et al. (2025a); Ma et al. (2026).
To address this challenge, recent VLA models adopt a “think-before-acting” paradigm through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning
Guo et al. (2025b); Ye et al. (2025); Yin et al. (2025).By reasoning over task goals, visual observations, and object relations before execution, these models decompose complex instructions and adapt action plans to environmental feedback.

Existing VLA paradigms
include language-based reasoning Zawalski et al. (2024); Lee et al. (2025); Qu et al. (); Huang et al. (2026a), which carry out reasoning in language domain and reasoning in vision,
exemplified by CoT-VLA’s decomposition of predicted goals into visual subgoals Zhao et al. (2025a)
and
VLA-Thinker’s repeated incorporation of intermediate state images Wang et al. (2026).
As shown in Figure 1(a), language-based reasoning loses fine-grained visual details and achieves lower success rates.
In contrast, incorporating updated visual information during reasoning can mitigate drift from the actual environment
Wang et al. (2026) (Figure 1(b)).

In general, existing approaches face two limitations: (i) reliance on observed states rather than future predictions, and (ii)
substantial computational overhead from repeated reasoning rollouts.
Specifically, existing approaches primarily reason over observed states and plan subsequent actions based on the current environment, without explicitly anticipating how the environment may evolve under different decisions. Meanwhile,
reasoning in VLA models need to perform full spatiotemporal reasoning rollouts repeatedly at every inference step, introducing substantial computation overhead.

To address these issues, we propose a visual reasoning framework for VLA models with two core mechanisms: latent spatiotemporal reasoning and scene gist memory.
Latent spatiotemporal reasoning
enables the model to imagine future scene evolution in visual representation space, exploring plausible action trajectories and their potential outcomes.
These imagined futures guide action selection, as shown in Figure 1(b).
It is inspired by human reasoning process, which imagines how a scene might unfold under different candidate actions and makes decisions based on expected consequences Atance and O’Neill (2001).
For example, when crossing a street, we consider multiple possible futures conditioned on our own actions such as crossing, waiting, or speeding up, then choose the safest action.
This anticipation
evaluates candidate behaviors through the imagined consequences rather than merely extrapolating scene evolution independently of actions Conti and Irish (2021).

To reduce computational overhead, our proposed Scene Gist Memory internalizes reasoning-derived scene–behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. This token captures general scene context and corresponding action patterns rather than preserving the complete future reasoning trajectory. During inference, the gist encoder predicts the Scene Gist directly from the current context, allowing the model to bypass the explicit future-reasoning pathway while retaining reasoning-derived behavioral guidance (Figure 2).
It’s inspired
by human behavioral psychology that repeated
experience
in familiar environments
helps consolidate learned behaviors into procedural memory involving the basal ganglia Wulf et al. (2010); Wood and Rünger (2016).
This memory supports rapid responses with less deliberation, reducing cognitive effort and decision time.
For example, familiarity with a home allows a person to head directly to the kitchen for coffee without searching the entire house. Repeated experience reinforces the association between the familiar scene and the corresponding navigation behavior.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Our framework incorporates Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning, enabling VLA models to learn to imagine task-relevant scene evolution in visual representation space. These anticipated scene dynamics guide action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation.

We further introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene–behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. It enables the model to
reuse this knowledge in corresponding scenarios, preserving reasoning benefits while bypassing explicit future imagination and full reasoning rollouts at inference.

Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our framework.
For example, IG-VLA achieves an 85.6% success rate on LIBERO-Plus’s challenging Language suite, outperforming the strongest baseline by nearly 6%.
Meanwhile, the gist policy requires only 169.5 ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000, achieving 6.38×6.38\times, 1.78×1.78\times and 1.55×1.55\times speedups over FastWAM-IDM (1,081 ms), FastWAM (1-step) (302 ms) and ImageWAM (263 ms), respectively.

1. Our framework incorporates Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning, enabling VLA models to learn to imagine task-relevant scene evolution in visual representation space. These anticipated scene dynamics guide action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation.

2. We further introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene–behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. It enables the model to
reuse this knowledge in corresponding scenarios, preserving reasoning benefits while bypassing explicit future imagination and full reasoning rollouts at inference.

3. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our framework.
For example, IG-VLA achieves an 85.6% success rate on LIBERO-Plus’s challenging Language suite, outperforming the strongest baseline by nearly 6%.
